en: Preface to the Reprint of the *Chànlín Sēngbǎo Zhuàn* (Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks of the Chan Forest). The *Chànlín Sēngbǎo Zhuàn* was compiled by the Chan Master Juefan of Xīnchāng during the early Xuánhuá era of the Song dynasty.
Juefan once read the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Tang and Song*, and because Dào Xuān was specialized in the Vinaya, his literary style was not [to Juefan’s] satisfaction.
Zhang: Zan Ning was erudite in his learning, yet his insight remained obscure. In his writings, he often resembled one groping for keys in the dark;
they could not be read as a coherent whole. Consequently, he became deeply inspired by the resolve to compose a comprehensive treatise. Throughout his travels to various regions, he...

Whenever he encountered a monk of vast learning, eminent character, and outstanding talent who was capable of baring his shoulders to shoulder the Great Dharma, he would invariably record their deeds by hand and preserve them.
Later, while residing at Gushan in Xiangxi, he finally brought forth all that he had collected;

following the model of the biographies in Sima Qian’s *Shiji*, he composed eulogies for each, totaling eighty-one individuals, which were compiled into thirty fascicles and titled with the present [name].

The title has already been carved into woodblocks for circulation. As years have accumulated, however, civil wars have broken out across the north and south over the past twenty years, resulting in widespread destruction by fire.
Of this book’s surviving copies, not even one in ten remains. Master Chan Ding of the Southern School currently resides at the famous monastery of Daci;
he laments that junior students of the later age do not see the complete whole of the Ultimate Way, nor the greatness of the ancients.

The Master then took the manuscript, re-carved it for publication, and widely disseminated it. Furthermore, he requested that I compose a preface to record the beginning and end of this work, so that it might be transmitted for all eternity.
In ancient times, the Left Scribe recorded words and the Right Scribe recorded deeds; thus, "words" became known as the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents).
The *Zuozhuan* records events as its substance, and Sima Qian relied upon it to compose the *Shiji*, wherein both words and deeds are fully contained.
This work by Juefan compiles the instructional sayings of the Five Houses and further records the life deeds of the various patriarchs;

regarding their genealogies, the origins of their entry into the Way, and the moments of clear verification at the time of their passing, there is nothing he has not carefully recorded and meticulously documented. This is because one listens to the words...
Observing through their deeds: since one has already recorded what they said, one ought certainly to record their actions as well.
Juefan may indeed be said to have captured the standard of Huijian. Yet some might say: "Huijian was a man of the world, whereas Juefan is one who has transcended the world.
The Way that transcends the world is transmitted from mind to mind; those verbal expressions and written characters [are irrelevant]."
This is not the ultimate realization of the Way. If one cannot remain unimpeded in this state, then the luminosity of one's own mind will become obstructed and obscured.
As for the Way, how could there be anything of it? Is this not a great error? Nevertheless, for those who study the teachings of the Buddha:

It is certainly not the case that one takes language and written characters to be the Way itself, yet it is also not the case that one enters the Way by departing from language and written characters.

Observe the masters of the past from India in the West and China in the East; there were indeed those who were thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka while simultaneously exerting themselves to propagate the Mind-Teaching (Cittamātra).
Such individuals include Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, Yongjia, and Guifeng. If students do not apply themselves with diligent effort, [they will fail].

In this regard, if one were to consider the mere rejection of speech and writing as Zen, and the silent illumination of the darkened mind as the sublime, then the subtle words of the Buddhas of the past and the regulations of the patriarchal masters would almost surely be extinguished.
Fearing this, Juefan composed this book; the Southern School likewise feared this and published it, desiring that all Zen monasteries throughout the world—
All follow the fundamental principles of their predecessors; thus, their words and conduct converge upon the same single Way as those eighty-one individuals recorded in the Biographies.

Therefore, the circulation of this book cannot be said to provide but a minor benefit. The Biographies state: "Though there be no more elders of mature experience, there still remain the exemplary precedents.
It further states: "The gentleman extensively recognizes the words and deeds of the past in order to store up his own virtue."

Virtue! May those who read this in the future exert themselves accordingly. Preface to the Re-engraved *Chanyuan sengbao zhuan* (Record of the Jewel-like Monks of the Chan Forest), composed on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month in the sixth year of the Hongwu era by Dai Liang, a man of Jiuling.
Mahākāśyapa closed his room and Vimalakīrti sealed his mouth, for the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is beyond words. Since the time of Caoxi, the single drop of water branched into five schools;

they established the fundamental tenets and revealed expedient means. Once the source of the Dharma was fathomed, the flow of its waves grew ever more vast, all returning to the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Yet, if one wishes to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, one must observe the conditions of time and season. From—
The great practitioners of the Dharma in ancient times were all men of extraordinary and eminent talent who did not submit to the constraints of the mundane world.
Therefore, they donned the black robes and shaved their heads, traveling far and wide to seek instruction and inquiry, never ceasing until they had realized the matter of their own enlightenment.
Indeed, some attained awakening through words, while others encountered the Way through a mere glance; in a single kṣaṇa, they transformed from the ordinary into the sublime.
The sages and the conditions of time and circumstance each differ; were it not for a complete record of their origins and conclusions, later students would have no basis for verification.
This is the reason for the composition of the *Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha*. This book has been transmitted for many years.

Like a flawless white jade set upon a brocade cushion, I beheld it with admiration. Its former repository was on Mount Lu, but it was subsequently lost in a fire. Now it resides at Fenghuang Temple in Qiantang.

The monk Guangyu of Mount Shan, fearing that this work might fall into oblivion, collated it against the original edition and carved it into woodblocks to share with practitioners throughout all quarters.
It took more than ten years for the book to be completed; his dedication was truly diligent. — Zhao Yuanzao of Weiting.

I met Yu once upon the lakes and mountains; our wisdom-torches illuminated one another, and he tucked his manuscript into his sleeve as he returned home, entrusting me with the request that I provide a turning word for it.
Although I and Yu had not yet met face-to-face, now, upon opening this book, I know his aspirations and inclinations. Though we are a thousand li apart, we share the same wind.
Furthermore, I see that Yu and Juefan, along with those eighty-one others, walk side by side, arm-in-arm; there must surely be a causal connection.
Issued from the Secretariat. To attain the meaning while forgetting the words is to enter this very Dharma assembly together; thus, the single assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly undispersed.
This is not beyond the bounds of possibility. Written with reverence by Zhang Hong of Linchuan during the first ten days of the middle spring in the Dinghai year of Baoqing.
In the *Preface to the Chanlin Sengbao Zhuan*, Juefan said to me: "Since the arrival of Bodhidharma, the Dharma was transmitted through six generations to Dajian (the Sixth Patriarch).
After Dajian, it split into two schools: one followed by the Shitou, Yunmen, Caodong, and Fayen lineages; the other by Mazu."
Linji and Yangshan were the founders of these schools, which constitute the Five Houses of Chan.

During the Jiayu era, the Chan Master Daguan Tanying once composed a biography for them, recording their karmic encounters and spoken words while omitting details regarding the full course of their lives and deeds from beginning to end.

Dehong maintained that since shadows arise from forms and echoes follow sounds, once these words are recorded, they constitute conditions for entering the Way and effects at the time of death that must not be allowed to go to waste.
He therefore compiled all the surviving fragments and miscellaneous records, supplementing them with the traditions of eminent monks from various quarters.
Furthermore, from the Jiayou era to the Zhenghe era, he extracted the lineages of the two houses of Yunmen and Linji.
Among his descendants, those who rose preeminently and stood out in excellence number eighty-one. For each, he composed a biography followed by a eulogy, totaling thirty fascicles.
This work was completed at the Southern Terrace in Xiangxi and titled *The Record of the Jewel Monks of the Chan Forest*.
He requested that I compose a preface for it. I sought out the book and examined it; its insights... [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
His learning was profound; his speech was expansive and correct; his conduct was simple yet complete; his expressions were subtle and elegant;
and his purport was vast, empty, and still—mysterious and deep indeed. As for his talent, he was the Sima Qian and Ban Gu of our school.
Had these eighty-one individuals been recorded in the annals, their brilliance would have been piercing and their character upright, shining like the five planets.
It is magnificent as it adorns the heavens; all people look up to it, perhaps because of this very book.
Now, when Juefan first read the words of Fenyang Zhao, he attained a sudden awakening and received formal certification from Yun'an Zhenjing.

He once encountered hardships and peril, coming close to death nine times, yet his mouth never uttered a word of grievance and his face never showed a trace of dissatisfaction. That which was manifested in his literary compositions was merely the surplus of his realization.

Biographies of the Jewel Monks of the Chan Forest:
The Master of the Stonehead Hermitage on Mount Nanyue, Volume One.
Compiled by the śramaṇa Huìhóng of the White Hermitage in the Song Dynasty.

Chan Master Caoshan Benji of Fuzhou (the sixth generation descendant of Qingyuan), whose name was Tanzhang, was the son of the Huang family of Putian, Quanzhou. From childhood, he was extraordinary and unconventional;

as a student, he could not bear to remain in the secular world. At the age of nineteen, he left home and entered Mount Lingshi in Fuzhou. After six years, he shaved his head and received the precepts.
[He was] complete [in his training]. At the beginning of the Xiántóng era, he went to Gāo'ān to pay his respects to Master Wùběn Jià. He remained in attendance for over ten years.

Master Jià, considering him to be like himself and capable of upholding the Great Dharma, subsequently caused his fame to surpass that of all in the monastic community. As he was about to take his leave, Master Jià said, "Come at the third watch; I shall instruct you in the details.
At that time, the one known as Shísū Āi (the Short Statured Uncle) learned of this and prostrated himself beneath the meditation seat. Master Jià—

He did not know [what was happening]. At midnight, the chapter was bestowed upon him—the *Precious Mirror Samādhi* (Pao-ching san-mei) previously entrusted by Yunyan, along with the "Five Ranks" (Wu-wei) manifest instructions and the "Three Kinds of Leakage" (San-chung san-lou).
Having finished, he bowed twice and hurried out. A short "uncle-master" called out, stretching his neck: "Dongshan’s Chan has entered my hands!

Guo-jia was greatly alarmed and said, "To steal the Dharma and vomit it up in vain—there is no way to remedy this. Later, everything happened exactly as he had said. [The *Precious Mirror Samādhi*...]
The Mirror Samādhi. Its verse says: "Such a Dharma has been secretly transmitted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
you have now obtained it—protect it well! Like snow in a silver bowl, or the bright moon hidden among egrets; though the likenesses are not identical, when mixed together, their places are known.

The meaning does not reside in the words; the responsive mechanism also follows. Movement creates a nest and a trap; a single deviation or a lingering glance leads to failure. Both 'avoidance' and 'contact' are not it; it is like the Great..."
A mass of fire is merely its form and color; it belongs to the defiled. At midnight it is perfectly bright, yet at dawn it is not revealed.
It serves as a model for all things, employed to uproot all sufferings. Although it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is not without expression.

It is like standing before a precious mirror, where form and reflection behold one another: you are not that, yet that is precisely you. Like an infant of the world, with the five features complete, he does not depart.

It does not come; it neither arises nor abides. It is pervasive and harmonious. Whether there is a phrase or no phrase, one will ultimately obtain the thing, for the words have not yet reached their full correctness.

The six lines of the hexagram *Lí* (Fire) are interchanged through the shifting of the biased and the correct; they are layered to form three, and when the transformations are exhausted, they become five. It is like the taste of the *zhìcǎo* herb; it is like a vajra scepter.
The center is perfectly poised in its subtle embrace, where "knocking" and "singing" are raised together. It penetrates both the source and the path, carrying them all along.
Flanking the path, they appear abruptly; thus there is auspiciousness. One must not offend or oppose them. They are the wondrousness of true nature, belonging neither to delusion nor enlightenment.

Through causes, conditions, and the proper season, they are silently yet manifestly revealed. Entering subtly into the infinitesimal, they are vast and beyond spatial location. A deviation of even a hair’s breadth fails to accord with the musical scales.

That there are now sudden and gradual approaches is established according to the specific circumstances of the teachings. Once these teachings are distinguished, they constitute the fundamental rules and measures. This is the penetration of the essence of the school.
Tending toward the ultimate, the flow of true permanence is constant; outwardly tranquil yet inwardly wavering, like a tethered colt or a crouching rat.

The former sages took pity on them and established the *dāna-pāramitā* of the Dharma. Following their delusions, they mistook black for white; only when these inverted perceptions are extinguished will they sincerely admit [the truth] and seek to align with the ancient tracks.
Please observe the ancients: when the Way of the Buddha was about to be perfected, he gazed at the tree for ten kalpas, like a tiger missing its prey, like a horse...
The white-footed horse [is recognized] by its inferiority; the precious stand and rare treasures are considered extraordinary.

A dark-skinned slave or a white ox—when Yi, through his skill and strength, shoots a target at a hundred paces, with the arrowheads meeting point-to-point, what has skill and strength to do with it? When a wooden man sings and a stone child dances, these are not reached by conscious cognition;
how could they possibly admit of deliberation? To serve a minister to his sovereign and a son to be obedient to his father—if one were not so obedient, [it would be impossible].

This is not filial piety. Not honoring and not assisting; acting secretly and employing [the mind] subtly, appearing as if ignorant and as if dull-witted—yet being able only to maintain continuity, one is called the "Lord among Lords.
The Verse on the Five Ranks of Ruler and Subject says: "Centered in the Right, yet Deviant: Before the moon becomes bright at the beginning of the third watch."
Do not be surprised that we meet yet do not recognize one another; hidden deep within, I still harbor the resentments of days gone by. "From the center, leaning to one side":
an elderly woman, losing her way at dawn, encounters an ancient mirror. Clearly facing each other, there is nothing more true than this; do not further lose your head by chasing after its reflection.

"Coming from the very center": within the midst of nothingness lies a path out of the dust. If you can simply avoid touching upon the taboos of the present age, you will surpass those who were severed in the former dynasty.
Tongue-talent. Reaching the ultimate within the partial. When two blades cross in combat, one must avoid them; a true adept is like a lotus in fire—possessing a natural air of loftiness.
Reaching the ultimate within the simultaneous. Not falling into existence or non-existence, who dares to harmonize with it?
Everyone desires to escape the common flow, yet when all is settled, they end up sitting in the coals. Regarding the three kinds of leakage, the verse says: First, the leakage of seeing.
Leakage (*āsrava*). First, leakage of the faculty (*indriya*): this refers to when the faculty does not leave its station and falls into the sea of poison. Second, leakage of emotion (*vedanā*):

this refers to when wisdom constantly turns away [from its object] and the locus of vision becomes biased and withered. Third, leakage of speech (*vāk*): this refers to when the essence is subtle yet the fundamental principle is lost, and the faculty is dim regarding the beginning and end.

The turbid wisdom of the student revolves and flows, never escaping these three kinds of leakage. There are three summary verses; the first is named "The Simultaneous Practice of Striking and Singing. The verse:
It is said: "The golden needle and double lock are prepared; flanking the path, they encompass all in concealment. The precious seal is wondrous in mid-air; layer upon layer, the brocade seams open.
Its second name is *Golden Lock of the Mysterious Path*. The verse says: "Interchanging, brightness contains darkness; when the function is equal, turning becomes difficult to perceive."

Exhausting one's strength, one seeks whether to advance or retreat; a golden chain and net cover it all over. The third [name] is "Neither Entering Principle nor Entering Phenomena. The verse says: Neither principle nor phenomena are entered;
The returning illumination cuts off the subtle and profound. Against the wind, there is neither skill nor clumsiness; Like lightning or a flash of fire, it is difficult to pursue.
At dawn, he left the mountain and traveled to Caoxi to pay respects at the Patriarch’s stupa. Returning from Luochuan, he settled at Linchuan, where there was a fine mountain.
Shui settled there permanently. Out of his aspiration for the Sixth Patriarch, he named the mountain Cao and addressed the assembly, saying:
"Monastics here, within this 'line of the robe,' must in principle understand and penetrate the matter that transcends [the mundane]. Do not treat it as trivial.
If you are clear in your capacity to take responsibility, you will turn all the sages behind yourself; only then will you attain freedom. If..."
It cannot be turned over. Even if you were to master it to the full extent, you would still have to stand behind him with palms joined and ask what great talk he could possibly speak.
If you can turn yourself over, then when all manner of coarse and heavy conditions arise, you will be able to exercise mastery over them.
Even if you fall down in the mud, you will still be able to exercise mastery. For instance, there was a monk who asked Youshan: "The teachings of the Three Vehicles..."
"Is there also the meaning of the Patriarchs within this? He replied, 'There is. [The questioner] said, 'Since there is, why did Bodhidharma come again?
He replied, 'Precisely because it exists that he came. Is it not so that one can attain mastery and turn back toward one's own self? As a sutra says:
'The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not achieve Buddhahood.'"
The Buddha’s Way says: "Kalpa" means stagnation. It is called the "ten completions," and it is also said to mean cutting off leakage. It simply refers to the ten paths being severed.
Because one does not forget the great fruit, it is called "staying fixedly in attachment," which is termed "accepting responsibility in a casual manner."
Regardless of status, whether noble or base, I have often observed that those in the monastic communities love to debate "this way" or "that way.
But can they actually establish the matter? Such talk is merely the spreading of paths toward future events. Have you not seen Nanquan say:
"Even if you were ten parts complete, you would still fall short of Old Wang by a single thread—this is truly difficult"? When the matter reaches this point, you must be extremely meticulous.
Only then does one attain clarity and mastery. Whether in heaven or hell, as a hungry ghost or an animal, it remains unchanged in all places;
one is fundamentally the same person as before, only that one no longer travels the old path. If there is a mind of longing [for the Way], [one shall surely return].

It results in further stagnation and attachment. If you can break free from it, what is there to choose? An ancient worthy said: "I only fear that you will not attain saṃsāra. Tell me, how would you respond?
Nowadays, people speak of a state of purity and prefer to talk about matters of the future; this ailment is the most difficult to cure.
If it were merely coarse and heavy worldly matters, they would be light; it is the disease of "purity" that is grave. It is just like this:
The flavor of the Buddhas and the flavor of the Patriarchs—both are merely attachments. The former master said: "To direct the mind toward them is to violate the precepts;

to obtain their flavor is to break the fast. Furthermore, what do you call "flavor"? It is simply the flavor of the Buddhas and the flavor of the Patriarchs. As soon as there is a heart of longing, one has violated the precepts.
If one speaks of breaking the fast or breaking the precepts as is done nowadays, then at this very moment of the three *karmavācanas*, one has already broken them.
It is understood. If it were coarse, heavy greed, anger, and delusion, though difficult to sever, they would actually be light.
If one is unconditioned, effortless, and pure, this is what is truly heavy—nothing can surpass it. The Patriarchs appeared in the world solely for this reason;
it was not for you alone. Do not treat this as a trivial matter in these times. It would be more expedient to practice as a black slave or a white ox than to be otherwise. Is it not so?
There is Chan and there is the Way. Yet you pursue them in all these various ways—seeking the Buddha, seeking the Patriarch, even up to Bodhi and Nirvana.
When will you ever find rest and fulfillment? All of this is but the mind of birth and extinction; therefore, it is not as good as being a black ox or a white cow.
Stupefied and ignorant, they know neither Buddha nor Patriarch, nor even Bodhi, Nirvana, or the causes and effects of good and evil.
They simply eat grass when hungry and drink water when thirsty. If one can act in this manner, there is no need to worry about not accomplishing the goal.
The Way cannot be calculated; it is only by knowing that there is [this reality] that one can shed hair and wear horns, pull the plow and drag the harrow.
Having attained this advantage, one may then begin to calculate a little. One does not see Maitreya, Akṣobhya, or the worlds of Sukhāvatī and so forth;
they are called "shameless" and "lazy bodhisattvas" by those of the higher path, and are also said to be subject to transformation.
Regarding birth and death, I fear that even this may be a slight laxity. As for the fundamental matter itself, how should one act?
One must be most thoroughly meticulous before it can be attained. Each person possesses their own ground of sitting; even if a Buddha appears in the world, you must not look down upon them.

Cultivate and practice with such realization; do not merely seek quick or clever results. If you wish to know this matter, even if you were now to become a Buddha or a Patriarch, it would still be just this.
This is it. One then falls into the three miserable realms, the hells, and the six paths of existence.
It is precisely this. Although it is of no use, one cannot yet escape it; one must become its master before one can. If you can become its master, that is immutability.
If you cannot become its master, that is changeability. Have you not seen Yongjia say: "Mang..."?
"Vast and unruly, one invites calamity and misfortune. [The questioner asks: "What is meant by 'vast and unruly, one invites calamity and misfortune'?
[He] says: "This very thing is it all. [The questioner asks: "How can one avoid this? [He] says: "If you know that there is [this], then you have attained it. Why would you need to avoid it?
Whether it be bodhi, nirvana, afflictions, ignorance, and so forth—it is not necessary to avoid any of them. This extends even to the coarse and heavy things of the mundane world."

Regarding such matters, one need only know that they exist and one will attain them; there is no need for excessive avoidance, for such avoidance is itself a form of conditioned transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Even attaining Buddhahood or becoming a patriarch, or reaching Bodhi and Nirvana—these are not minor calamities. Why is this so? It is solely because of conditioned transformation.
If one does not undergo transformation, one must achieve freedom in every encounter before it can be attained. —Master Xiangyan Xian.
There was a monk in the assembly who asked, "What is the Way? Xian said, "A dragon’s roar within a withered tree.
He asked again, "What is one who is on the Way? Xian said, "Eyes within a skull. The monk did not understand;
he took his leave and went to Shishuang, where he asked the various Chan masters, "What is the dragon’s roar within a withered tree? They replied, "It still carries a trace of joy. He asked again.
"What are the eyes within the skull? Zhaozhou replied, "They still carry consciousness.
The monk did not understand and asked Changqing, "What is the dragon’s cry within the withered tree? Changqing replied, "The life-blood is unbroken.
He asked again, "What are the eyes within the skull? Changqing replied, "Dry, yet never exhausted. He asked again, "Is there anyone who can hear them? Changqing replied, "Everyone."
Throughout the great earth, there was not a single person who had not heard it. He asked again, "I do not yet know what chapter or verse this is.
The Master replied, "I do not know what chapter or verse this is; those who hear it shall all perish. He then composed a verse: "The dragon’s roar from a withered tree is the true seeing of the Way;
The skull, though devoid of consciousness, has its eyes first opened. When joy and cognition are exhausted, all news and signs vanish; How can a person distinguish the clarity within the turbidity?"
There was a monk who made his robes from paper; he was known as the "Paper-Robed Wayfarer. He had come from Dongshan.
Chang asked him, "What is it like beneath the paper robe? The monk replied, "Once this single garment is hung upon the body, all ten thousand matters are as they should be.
Chang asked again, "What is the function beneath the paper robe? The monk stepped forward, bowed with palms joined, and said, "Yes," and immediately took them off. Chang laughed and said:

"You only understand going in this way; you do not understand coming in this way. The monk suddenly opened his eyes and asked, "When the single, spiritual, true nature does not rely upon the womb, what then?
Chang said, "That is not yet wonderful. The monk asked, "What is wonderful? Chang said, "Neither borrowed nor not borrowed.
The monk withdrew to sit in the hall and passed away. Chang composed a verse, which says: "The nature of awakening is perfectly bright and clear."

The formless body: do not, through your perceptions and views, falsely distance yourself from or draw near to it. If your thoughts differ, you will obscure the profound essence; if your mind deviates, you will not be a neighbor to the Way.

The Ultimate Way is profound and vast; it cannot be proclaimed through words. If proclaimed through words, it would not be the true pointer. Who could say that "this" exists? It is the conduit everywhere one touches. How can it be illustrated by "true" or "empty"?

Should one attempt to distinguish between "true" and "empty," it is like reflections appearing in a mirror. Although existence and non-existence are manifested, they do not cause harm wherever they appear.
Without injury and without location, what restriction or obstruction can there be? Not achieved through effort, by what dharma could it be so?

Whether the dharma is thus or not thus, both are but teeth and lips. If one presents it in this way, the fundamental principle (zong) is buried; yet the principle is not presented through intention, for it cannot be seen or heard.
Seeing and hearing are not liberated; they are like the moon in water. If one is not clear regarding this, it instead becomes a superfluous dharma. A single dharma has form, which obscures your eyes.
When the eyes are obscured, the world appears rugged and treacherous. My school is extraordinary; it is manifest and brilliant in the very presence of reality.
The Buddhas and sentient beings all receive the power of this grace; it is not something to be found by bowing one’s head or through discursive thought.

It shatters the gateway of the face and covers heaven and earth. You must realize it quickly and cast off the sensory faculties and their objects. Yet, as for those who do not understand, they merely prattle on about "now."
In the autumn of the third year of the Tiānchéng era of the Later Táng (the Wǔzǐ year), Fǎchēn returned once more to his former residence in Míncéng.

He traveled extensively through the various monasteries near the city before returning to his quarters, where he manifested a slight illness. After bathing and sitting upright, he passed away. He had lived for sixty-two years and spent forty-two summer retreats in the monastic life.
His remains were cremated, and śarīra relics were collected to build a stūpa. Among those who had received the Dharma from him, the foremost was the Chan Master Qīngliáng Yì.
The Master:
Chan Master Yi of Qingliang in Jinling (Fayan). The Master’s name was Wenyi.
He was the son of the Ru family of Yuhang. At the age of seven, his brilliance manifested; he relied upon the Vinaya master Quanwei of Xinding.
The Master shaved his head and went to the Kaiyuan Monastery in Yuezhou to receive full ordination from Vinaya Master Xijue.

When Master Jue’s influence flourished in Siming, the Master went there even more frequently to study the *vinaya*. He was skilled in literary composition, which greatly amazed Master Jue. Shortly thereafter, he took his leave.
Initially, he visited the practitioner Changqing Leng, but attained no realization. Together with Shanxiu and Hongjin, he traveled from Zhangzhou to the region beyond Lake Dongting.
Just as he was about to set out, it began to rain. The mountain stream became so turbulent that it could not be crossed. Looking toward the corner of the city wall, he saw an ancient temple;

he unpacked his belongings and took rest beneath its gate. The rain did not stop, so he entered the hall. An elderly monk sat by a brazier on the floor; seeing Yì, he asked him, "Where are you going on this journey?"
He said, "I am going on a pilgrimage. He was asked again, "What is the matter of pilgrimage? He replied, "I do not know. [The Master] said, "Not knowing is most intimate.
Fayi became even more suspicious of this. The three men were sitting by a fire and brought up the words of Master Sengzhao.

When they reached the passage, "Heaven and earth share the same root as I," the old monk further asked, "Are the mountains, rivers, and great earth the same as oneself, or are they different? Fayi said, "They are the same. Facheng [said, "They are different"].
He held up two fingers and, looking intently at him, said, "Two. He then immediately rose and departed. Fayu was greatly astonished.
He walked all around the corridors and read the characters on the master’s forehead, which said, "Stone Mountain Dizang. He turned to speak to Huixiu and the others, saying, "This is Master Chanben.

He intends to stay here. Before he had finished speaking, Chanben arrived again. The rain had already ceased, and Fayu had completed his preparations for departure. As Chanben saw him off, he asked: "Master..."
While Zuo was discussing the common teaching that "the three realms are mind-only," he pointed to a stone in the courtyard and asked, "Is this stone inside the mind or outside the mind?
Daoyi replied, "It is inside the mind. Daolin laughed and said, "For a wandering monk, what is the reason for placing a block of stone upon his head?
Daoyi had no reply. Thereupon, they both sought definitive resolution and subsequently both emerged into the world; Daoyi resided at [Yunmen].
At Chongshou Monastery in Linchuan, the monk Zifang asked, "Master, you have long been close to Changqing, yet you instead succeeded Dizang.
What was your intention? Yiyu replied, "Because I did not understand Changqing’s saying: 'Among the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed.
Zifang held up his whisk and showed it to him. Yiyu said, "Do you negate the myriad phenomena, or do you not negate them? Zifang said, "I do not negate them."
Yangyi said, "The body alone is revealed. Zifang said, "Wiping away the myriad phenomena. Yangyi said, "Within the myriad phenomena..."
At this, Zifang realized the essential meaning and sighed, saying, "I have nearly spent this life in vain. He further said to his disciples, "Zhaozhou said, 'Do not exert effort;
these are excellent words. Why not simply proceed as before? Even in worldly dharmas there are gateways;
how could the Buddha-dharma lack gateways? It is precisely because we do not proceed as before that the Buddhas and Patriarchs rely solely upon proceeding as before."

It is attained within the old midst, like the midnight bell; not even a hair’s breadth of difference is seen. To attain such perfect fitness, at the time of hearing there is not a single sound of clamor.
Why is this? Because it accords with the proper occasion. To speak of "death" when there is no mind is not actually death.
To stop at anything is simply to fail to remain with the original state. Suddenly, when hearing occurs out of its proper sequence, everyone is startled and says, "The bell has sounded strangely.
Furthermore, if one were to say today, "The early summer is gradually heating up," it would be incorrect; for though it is but a single day apart, how much difference can there be?
To say this on the first day of the fifth month would be a deception; you must know that the difference is but a hair’s breadth.

It is not permitted. Within the context of expedient means, to say to the Venerable Elder that it is "not the right time" is merely a deception; therefore, one does not revert to the old ways. Master Bao said:
"If you are willing for a moment and do not pursue [thoughts], how could there have been any difference throughout kalpas from this very day?

Do you understand? This very day is simply the same as kalpas of dust; it is merely a matter of putting on clothes and eating food, walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, attending morning inquiries and evening requests.
If everything remains as it was, you will simply be a person of no concern. It is also said: "Seeing the Way is the foundation; clarifying the Way is the achievement.

Only then can one attain the power of great wisdom. If you have not yet attained this, you must ensure that all things within the Three Realms that are objects of attachment are completely eliminated.
If even the slightest trace remains, you have not yet reached the goal. It is just like when you sleep: you do not feel anger, and you are naturally at ease.
This is the delusion of the three realms. When one becomes habituated to objects of perception, one fails to maintain clarity and thus falls into confusion;
this is precisely due to the chaotic interference caused by you all. The ancients called this "intermingled gold with dross"—it is indeed the genuine gold, but what can be done about the ore?
If you can see through to the very bone and marrow, that is the power of you all. If you cannot yet do so, what else is there for you to observe? Lou.
Regarding the halls, pavilions, and towers: the various sages have not necessarily always held your hand, nor have you necessarily followed their practice;

it has been thus throughout antiquity and the present. It is also said: for those who have left the household life, it is simply a matter of being in accord with the time and its seasons. When it is cold, it is cold; when it is hot, it is hot.
If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the causes and conditions of the seasons. The skillful means of the ancients and the present are not few. (Stone)
At the beginning of his reading of *Zhao Lun*, when he reached the passage, "To take all things as oneself—can this be anything other than the Sage?", he remarked:

"The Sage has no self, yet there is nothing that is not his own. Thereupon, he composed the *Cantong qi*. Its opening lines state, "The mind of the Great Immortal of the land of Zhuyi (India) does not exceed these words.
Throughout the middle sections, it speaks only of ordinary matters. Indeed, for one who wishes to realize all things as themselves...
"Go! Indeed, throughout the entire earth, not a single dharma is to be seen. He then further instructed them, saying: "Do not let your time be spent in vain. This is why I tell you all:
simply act according to the occasion and the season, and you will attain it. If you miss the timing and lose the opportunity, you are wasting your time.
To perceive form within that which is not form—to perceive form where there is no form—is precisely what it means to miss the timing."
You have missed the point. Furthermore, tell me: can you truly understand form as being non-form? If you understand it in such a way, there is no connection at all;
this is precisely what is called "running back and forth in deluded madness. What use is there in that? It is best simply to pass your time by maintaining your proper measure.
Once, he pointed to a bamboo and asked a monk, "Do you see it? The monk replied, "I see it. Fayi said, "The bamboo comes into the eye; the eye goes to the bamboo.
The monk said, "It is not like that at all. Fayi laughed and said, "Why such a panic? He had a verse which says: "The three realms are mind-only."
The myriad dharmas are consciousness-only; consciousness-only is mind-only. The eye and sound, the ear and form: form does not reach the ear, so how could sound touch the eye?

Through the eye and form, the ear and sound, the myriad dharmas are accomplished. If the myriad dharmas were not dependent on conditions, how could one contemplate them as being like illusions—the great earth, the mountains, and the rivers?
Who remains firm and who undergoes change? On the seventeenth day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Xiande era (the Wuma year), he manifested illness.

having bid farewell to the assembly, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. His countenance remained as if alive for a long time. He had lived seventy-four years in the world and had sat in meditation for fifty-four years. — By Master Xia.
Your Excellency Li Jianxun and those below him, dressed in plain white robes, escorted the whole body to the Danyang District of Jiangning to erect a stupa.
He was posthumously titled the Chan Master Dafa Yan.

The eulogy says: When Xuansha discussed the three phrases, there was originally no mention of wheels of gold, silver, or copper; otherwise, it would have been perilously close to the teachings [of the scriptures].

How could there be any difference between them? Master Zhancheng was profound, subtle, and vast; he sought only to see directly and immediately, regarding the formulation of "superfluous dharmas" as essential, which cannot be encompassed by the three phrases.
Furthermore, he remained as he was, using the "phrase that cuts off leakage" for the sake of others, yet he placed considerable emphasis on formal boundaries.
Yongming was his direct descendant; how could he not be what is called a true scion of the deep mountains?

His name was Qìngzhū. He was the son of the Cén family of Xīngǎn in Lúlíng. From birth, he was of divine brilliance and possessed a refined and tranquil bearing.
At the age of thirteen, Xia traveled alone to Nanchang. He was captivated by the Western Hills and went there to sightsee, forgetting to return.
The śramaṇa Shao-luan, having conversed with him, marveled at his extraordinary nature and said to others, "This boy exerts himself in such a manner; his future potential is difficult to measure.
He took him in and attended to all his needs as if it were but a single day for ten years. Only then did he shave his head and go to Mount Song to receive full ordination. At that time, in Luoyang...

The monks requested to register their names for manual labor, working diligently among the mortars and pestles for a very long time. One day, when Master You saw them winnowing grain, he observed them.
Dongshan said, "The offerings of the donors must not be scattered. Yunwu replied, "I dare not. Dongshan bent down, picked up a single grain of rice, and said, "Is this not what was scattered?
The monks were at a loss for a reply. Dongshan said, "Do not underestimate this single grain; hundreds of thousands of grains are born from this one.
They said, "It is so. But from where does this grain arise? Dongshan laughed heartily. The next day, he ascended the seat.
He said, "There are insects in the rice for the great assembly, yet my doubts remain ultimately unresolved.
He then went to rely upon Master Zhiduowei of Daowu and asked him, "After the Master has passed away, if someone asks about the ultimate matter, how would you respond to them?"

Zhu repeated his previous words. Huizhi immediately rose and departed. At this, Zhu realized the meaning of the matter; at that time, he had only been a monk for two summer retreats.

It is said: The temporal teachings of a single era were intended to rectify the conduct of people of that time; yet whatever origins they may have, they all ultimately fall into the "present moment. Even reaching the point where the Dharma-body is no longer a body is called the ultimate pinnacle, yet we śramaṇas lack any path toward it. If one attempts to divide it, one errs; if one does not divide it, one remains stuck in the mud and water. This is simply due to the mind and its intentions, leading to false claims based on what has been seen and heard. A monk asked: [The Master] said: "Monks, do you understand? The monks replied, "We do not understand. The Master said, "If you do not understand, how can you say you understand? If you say you understand, how can you say you do not understand? To say you understand when you do not is delusion; to say you do not understand when you do is ignorance. Delusion and ignorance—what difference is there between them? If you can see through this, you will know that the Buddha-nature is neither within nor without, neither inside nor outside. It is not something to be grasped by the mind or intellect, nor is it something to be attained through hearing or seeing. It is like the great ocean: though the waves are vast, their nature is always moist; though the clouds are many, their essence is always water. When the wind ceases, the waves subside, yet the moisture remains; when the clouds disperse, the rain stops, yet the water remains. Thus, the myriad phenomena arise from the One, yet the One is never exhausted. If you can realize this, you will see that the ten thousand dharmas are originally the One Mind. Do not seek elsewhere; do not create further complications. Just as the moon is reflected in the water, the reflection is not the moon, yet without the moon there would be no reflection. The moon is not in the sky, nor is it in the water; it is simply because of the water that the moon appears. Therefore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says, 'To see the Buddha with the eye of wisdom is to see the Buddha. If you can see thus, you will see that the Buddha is not a person, and the person is not the Buddha. To speak of the Buddha as a person is to fall into the error of attachment; to speak of the person as the Buddha is to fall into the error of emptiness. Only when you transcend both person and Buddha will you be free from birth and death. This is what is meant by 'the Dharma-body is non-body. If you can attain this state, you will be able to turn the wheel of the Dharma and benefit sentient beings. But if you remain caught in the duality of subject and object, you will merely be adding fuel to the fire of affliction. The monk then asked: "What is the meaning of this? The Master said: "The meaning is that the Way is not something to be sought through words or concepts. It is like a mirror reflecting images: the images come and go, but the mirror remains still. If you can be like this, you will be able to respond to all situations without being bound by them. The monk bowed and withdrew. The Master said: "This is why I say that the teachings of the past are all contained within the present. If you can grasp this, you will see that there is nothing to attain and nothing to lose. This is the true path of the śramaṇa. The monk asked: "How should one practice? The Master said: "Practice means to let go of all attachments and to dwell in the state of non-abiding. Do not follow after thoughts; do not cling to appearances. Just as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, so too should you let go of all things as they arise and pass away. This is the way to enter the gate of the Dharma. The monk asked: "What is the ultimate goal? The Master said: "The ultimate goal is to realize that the self is empty and the dharmas are empty, and to abide in the state of great liberation. This is what is called 'the Dharma-body is non-body. The monk asked: "How can one reach this state? The Master said: "By cutting off the flow of thoughts and returning to the source. When the mind is still and the senses are clear, you will naturally see the true nature of reality. The monk asked: "Is there a specific method for this? The Master said: "There is no fixed method. Each person must find their own way according to their capacity. Some may find it through meditation, some through recitation, some through service, and some through study. But in the end, it all comes down to letting go of the self and opening up the mind. The monk asked: "What is the difference between a sage and an ordinary person? The Master said: "The difference is simply in the degree of awakening. An ordinary person is deluded by appearances; a sage is awakened to the truth. Yet, even a sage is not separate from the ordinary person; it is only a matter of whether one is aware or unaware. The monk asked: "How can one become aware? The Master said: "By practicing mindfulness and maintaining awareness at all times. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, do not let the mind wander. Always keep the mind focused on the present moment. This is the way to cultivate mindfulness. The monk asked: "What is the meaning of mindfulness? The Master said: "Mindfulness means to be aware of the nature of the mind. The mind is originally pure and bright, but it is obscured by delusions. Through mindfulness, one can remove these obscurations and reveal the original purity. The monk asked: "How can one remove these obscurations? The Master said: "By practicing the four foundations of mindfulness: mindfulness of the body, mindfulness of feelings, mindfulness of the mind, and mindfulness of dharmas. By observing these four objects, one can see through the illusions of the world and return to the source. The monk asked: "What is the result of this practice? The Master said: "The result is liberation from suffering and the attainment of nirvana. This is the ultimate goal of all Buddhist practice. The monk asked: "Can one attain this goal in this very life? The Master said: "Yes, if one practices diligently and without distraction. But one must not be impatient; the path requires patience and perseverance. The monk asked: "What should one do if one encounters obstacles? The Master said: "Do not be discouraged. View obstacles as opportunities for growth. Every difficulty is a test of one's resolve. If you can face challenges with a calm and steady mind, you will eventually overcome them. The monk asked: "How can one maintain a calm and steady mind? The Master said: "By cultivating equanimity. Equanimity means to remain balanced in all circumstances, whether favorable or unfavorable. Do not be elated by success or dejected by failure. Maintain a constant attitude of acceptance and understanding. The monk asked: "What is the meaning of acceptance? The Master said: "Acceptance means to accept things as they are, without resistance or rejection. It is to see the impermanence of all things and to let go of attachment to them. When you can accept things as they are, you will find peace and tranquility. The monk asked: "How can one let go of attachment? The Master said: "By realizing the emptiness of all things. Emptiness does not mean nothingness; it means that things have no inherent existence. When you see that all things are empty, you will naturally let go of attachment. The monk asked: "What is the relationship between emptiness and compassion? The Master said: "Emptiness and compassion are two sides of the same coin. True emptiness gives rise to true compassion. When you realize the emptiness of the self, you will feel compassion for all sentient beings who are likewise deluded. This is the essence of the Bodhisattva path. The monk asked: "How can one manifest compassion? The Master said: "By acting with kindness and benevolence. Compassion is not merely a feeling; it must be expressed in action. Help others whenever you can, and treat everyone with respect and dignity. The monk asked: "What is the ultimate goal of the Bodhisattva path? The Master said: "The ultimate goal is to achieve perfect enlightenment and to lead all sentient beings to the same state of liberation. This is what is called 'the vow to save all beings. The monk asked: "How can one make such a vow? The Master said: "By generating the bodhicitta—the aspiration for enlightenment. This aspiration is the foundation of the Bodhisattva path. Once you have made this vow, you must remain steadfast in your practice until the end of samsara. The monk asked: "What is the meaning of bodhicitta? The Master said: "Bodhicitta is the mind that seeks enlightenment for the sake of all beings. It is the mind that is free from selfishness and is dedicated to the welfare of others. This mind is the source of all virtue. The monk asked: "How can one generate this mind? The Master said: "By contemplating the suffering of others and the rarity of the opportunity to encounter the Buddha-dharma. Reflect on the fact that all beings have been your parents and kin in past lives. Generate a heart of gratitude and a desire to repay their kindness. This is how to generate bodhicitta. The monk asked: "What is the difference between bodhicitta and ordinary compassion? The Master

When Emperor Xizong of the Tang dynasty heard of his fame, he dispatched an envoy bearing a purple *kāṣāya* robe as a gift, but he would not accept it.

On the twentieth day of the second month in the fourth year of the Guangqi era (the Wushen year), he passed away while sitting peacefully. He had lived for eighty-two years and sat in meditation for fifty-five years.
In the ninth month of summer, his entire body was interred in the northwestern corner of the monastery. He was posthumously titled Puhui, and his stupa was named Wuxiang.
He had two principal disciples who attained the Dharma: Zen Master Wen of Longhu and Zen Master Qian of Jiufeng.
Chan Master Wen of Longhu in Shaowu was named Pumen.
He was the crown prince of Emperor Xizong of the Tang dynasty. From birth he was auspicious; his features and bone structure were as pure and elegant as a painting.
He abstained from meat and pungent roots. Emperor Xizong doted on him, yet because the prince lacked any intention to govern the world, [the Emperor] employed every means to cultivate him.
He wrote this and never looked back again. Hearing of the "Wind of Frost Flowers," he longed to see it even in his dreams. In the first year of the Zhonghe era, the empire was in great chaos;

Emperor Xizong fled to Shu, and the princes and members of the imperial clan all went into exile, failing to protect one another. [The Master] heard that [the Emperor] had cut his hair and wandered away, with no one knowing his whereabouts.
He traveled to Shishuang, where those who spoke with him marveled at him, saying: "You have mounted the power of your vow..."
He came and was born into the family of an emperor and king. He left his station to follow me; he is like a lotus blooming from within the fire.

Hearing that he had entered the room at night, he earnestly said, "Master, regarding the matter of the Patriarch’s special transmission, would you be willing to entrust it to me? Mazu said, "Do not slander the Patriarch. He replied, "The principles of the world are grand and flourishing;
how could they have been established falsely? Mazu said, "Is this a real matter? He asked, "What is your intention, Master? Mazu [remained silent].
He said, "I shall tell you the secret once the mountain over which I sit nods its head. Upon hearing this, the man bowed his head in thought and exclaimed, "How extraordinary!

He broke into a sweat and prostrated himself twice. That very day he took his leave. When he reached the outskirts of Shaowu, he saw the mountains rising up lush, profound, and beautiful. He questioned the elders there.
"Is there anyone living there? He replied, "There is an ascetic who dwells within it. Hearing this, he cleared away the grass and, following the rising smoke, proceeded alone toward the site.

When the ascetic saw him arrive, he joyfully yielded his hut to him, saying, "Venerable sir, you should establish yourself here. He then performed a long bow and departed, with no one knowing where he went.
[The Master] heard that [the ascetic] lived for over ten years, eating the fruit of trees and drinking from mountain streams. One day, an old man appeared...
A man came to pay his respects. Wumen asked, "Where is your home, sir? What do you seek by coming here? The old man replied, "My home is on this mountain.
I have a request of you, Master. However, I am not a human; I am a dragon. Because I have been negligent in my duties as a rain-bringer, the heavens have punished me, and I am due to die.
I rely upon the power of the Way to escape this fate. Wumen said, "You have incurred the wrath of the Supreme Deity; what power do I have to help you?"
He applied himself with diligence. Although the man had intended to change his form and approach, he suddenly lost sight of where the old man was.
Looking beside his seat and couch, he saw a small snake about a foot long that had slithered into his sleeve and coiled itself there. At nightfall, wind and thunder swept over the couch;

lightning crashed and rain lashed down, causing the mountains and peaks to tremble and shake. Yet he heard [the sound] while sitting upright and unshaken. When dawn arrived and the sky cleared, the snake remained hanging from his sleeve.

He fell to the ground and departed. Shortly thereafter, an old man arrived and wept, saying, "Were it not for the power of a Great Being, this mountain would have been defiled by the stench of blood and flesh.

How may I repay such profound kindness? He then hollowed out the base of a cliff to form a spring, saying, "In the future, when many people gather here and there is no water, how will they establish a monastic community?
This spring is provided so that you, Master, may remain. The spring has now become a lake.
On a mountain halfway up was a place known as Longhu (Dragon Lake). When the people of the region heard of his deeds, the wealthy contributed their wealth and the poor offered their labor;
thus, the halls and pavilions were completed in a short time. Wandering monks arrived there as if returning home.

Beside the lake was a deity of extreme power over fortune and calamity, whom the local customs of this region revered with awe, making offerings of sacrificial animals during the four seasons. Hearing that [the Master] had arrived at the temple on foot, he made a covenant with him.

He replied, "If you can eat vegetarian food and observe the precept against killing, then you may become my neighbor. Otherwise, those whose paths differ do not consult one another; what mountain could you not dwell upon?
That evening, the elders of the village dreamed that a deity told them: "I have heard that the Meditation Master has conferred the precepts upon me.
I shall no longer consume offerings of blood. For my sacrifices, it will suffice to provide as much food as is offered to a bhikṣu. From then on...
This deity manifested miraculous traces to protect this mountain. Hearing that [the Master] was about to pass away, he struck the bell to assemble the congregation.
He sat in the full lotus posture and spoke a verse: "I fled the world's hardships to leave the household life; The Master pointed out to me a place of rest.
I have dwelt on this mountain and gathered the assembly for thirty years; I did not wish to bestow [this teaching] lightly upon others. Today I speak it clearly to you: I now withdraw [my hand]."
He instructed them, "Listen attentively now. Thereupon, he closed his eyes and sat upright. After a long while in profound stillness, when they shook him, he had already passed away.
His remains were enshrined in a stupa at the mountain where he resided, and he was posthumously titled Chan Master Yuanjue (Perfect Enlightenment).

The official histories do not record his personal name, but merely list two sons of Emperor Xizong: Prince Jian, Chen, and Prince Yi, Sheng. Furthermore, the biographies fail to record their mother’s surname, their official ranks, or the dates of their deaths; this is all that is heard.
At the place where he received the precepts and full ordination, he recited a verse: "I fled from worldly hardships to leave the household life.
One wonders if Shishuang was also his tonsure master.
This refers to Chan Master Jiufeng Qian of Yunzhou.

The Chan Master’s name was Daoqian. He was of the Liu clan and a native of Hougan in Fuzhou. His appearance was open and expansive, and his intellect was brilliant; his presence commanded the monastic community.
When he reached the age of "frost-flower" (thirty), the various Chan masters saw him and said to others, "This practitioner is a true talon and fangetooth of the ancestral school.
When Zhuhui passed away, Daoqian served as his attendant. The assembly requested that he take the seat of the First Seat in the hall and succeed Zhuhui.
As the abbot was discussing this with the assembly, Xuefeng Qian addressed them, saying, "This will not do; you must clarify the meaning of our former teacher before proceeding.
The assembly asked, "What was the former teacher’s intention? Qian said, "It is just as it was said: 'The incense burner of an ancient temple—how do you understand the single white chain?
The first seat replied, "This clarifies matters on the side of the single color. Qian said, "In that case, you truly do not understand the former teacher’s intention."
Thereupon, the first seat-holder arose, lit incense, and made a vow, saying: "If I have realized the meaning of my late teacher, may the incense smoke vanish as I depart this life;
if not, may I be unable to depart when the smoke vanishes. As soon as he had finished speaking, he passed away. [Dongshan] reverently patted his back and said:
"To sit and die or stand and pass away is not unknown; yet even if the Head Seat has realized the meaning of my late teacher, it is not yet complete. He then lived in a hut at Puhui.
After three years by the side of the stupa, he departed and practiced walking meditation beneath Mount Moshan, where he resided at Chongfu Temple.

A monk asked him, "What kind of practice does one who is neither human nor intermediate perform? He replied, "The practice of an animal. The monk asked, "And what kind of practice does an animal perform?"

[The Master] said: "Uninterrupted practice. [The Disciple] said: "This is still a person on the path to longevity. [The Master] said: "You must know that there is a life not shared [with others]. [The Disciple] asked:
"What kind of life is it that is not shared? [The Master] said: "The life-force of longevity is not permanent. He spoke again: "Can the great assembly attain this life?
If you wish to know life: flowing springs are life; profound stillness is the body. The thousand waves competing to rise—this is Mañjuśrī."
The realm is a single expanse of clear sky; this is the bed and couch of Samantabhadra. Next, borrowing a single phrase is like pointing at the moon;
within it, the matter is the speaking of the moon. This is the matter of the ancestral school of the Gate of the Patriarchs, like the official seal and credentials of a military governor.
For instance, before the various former worthies had established so many designations and explanations, by what standard or form did people then proceed?
Consider this: here, there is no need for the "three inches. Try to understand it! There is no need for the faculty of hearing—try to listen!
There is no need for the two eyes—try to discern it clearly! Therefore it is said: "Before the sound, nothing can be cast out;
after the phrase, no form is hidden. The entire universe is, in its entirety, your own true self. Where, then, would you place your eyes and ears?
Do not, through the nose or tongue, attempt to calculate or construct an understanding based on the faculty of the mind; even until the end of the future, there will be no possibility of rest.
Therefore, the ancients said: "To seek to learn the profound mystery with the mind and intellect is much like heading west while actually traveling east."
Previously, when the Great Master Mazu passed away at Kaiyuan Temple in Yuzhang, his disciples Huaihai, Zhizang, and others interred his śarīra at Shimen in Haihun.
Huaihai also lived in a grass hut at the stupa for over ten years, after which he traveled up the Feng River to Chelun Peak.
There he met the ascetic Sima Tuo, who urged him to remain; consequently, he never returned to Shimen again. Qian [proceeded] from there...
Jiufeng went there to travel and study, eventually establishing a Dharma assembly and becoming the first patriarch of Letan, continuing the legacy of Master Hai.

At the beginning of the Shunyi era of the Wu dynasty, he informed the assembly, sat peacefully, and passed away. His stupa was erected to the west of the temple; he was titled Yuanji (Perfect Quiescence) and posthumously honored with the title Chan Master Da Jue (Great Enlightenment).
His foremost disciple who received the Dharma was Master Yin.
Chan Master Yin of He Shan in Jizhou:
The Chan Master’s name was Yin. Born into the Wu clan, he was a native of Fuzhou.

At the age of seven, Chan Master Cunen of Xuefeng saw him and, admiring his purity and integrity, persuaded his parents to let him become a monk. At twenty, he shaved his head, received full ordination, and took his leave.

Yinyuan traveled to Jiufeng to visit Master Qian. Qian asked him, "You have come from afar; what have you seen? By what path should one transcend birth and death? Yinyuan replied, "The profound darkness has been cleared away, yet the blind remain blind. Qian laughed and waved his hand at him, saying, "The Buddha-dharma is not like this. Yinyuan was displeased and asked, "Is there no expedient means? Qian said, "Ask me yourself. Yinyuan then restated his previous words. Qian said, "I am deaf. Yinyuan said, "I am blind. Qian said, "If you are blind, how can you see my deafness? Yinyuan said, "If you are deaf, how can you hear my blindness? Qian laughed and said, "You are indeed blind! Yinyuan bowed and withdrew. Later, he went to Mount Lu and studied under Master Daowu. One day, Daowu asked him, "Where have you come from? Yinyuan replied, "From Jiufeng. Daowu asked, "What did Jiufeng say to you? Yinyuan recounted the previous dialogue. Daowu said, "Jiufeng is a man of great capacity; why do you not go back and ask him about 'deafness'? Yinyuan returned to Jiufeng and asked about "deafness. Qian said, "When the sound of a single finger snaps is heard throughout the Dharma realm, who is it that does not hear? Yinyuan was greatly enlightened. He then composed a verse: "A single snap of the fingers / Resounds throughout the ten directions / The deaf hear it clearly / And the blind see it distinctly. Qian said, "This is still not it. Yinyuan then composed another verse: "A single snap of the fingers / Resounds throughout the ten directions / The deaf hear it clearly / And the blind see it distinctly. Qian said, "This is it. Yinyuan then took leave of Jiufeng and went to stay at Mount Dongping. Later, he visited Master Xuefeng. Xuefeng asked, "Where have you come from? Yinyuan replied, "From Mount Dongping. Xuefeng asked, "What is the news from Mount Dongping? Yinyuan said, "The old fellow is dead. Xuefeng said, "How long has it been since he died? Yinyuan said, "It has been thirty years. Xuefeng said, "If so, why do you still smell of incense? Yinyuan said, "Because I am still alive. Xuefeng said, "If so, when will you die? Yinyuan said, "I will die when I am tired of being alive. Xuefeng said, "When you are tired of being alive, you will die; when you are tired of being dead, you will live. Living and dying are both free. Yinyuan then composed a verse: "Thirty years ago I met the old fellow / Today I see him as before / Living and dying are both free / The whole world is a single body. Xuefeng said, "You have attained the marrow. Later, Yinyuan stayed at Mount Yunju. One day, while sitting in the hall, he suddenly called out, "O monks! When the assembly responded, he said, "The Buddhas of the three times all emerge from here. He then composed a verse: "The Buddhas of the three times all emerge from here / The patriarchs of the ten directions also arise from here / If you wish to know the source of the Way / Just look at the tip of a single hair. He then passed away. His stupa was named "Dong" (East). This is why he is called Dongshan. Later, Master Shoushan Shengnian of Mount Nanyue visited Dongshan. When asked about this, he said, "I saw how diligent the servant was toward her mistress. Consequently, he remained in attendance for more than ten years.

When Huiqian moved his residence to Shimen, he followed him there as well. Upon Huiqian’s death, he departed to travel to Luling; arriving at Yongxin, he beheld the extraordinary and magnificent beauty of the mountains to the southeast.
He then followed the course of the water and arrived at the site of an old temple. This was likely where the eminent monk Da-xi Dao-chang had resided during the Wende era;

he subsequently settled there, and students gathered like clouds. When the Later Ruler of Tang heard of his reputation, he issued an imperial decree for him to come to Jinling to inquire about the essentials of the Buddha-dharma.

After some time, by imperial command, he was invited to reside at Xiangguang Temple in Yangzhou. He declined the offer with earnestness and returned to the Western Mountains, where he was subsequently summoned to reside at Cui... [temple].

Yan also resided at Shanglan Temple, where he was granted the title Chan Master Chengyuan. In the second month of the first year of the Jianlong era (the Gengshen year), he manifested a slight illness.
On the second day of the third month, he ordered his attendant to open the abbot’s quarters and assembled the great assembly, saying:
"Those who come here to study later have not yet recognized Heyang; recognize him right now! Thereupon, he passed away peacefully. He had lived for seventy years.
He spent fifty summer retreats there. His posthumous title was Chan Master Faxing, and his stupa was named Miaoxiang (Wondrous Appearance).
The eulogy says: Shishuang said, "The entire realm has never been hidden. Yet when his disciple, Master Wen, was about to pass away, he said, "Today I shall speak clearly to you;
listen well as I close my eyes. Jiufeng said, "The entirety of heaven and earth is you."
When a person is in their own body, where do they place the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue? When Master Yin, his son, was on the verge of passing away, he said:
"Those who come later as students have not yet recognized Heishan; recognize him right now!

I observe that the words and deeds of this father and son, these brothers, are like a form appearing when a shadow is cast, or a sound echoing when a valley is called. Yet, even among the Chan practitioners of recent times, there are still those who linger in contemplation—how can this be?
