Composed by the Chan Monk Huìhóng of the Míngbái Ān in the Song Dynasty.
Chan Master Yúnjū Hóngjué Yīng:
The master’s name was Dàoyīng. He was a native of Yùtián in Youzhōu and was born into the Wáng family. While still a young child, his bone and spirit...
He was profound and steady; his speech was sparse while his principles were abundant. At the age of ten, he left home at Yan-shou Temple in Fan-yang.

Another fifteen years passed before he became a full-fledged monk (*bhikṣu*). His master had him study the *Vinaya*, but this was not to his liking, so he abandoned it to travel as a wandering mendicant.

Upon reaching Cui-wei, he encountered a monk who had come from Yu-zhang. During a conversation at night, they discussed the Dharma seat of Dong-shang; thereupon, he traveled south with only a single alms bowl.
When Xinfeng was established, he went to pay his respects to Chan Master Wuben Jia. Jia asked, "What is your name? He replied, "Daoying.
Jia said, "Why not say something further beyond that? He replied, "Beyond that, one is no longer named Daoying. Jia was pleased and considered him a man of realization.
His manner of responding was like that when he first met Yunyan; [Zhao] Rong considered him to have entered the inner chamber and attained profound penetration.
He remained behind at Yunfeng, where he built a hermitage to dwell. Once a month, he would come to visit Guishan Jia. Jia rebuked him, saying, "You have not yet forgotten worldly attachments;
this is a distraction from the Way. He then burned the hermitage. He subsequently left Haihun and ascended Mount Oufu—located on the northwestern slope of Mount Lu—which towers over the world.
It was a place of extreme desolation. He built a hut by binding it to a tree and lived there, naming it Yunju (Cloud Dwelling). Disciples also sought him out, gathering wherever he stayed;

thus, beneath the trees and among the mountains, temporary shelters were gradually established. Preaching the Dharma beneath one such shelter, he said: "What complicated matters are there in the Buddha-dharma?
Practice is all that is required. Simply know that the mind is the Buddha; do not worry that the Buddha cannot understand your speech. If you wish to attain this, act accordingly.
As for the matter, one must still be such a person. If one is such a person, what is there to worry about?
If you say that such a matter is difficult, consider the ancient masters of old: they were pure and simple, acting according to their true nature, and never devised anything artificial.
When someone asked, "What is the Way? they would sometimes answer with a brick, a tile, or a wooden head. Why? Because they all valued the original foundation beneath one's feet.
Truly, there is power; this is none other than the inconceivable person who can grasp soil and turn it into gold.

If such a thing did not exist, even if you were to speak with great eloquence—like weaving together flowers and brocade—it would be nothing more than empty words. To say directly, "I emit light and shake the earth," is beyond all that exists in the world.

Even if one were to exhaustively explain it until one’s head was cut off, no one at all would believe or accept it. From the very beginning, it has been beneath one's own feet, yet it is void and non-existent.
"Power! You all are like hunting dogs; you only seek out that which has left tracks.

If you encounter a wild sheep with its horns caught in a tree, not only will you see no tracks, but you will not even recognize its scent. A monk then asked, "What is it like when a wild sheep’s horns are caught in a tree?
He replied, "Six times six is thirty-six. The monk asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. He replied, "Have you not heard it said..."
There are no traces. He asked again, "The World-Honored One has secret words; Kāśyapa did not conceal them. What are the World-Honored One’s secret words?
[Linji] called out the questioner’s name and said, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. [Linji] said, "If you do not understand, the World-Honored One has secret words.
If you do understand, Kāśyapa did not conceal them. Then he said, "When members of the Sangha speak and breathe, they must..."
There is a reason for this; do not treat it with indifference. What kind of place is this? How could one accept it so easily?

Whenever you ask about a matter, you must recognize what is good and what is evil. If you do not distinguish between the honorable and the lowly, or the noble and the base, and fail to understand what constitutes an offense, speaking recklessly at random will yield no benefit.
You merely travel from house to house, seeking out similar words wherever you go; that is why you have come to search.
I have always told my brothers: "Do not take offense at our differences. I fear that many of our fellow students will depart; therefore, by all means, do not bring them here.
If they are brought here and speak words that do not accord with ours, you must still observe them. This is no small matter for an eighty-year-old elder to enter the examination hall;
it is no trivial or casual affair. A single word out of alignment, and one is separated by thousands of miles."

It is difficult to bring [the mind] under control. This is because the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*) are easy to neglect; one must apply oneself with all one's might. There must be a specific reason for striking the bone and breaking the marrow.
One’s words must be like tongs, like pincers, like hooks, and like locks; they must be taught so that they continue in an uninterrupted succession, only then will it be achieved.
It is fully present in every head and clearly manifest in every object; is this not the attainment of the wondrous matter? This kind of study requires great care and thorough investigation;
you must be precise and exact, reaching a point where there is no error. When you arrive here, what room is there for hesitation? What room is there for deliberation?
Those who move forward must always remain solemn and cautious, with wings tucked in, only then will they succeed. If...
One who knows this naturally understands how to guard and cherish [the mind], never speaking recklessly even once in ten instances; they stop nine times out of ten.
Why is this? It is for fear that there may be no benefit. One who has realized the essence is like a hand fanning the moon in pursuit.
Mold even forms upon his lips; this is not a matter of forced effort, but occurs spontaneously and naturally. To attain such a state, one must be such a person.
Since one is already such a person, there is no need to worry about such a state. Yet, such a state is difficult to find.
It is further said: "Even if you were to master the matters on the Buddha's side, you would already have misapplied your mind.

Have you not seen that even when the ancients caused the heavens to rain flowers and the stones to nod their heads, it still had nothing to do with their own self? What else, then, is this trivial business?
Now, you intend to take this limited body and mind and apply them toward the infinite; what connection could there possibly be?"
It is like trying to force a square block of wood through a round hole; there will inevitably be some degree of friction and difficulty.

If there were no such matter, even if you could speak with the profusion of clustered flowers and brocade patterns, it would be of no use; you would still remain within the realm of emotional consciousness.

If all matters must be brought to their ultimate exhaustion right here, only then can one be free from fault and emerge from the body. If there is even a single hair’s breadth left unexhausted, [you have not succeeded].
One is immediately burdened by worldly entanglements; how much more so when they become numerous? To deviate by even a hair’s breadth is to commit a transgression as vast as a mountain.
As the ancients said: "The place of study is not mysterious; it is entirely a matter of common custom. Things of the inner chambers that one cannot relinquish all constitute leaks."
You must directly take it up right here. When going and coming are both exhausted and all affairs are brought to an end, only then will you be free from fault.

It is like a person who has attained realization in every situation and is thoroughly proficient in every matter; such a one is merely called a "person of affairs accomplished," but is never called "Noble and Precious.
From this, one should know that the path of the Noble and Precious is distinct by itself; it is like the most profound and most precious thing in the world.
It must not be brought before those who are honorable and noble; one must know that it is inconceivable and should not be treated with mere superficial interest.
Thus the ancients said: "It is like two mirrors facing each other; their radiance reflects one another, and there is no waxing or waning.
Is this not a state of uniformity? Yet even so, it is still called a matter of reflected images. It is like when the sun rises and its light illuminates the world—this is clarity.
"Lǎng is one half. What is that other half called? People nowadays have not yet recognized it;

they take the coarse and superficial matters of light and shadow, doors and thresholds, to be the affairs within the house—how could this possibly suffice? It is further said: 'The one who attains it does not treat it as trivial;

Amidst the multitude, one is as if not among the multitude."
To be amidst the multitude as if not amidst the multitude; to be in the body as if without a body; to dwell in the world as if without a world—is this not to have no defilement disturb one’s virtue?
To transcend the myriad categories and be liberated from all fetters. Even if a thousand or ten thousand people attain it, they still consider the Way not to be for their own sake.
If you were to attain it now, it would be identical to what was attained at the beginning. As the ancients said: "Having realized the matter of that other shore, yet..."
"Bring your baggage here. "What is there to do over there? "And what about bringing your baggage here? Therefore it is said: "If you have it, do not bring it;

"If you wish to realize this matter, you must be like one who has taken his last breath; only then will you be in accord with that person."
If you can grasp the intent of this person, only then will you have a share in speaking even a few words; only then will you have a share in carrying on the journey.
To be absent for even a moment is like being dead—how much more so now, when one is away for years and months!
If one were truly long gone, why worry that household affairs would not be settled? If you wish to know what has occurred over a long duration, it lies entirely in the present. It is just like this.
If you attain it now, you will attain it for all eternity. It is like a person who has traveled through a thousand villages and ten thousand miles to return home;

upon arriving, it is right here. Thus, if it is so, then everything is entirely so; if it is not so, then everything is entirely not so. One reaches the point where a radiant flame arises from the crown of one's head.
Nor is it so. It can do all things, yet all things do not constitute the Way. All day long one covets what lies ahead, thereby losing what lies behind;
if one looks at what lies behind, one loses what lies ahead. It is like a person who does not move forward—what matters would there be behind them?
A monk asked: "When someone enters wearing brocade and embroidery, why is it that after seeing the Master, they are left with not even an inch of thread?"
He hung it up and said, "Even if one were to walk upon the crystal palace and fall down, it must be shattered to pieces.
He then said, "If there were even a hair’s breadth remaining that was not discarded, one would be burdened by dust; how much more so if there were more? Have you not seen the common saying:

A sound of gold. There is no need to turn your head back and look; what other use would there be?

Have you not seen how the Second Patriarch at that time was one who had extensively studied the *Shi* and *Shu*, and whose mastery of the Three Baskets of the Holy Teachings was like looking into the palm of his hand?

For what reason did he still seek from Bodhidharma the settling of his mind? From this, one knows that the matters within this gate are no ordinary affair. Therefore it is said: "The wise person does not rely on words."
To seek within the "middle" is to take it up; how could one who has attained the person seek it by speaking of a middle? This is not to be distinguished from ordinary folk.

When all myriad entanglements cease, the Way is for a moment no longer on the road; there is then a source from which it comes. It is not only that evil associates cannot be found, but even good associates cannot be found.
Where have they gone? They have gone throughout the entire body; they have gone home; they have gone to pay their respects. Only then is one liberated from all realms of existence.
He departs through the gate. Having departed, he leaves the cage behind; he has escaped from danger and hardship. He is an extraordinary person. It is also said:
"If one observes an object as clearly as looking at it in the palm of one's hand, then with certainty, one may follow conditions. If it is so for one, it is so for ten thousand.

Among ten thousand, it is difficult to find even one or two. One or two cannot be found. Does this not show that those who manifest illumination are easy to find, yet those who manifest their own nature are rare?

Such people are indeed difficult to find; it is not that they do not exist at all, but rather that they are rare. If you have not yet attained such a state, do not force yourself to act as if you have.

To force oneself leads to the arising of affliction; when affliction arises, one retreats from the Path. When one retreats from the Path, transgressions come upon the person, and thus one will not attain realization.
Why do you speak such grand words? Since you have left the household life, you are like a prisoner released from jail. You must practice few desires and contentment.
Do not covet worldly glory. Endure hunger and thirst; set your will upon non-action (*wuwei*). Having entered the Buddha-dharma, through ten births and nine deaths, do not abandon one another.
Entering life and facing death, do not violate the Buddha-dharma. Be as firm as cutting through nails or iron; do not betray the Tathāgata. There is no need for much ado;
each person should understand this for themselves. If there is business, come forward; if there is none, do not stand about. [This is] the charge of the Abbot.
For thirty years, his Way spread throughout the world, and his assembly reached fifteen hundred people. Zhong Wangshi of Nanchang revered him, vowing to take him as his teacher for all generations.
In the autumn of the first year of the Tianfu era of the Tang dynasty, he manifested a slight illness.

On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month, he expounded the final skillful means for the great assembly, recounting the intent behind the beginning and end of his appearance in the world. The assembly was moved with grief.

Chan Master An of Luopo in Lizhou was named Yuan’an.
Born into the Dan clan, he was a native of Nanyou in Fengxiang. In his youth, he relied upon Vinaya Master You of Huaien Temple, where he shaved his head and received full ordination.
Having grown up, he became proficient in the sutras and śāstras. He first visited Cuiwei, but attained no realization there. He then traveled north.
Upon arriving at Linji, Linji remarked that he was sharp and quick-witted and could be taught. An departed with a sense of self-assurance. He went to Jiashan and built a hermitage on a tomb mound.
Jiashan marveled at this and sent a letter to An. He instructed his messenger, saying, "If this monk does not open the letter upon receiving it, he will come tomorrow;
if he opens it, he will not come. When An received the letter, he indeed set it aside without replying. The messenger...
He reported this in full to Jia Shan. Jia Shan said, "He will surely arrive by dawn or dusk. Shortly thereafter, news arrived that Huian had reached the vicinity.
From afar, Jia Shan saw him and shouted, "A rooster nesting in a phoenix's den—it is not its kind! Get out! Huian then asked, "I have come from afar to pay my respects;

[Zhaozhou] was mistaken. Jia Shan said, "Stop, stop! Do not be so hasty or precipitate. The clouds and moon are the same; the streams and mountains are each different.
It is not that one cannot cut off the tongues of all people in the world, but how, O *dānapati*, can you make a tongueless person speak?"
An was at a loss and did not know how to answer. Jia Shan struck him with his staff. After Jia Shan passed away, the assembly appointed An as his successor.
Having resided there for a long time, he later moved to Lopu and said to the assembly: "The final word is where one first reaches the secure barrier;

it blocks the vital ford, allowing passage neither to ordinary people nor to sages. If you wish to know those of the highest caliber, they do not take the words and teachings of the Buddhas and patriarchs and paste them [upon themselves]."
Upon the forehead, like a tortoise bearing a map, one brings upon oneself the calamity of losing one’s life. A single path leading south—those with wisdom know it to be superficial.
To study the Way, one must first recognize one’s own fundamental principle; only then can one act spontaneously without failing to meet the requirements of the moment.
It is just like before even a trace of a sharp edge has appeared: there is neither "this" nor "that. Yet, the moment a fleeting perception of seeing or hearing arises, there is already [distraction].

He replied, "This question is not weak. It is like asking, 'What is the Prince’s body?

He replied, 'When the Master sees the Venerable ask, then in the midst of that question and answer, do not allow the faculty of thought to take root. He once said: 'In general, regarding words and phrases...'"
One must first sever all leakage; yet those who study now vie with one another to hasten toward the realm of the subtle and wondrous, desiring to see the mind of the Patriarchs.
Is this not like heading for Yan while intending to reach Yue?
Chan Master Xuan of Jiufeng in Yinzhou was named Tongxuan.
He was born into the Cheng clan; his ancestors were from Changshou in Yingzhou. In his youth, he relied upon the śramaṇa Huichao of Renwang Monastery in Ying.
Huichao observed him in secret and found that while his exterior was pure and profound, his inner nature was exceptionally sharp and awakened. Huichao regarded him as extraordinary.

He shaved his head and received full ordination, immediately traveling to the capital of Luoyang to study the Vinaya-piṭaka. Later, he departed for Wuling to visit Chan Master Shenguang Jian of Deshan.
At that time, Master Jian was already advanced in years, and his monastic style was increasingly rigorous; no one among his disciples had yet encountered him.

Yet Huian alone regarded the profound as extraordinary. However, his understanding of the profound did not reach full penetration. He took his leave and went to Gao’an to pay his respects to Chan Master Jia.

Master Jia was delighted when they conversed; he patted him and said, "In your palm lies a divine pearl. You display it to people in broad daylight, yet even then people brandish their swords against you—how much more so in the dark of night!
You are indeed precious. Huian replied, "It is simply that I do not recognize the pearl. If I were to recognize it..."

There was also no distinction between day and night. Jia praised him, calling him a "superior man. After Jia passed away, he lived in a grass hut beside the stupa for three years, and those who came to study under him increased daily.
Huian said, "In times of great peace, one eats when hungry and sleeps when weary; what else is there to do? I am fundamentally without affairs.
For you to come seeking me like this is to create affairs where there are none. To create affairs where there are none—this is truly to create affairs."
This is what practitioners of the Way dread. Why not each of you retire to your own places? At the beginning of the Zhonghe era, he took his leave of the stupa and traveled north for a long time.
Returning south, he took up residence in Yuzhang. Zhong Wang of Nanping treated him with the etiquette of a disciple, serving him as his teacher from the south.
Xuan grew weary of living in a city and desired to transcend the world in the mountain forests; the King purchased Mount Mo for him and built a vihāra there, naming it Longxing.
Ji invited him [to stay], and students flocked to him like grass bending in the wind. Someone asked, "Can one's own mind and another's mind see each other?

Xuán replied, "If you cannot even see your own self, how can you observe another? He was asked again, "How does one thoroughly comprehend the nature of sin and merit so that no distinction between them remains?
Xuán replied, "Fine silk and linen do not ward off the cold. On another occasion, he once asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from?"
[The monk] said, “From the Min Ridge. Xuán said, “It is not easy to travel such a great distance. The monk said, “It is not difficult; as soon as one moves a step, one arrives.
Xuán asked, “Is there anyone who does not move a step? The monk replied, “There is. Xuán asked, “How can such a person arrive here?

The monk was unable to answer. Xuán drove him away with his staff. Xuán then said to his disciples, “The meaning of the Buddhas and the meaning of the Patriarchs are like the opening and closing of a hand.”

The former master established the five ranks to clarify the fundamental tenets of Yunyan. It is like a divine physician treating an illness; his medicine is merely that which is used in daily practice.
In speech, he avoids absolute certainty, not wishing to sever the continuity [of the lineage]; in his spiritual mechanism (*ji*), he avoids offense, not wishing to defile it.
Yet, because the students' faculties and thoughts are not yet refined, they seek only the "nine-fold elixir," claiming it can raise the dead. This is...
This is not so. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there is a chapter titled "The Phantom City. This was spoken by the Buddhas and Patriarchs in secret;
read it thoroughly and clearly. The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū had a lifespan of five hundred and forty million *nayuta* kalpas.
Having sat at the site of enlightenment and defeated the armies of Māra, he was on the verge of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet the teachings of the Buddhas did not appear before him.
[The Buddha] sat before [him] in the full lotus posture for one *kṣudra-kalpa*, and even up to ten *kṣudra-kalpas*, without moving body or mind;
yet the teachings of all Buddhas still did not appear before him. To say "on the verge of accomplishment" means one *kṣudra-kalpa*;

to say "ten *kṣudra-kalpas*" refers to that which is defiled and that which is severed. Furthermore, it is said: at that time, the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven first [offered] to that Buddha...
Beneath the Bodhi tree, he spread a lion throne one yojana in height. Upon this throne, the Buddha was to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Just as he sat upon this throne, the Brahma kings rained down various celestial flowers.
The area was a hundred yojanas across. From time to time, fragrant breezes blew away withered flowers and rained down fresh ones;
in this manner, it continued without ceasing for ten minor kalpas as he made offerings to the Buddha. He constantly struck the celestial drum, while the other devas performed heavenly music.

This flower rained down constantly. The devas of the Four Great Kings, in order to make offerings to the Buddha, constantly struck celestial drums, while the other devas performed celestial music for ten intermediate kalpas until his parinirvāṇa; it was likewise so throughout that time.
O bhikṣus, after the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū had passed ten intermediate kalpas, the Dharma of all Buddhas appeared before him, and he attained unexcelled [enlightenment].
"Attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. To say that "ten small kalpas have passed" refers to the principle of the interplay between the provisional and the ultimate.
The Patriarch said: "How could it not be so for those who rely on the teachings to awaken to the fundamental source?

On the seventeenth day of the second month in the third year of the Qianning era of the spurious Tang dynasty, he rose at dawn and exhorted his disciples, saying: "Do not let your time be spent in vain; do not let the offerings of the faithful go to waste. Having...

Having already left the household life, he took only the Way as his path; thus he was called a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). Thereupon, remaining in silent meditative concentration, he passed away on the twentieth day of the third month.
He had lived in the world for sixty-three years and spent forty-two summer retreats in seated meditation.

The commentary states: Yantou said, "One need only recognize the fundamental principle (gangzong); fundamentally, there is no substantial dharma. His profound words avoid the trap of total perfection;
he does not wish to sever the continuity, nor does his mechanism of response allow for offense. That which is untainted is the fundamental principle.

He even cites the *Lotus Sūtra* to provide proof, clarifying the esoteric teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs so that there is no lingering doubt. To rely on the teachings to awaken to the fundamental principle—how could this possibly be in vain?
How lamentable! When I arrived at Jiufeng, I paid my respects at his stupa; the stone stele was already broken and ruined, so it could not be read.
There was a wooden stele with an inscription, the gist of which was as follows. Why is it that the descendants of his lineage today do not equal the fundamental principles revealed by Xuán?
Chan Master Qi of Yunju in Nankang: The Chan Master’s name was Daoqi.
Born into the Jin clan, he was a native of Nanchang. In his youth, he relied upon Chan Master Mingzhao of Baizhang and received full ordination.

His spiritual disposition was sharp and keen; whether walking, practicing, or sitting in meditation, he was constantly preoccupied with the fact that he had not yet clarified his own fundamental matter. Carrying a single almsbowl...
Having traveled extensively through the monastic communities (*saṃghārāma*), his mind of study never ceased. At that time, Chan Master Faden was residing at Shanglan in Nanchang;

Zhiqi went there together with others to rely upon him. Faden appointed him as the Librarian (*zhizang*). One day, Faden happened to see him and called out, "Every time I see you raise the dialogue regarding the Patriarch’s coming from the West, how do you, the Librarian, deliberate upon it? Zhiqi replied, "Neither East nor West. Faden said, "If..."

"If you understand it in this way, there is no connection at all. [Zhaozhou] asked, "I do not yet know what your honorable intention is. Faldeng remained silent for a long while and then said, "What intention is there in coming from the West?
At these words, Zhaozhou suddenly awakened to the essential meaning. He first resided at Dayu in Gaoyang, where he composed the *Souxuan Nianqian Guizhe* (Searching the Profundities:
Verses on Holding up the Ancients), which circulated widely throughout the various regions. He was known as Dongchan. He once said to his disciples:
He said: "Dharma said: 'In this land, among all the sutras, only the Laṅkāvatāra can serve as a seal for the mind. As I read this sutra, a verse says: "All phenomena have no essence;
they are taught to be nothing but mind. Failing to see one's own mind, one gives rise to conceptual discrimination."'"

He may truly be called the Great Compassionate Father. His discourse is an ultimate expression of reality as it is; it is simply that we ourselves fail to receive it, thereby turning our backs on his boundless grace—an offense as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Someone might ask: "In that case, does seeing one's own mind immediately sever all conceptual discrimination?
Zhi said: "It is not so. It is like training a horse: when the horse sees its own reflection, it is not startled. Why? Because it knows [itself]."
Because its shadow issues forth from one's own body, I know by this that while discursive thought is not severed, the characteristics of the mind are also relinquished.
Observe right now before you as it truly is; not even a hair’s breadth is seen. The Patriarch said:
"If you see the present, you should also see the past and future. If you do not see the past and future, you should not see the present either. This...
His words were clear and distinct, yet people remained deluded and confused. Someone asked Longji, "All bells and drums are fundamentally without sound;
how can one believe that they are soundless? Longji replied, "The Patriarch said: 'Just as with the sound of a drum, there is no creator and no place of abiding.
Because it is ultimately empty, it merely deceives ordinary people. If the sound of the drum were truly existent, then the sound of the bell would likewise [be so]."
"Striking [the bell] and responding [to the drum] should not be conflated. Thus Xuansha said: 'In the bell there is no sound of the drum; in the drum there is no sound of the bell.

Bell and drum do not intersect; every phrase is without before or after. If one does not realize the quiescence within the very substance [of these sounds], how could every phrase be without before or after?
Later, he moved to reside at the Shuanglin Chan Monastery on Mount Yougu, and subsequently transferred his residence to Yunju.

This lasted for twenty years in total. In the third year of the Zhide era, the *dingyou* year, in the ninth month, he manifested illness. On the eighth day, at the hour of *shen*, he ordered the bell to be struck to assemble the community.
Once the *vina* had announced that the assembly was gathered, he laughed heartily and recounted the origins of his renunciation from beginning to end.

He then bowed in thanks to those who had assisted him in the monastic community, saying: "Today, this old monk, pressed by the mutual forces of wind and fire, has come specifically to meet you all. Furthermore—"
"In what place do you see? Do you see it in the four great elements and five aggregates? Or do you see it in the six entrances and twelve bases?
Since these various places cannot be seen, who is it that is questioning me right now?
After a long silence, he said, "After my passing, you should entrust the affairs of the monastery to Qi Gui. Thereupon, he passed away.
He lived through sixty-nine years of the world and sat in meditation for forty-eight summer retreats.
The eulogy states: I have previously composed an inscription for the Great Fool (Dayu) at Dongchan Temple. That inscription recorded the karmic conditions for his realization of the Dharma.

Regarding the statement by Faden, "What profound meaning is there in that which came from the West? when compared with the *Chuan deng lu*, the phrase "In his own house, there are naturally descendants" is an error.
Long ago, there was a monk who asked Zhaozhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhaozhou replied, "The cypress tree in the courtyard.
He then followed this by admonishing him: "If you are willing to accept what I have said, then I have failed you;
if you are not willing to accept what I have said, then I have not failed you. Yet those who are dim-witted plagiarize [his words], thereby distorting the ancient [teaching].
The intentions of men are incomplete; the harm they cause is extreme. Therefore, I have recorded this together.

Chan Master Rui-lu Xian, whose ancestral name was Benxian, was born into the Zheng clan and was a native of Yongjia in Wenzhou. From his childhood, he found no pleasure in remaining in the secular world.
At age twenty-five, he went to rely upon a certain śramaṇa at Jiqing Monastery and became a śrāmaṇera.
He then traveled to Tiantai Guoqing Temple to receive the full precepts. He immediately visited National Teacher Shao, serving him diligently for ten years.

While residing at Ruiluo Monastery, his feet never stepped into cities or towns, his hands never handled wealth or silk, he did not provide bedding, and he did not wear silk garments; he maintained the midday meal as his only sustenance throughout the day.
He sat in meditation until dawn, instructing and guiding his disciples for over thirty years; his resolve became ever more rigorous. He said to the assembly:

"When I first saw [the Master of] Tiantai, I attained realization upon hearing his words. Yet for a thousand days thereafter, throughout the four modes of deportment, it was as if something were obstructing my breast, like living with an enemy.
One day, I suddenly had a forceful awakening, like feeling my nose while washing my face."
Kong composed three verses, saying: "It is not the wind or the banner that moves; it is the mind of benevolence that moves. This has been transmitted from of old until the present day.
Hereafter, those who wander as water and clouds wishing to understand: the Patriarch was truly a fine connoisseur. He further said:

"If one sees the form and thereby sees the mind, when people come to question you, you will find it difficult to answer. If you seek to explain it through various principles, you will fail the Master’s intent."
He produced three pieces of patched robes (*kāṣāya*). He further said: "Throughout vast kalpas, it has always been thus. Thus, it is the same as heaven and the same as earth.
Being the same as earth and the same as heaven, what form could it have? What form it has, there is nothing that is not it. He then further said: "The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra proclaims:"

"The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm. Is this not truly so? For instance, since the Buddha-body already fills the Dharma-realm, there would be no place left for the realms of Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, humans, devas, asuras, hungry ghosts, animals, or those in the hells to dwell.
Such reasoning is utterly preposterous. It is commonly said that all phenomena...
Birth is merely what is manifested by the mind. Now tell me: are the five sense organs and the six objects they encounter the same as you, or are they separate?
If they are the same, why do they not become a single mass? If they are separate, how can it be said that there is only this one mind?
You must apply yourself with utmost vigor; the Buddha-dharma is no trivial matter. On the second month of the first year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, he addressed his disciples...
The disciple Rujiao said, "Build a 'egg-stupa' for me; once the stupa is completed, I shall depart. On the full moon day of the eighth month, the construction was finished.
Monastics and laypeople from near and far came to build up the mountain, fearing only that they might be too late. On this day, it was as if he were at home. At the hour of noon—
Anzhu sat upright in his quarters, his hands forming the *ratnamudrā*. He said, "Ruozhou, the ancients said:
'Mounting the tiger’s head while reaching for its tail—what about the matter in the middle? Ruozhou replied, 'It is simply Ruozhou. Anzhu then said, 'Ask me.'"
He asked this while riding on the tiger’s head and reaching for its tail: "As for the matter in the middle, what is it? Xian said, "I cannot bring myself to play with this either.
Thereupon, he suddenly opened one eye, looked with a faint gaze, and passed away peacefully. He had lived in the world for sixty-seven years.
He sat in meditation for forty-two summers. The high officials reported these matters to the throne, and an imperial edict was issued for his home province to conduct regular inspections.

Thus, Ruzhou presented the collection of his lifelong writings, the *Zhulin ji* (Bamboo Grove Collection) in ten fascicles, containing over one thousand poems and prose pieces, to the imperial court for submission.
By imperial decree, it was stored in the Secret Archives (*Bige*), and Ruzhou was specially granted the purple robe.
The commentary states: Having read the earlier biographies and compared them with the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), I find they differ slightly in detail and brevity.

Indeed, the mind of one’s own nature does not exist externally; when delusion is exhausted, one returns to oneself. Thus, at the moment of birth and death, one attains such transcendence spontaneously.
Yet I have always marveled that while the sagely predecessors possessed eloquence and wit in their daily lives that were unassailable, on the day of their passing, they all withdrew their radiance.
Mengqi asked, "Dongshan said, 'My name for idleness has already faded away,' and Linji said, 'Who knows that my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye will perish with this blind donkey?
Now Xian also says, 'I too cannot bring it forth. Alas! Is there not a profound essential meaning here?"
*The Record of the Jewel-like Monks of the Chan Forest*, Scroll Seven;
*The Record of the Jewel-like Monks of the Chan Forest*, Scroll Eight.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huìhóng of the White Hermitage, Song Dynasty.
Chan Master Yuantong Yuede: The Chan Master’s name was Yuede.
He was born into the Huang family of Lin’an, Hangzhou. At the age of seventeen, he served the Elder Qin of Dongshan as his teacher;
he shaved his head and received full ordination. His spiritual demeanor was serene and profound; he was empty within and plain without, taking diligent practice as his Buddha.
At the age of twenty-four, he traveled extensively throughout various regions, wandering freely among the monastic assemblies.

Upon reaching Qingxi in Xiangzhou, he visited Master Jin, where he stayed for a long time before departing. During the reign of the Li family who held the kingdom of Jiangnan, Zhide lived incognito at Shanglan Temple in Nanchang.
When Song Qi, the Duke of Chu, arrived at the sutra hall, the monks hurried forward to welcome him; however, Zhide merely looked on.
The scripture remained as it was. Duke Song stood by his side and glanced at it, but Huide did not look back or respond much.

Duke Song asked, "What scripture is the Senior Monk reading? Huide held it up for him to see; the Duke marveled at this and earnestly requested that he reside at the monasteries of Sheli, Yougu, and Shuangling.
Huide was unconcerned with staying or leaving; wherever he went, he would simply sit in silent repose, yet his disciples naturally gathered around him.
Guījǔ wore a single-layered dharma-robe throughout his life. He would thread cords through the folds of the garment; at night, he would stretch out the robe to serve as a blanket.
When the Ruler of the Later State heard of his reputation, he summoned him to Jinling and inquired about the essentials of the Buddha-dharma.

Guījǔ was retained in the imperial palace, and a temple was subsequently established for him to reside in. After the death of Prince of Xuancheng, her son by Empress Zhāohuì, she donated funds to build a temple in Lú.
On the northern slope of the mountain, below Stone-Ear Peak (Sekiribō), on the day the foundation was laid, a golden image of Avalokiteśvara was discovered within the earth;

it was bestowed the name Enmyō (Perfect Pervasion). Later, when the court dispatched an envoy to demand retribution from the Southern Dynasties ruler, who subsequently surrendered his territory, Hu Ze occupied Jiujiang and refused to submit.
The vanguard of the Great General Cao Han crossed the river and entered the temple.
The Chan practitioner started in alarm and fled. Huide sat as calmly as on any ordinary day. When Zhang Han arrived, Huide did not rise nor offer a bow.

Enraged, Han shouted, "Elder, have you not heard of the General who kills men without blinking? Huide stared at him intently and said, "How do you know there is no monk here who does not fear birth and death?
Han was greatly amazed and his respect increased. He then asked, "For what reason did the Chan practitioner [flee]?"
Sengde said, "Beat the drum and they will assemble of their own accord. Liu Han dispatched his subordinate officers to beat it, but none of the Zen practitioners came. Han asked, "Why have none come?
Sengde replied, "It is because you have a murderous intent; that is why they do not come. Sengde rose and beat it himself, and the Zen practitioners then assembled.
Han bowed twice and asked for a strategy to ensure victory. Zhide replied, "This is not something one who practices *dhyāna* would know.
On the seventh day of the tenth month in the second year of the Taiping Xingguo era, he ascended the hall and said, "Today is the day I shall sever my worldly ties.
He left his patched robe and the wooden clogs he wore behind in the mountains, instructing his disciples to stack blue stones to form a stupa, saying, "In the future..."
The stupa was made red. When I arrived there once more, he had already passed away. He lived for eighty years and sat in meditation for sixty-three summer retreats.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Daoji.
Chan Master Guangyong of Nantaguan:
The Chan Master’s name was Guangyong. He was the son of the Zhang family of Fengcheng in Yuzhang. On the evening his mother nursed him, a divine light illuminated the courtyard.
The horses in the stables were all startled; thus, he was named Guangyong (Surging Light). At the age of seven, he recited the *Shi* and *Li* classics and understood their great principles.

At thirteen, he studied the sutras and treatises, being able to provide exegesis immediately. There was an eminent elder at Kaiyuan Temple whose name has been lost to history, who possessed extraordinary interpretive abilities.

Upon seeing Guangyong, he sighed and said, "A brilliant talent within the Dharma," and bestowed upon him the essential meaning of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*. At that time, [he] looked up in admiration...
Chan Master Shanji resided at Shiting Temple in Nanchang. Yuong’s father served him and received the tonsure.
At the age of nineteen, he went to Xiangzhou to receive the full precepts from Vinaya Master Zai of Shoushan Temple. He then traveled north to visit Linji, who said:
"Your teacher has clear vision, yet you do not serve him; for what purpose do you travel so far? Yung then returned south. For many years he applied himself with diligence.

Previously, whenever anyone came to pay their respects at Shiting, he would invariably ask, "What have you come for? If the visitor replied, "To pay my respects to the Master," he would ask again, "Have you seen the Master?
If they replied, "I have," he would ask, "How is the Master like a donkey? No one among those who came to study was able to answer.
Touei-duei (Huide) also failed to provide a response. Suddenly he questioned Yong (Yongjue). Yong replied, "When Guangyong saw the Master, he did not resemble a Buddha either.
Shiting asked, "If he did not resemble a Buddha, what did he resemble? Yong said, "If there were anything further for him to resemble, how would he differ from a donkey?
Shiting was greatly startled and said, "Both the mundane and the sacred are forgotten; when emotion is exhausted, the essence is revealed. I shall test you with these words."
"Twenty years have passed, yet no one has reached a definitive resolution. Alas! You are truly of keen faculties; you must take this upon yourself. I cannot exhaustively explain it all;
you shall know it for yourself in another day. He pointed at him and said to the people, "This son is a flesh-and-blood Buddha; he can transform others.
After Shiting passed away, Yong burned his third finger as an offering to the Dharma, and then burned his second finger as well.

To repay his parents' kindness: In the first year of the Tianyou era of the pseudo-Tang dynasty, Zhong Chuan, the Prince of Nanping and Regional Commander of Nanchang, received him with full ceremonial courtesy at his residence.
When [Huiyuan] did not rise for him, the prefects and magistrates arrived and likewise he did not rise. Laypeople and monastics gathered in great numbers, yet he still did not rise.
They then petitioned him together, saying, "If you do not rise, it will bring reproach upon the commandery and the counties. Thereupon, having no other choice, he complied.
He succeeded to the Dharma seat at Shiting, and students gathered around him like clouds. In the autumn of the fourteenth year, he returned to Mount Yang.
In the summer of the second year of the Shengyuan era of the Pseudo-Tang dynasty, he passed away without illness. He had lived for eighty-nine years and sat in meditation for seventy summers.
Chan Master Shouchu of Dongshan: The master’s name was Shouchu.

He was born into the Fu clan and was a native of Liangyuan in Fengxiang. As a child, whenever he heard the sound of bells or Buddhist chanting, he would immediately stop eating and sit upright for the entire day.
His mother, Lady Lü, tested him by not feeding him; yet he neither ate nor asked for food. He was sixteen years old.

Kneeling, he requested to leave the household life. Lü granted his request. He followed the śramaṇa Zhishen at Mount Kongtong in Weizhou to have his hair shaved, and then went to Jingzhou Śarīra Monastery to receive full ordination from Vinaya Master Jingyuan.
Having begun his studies in the school of the Vinaya, he would fall asleep while sitting with his scroll in hand.
Leaving behind the regions of Xian and Qin, he traveled south from Xianghan to Changsha, where he sat in summer retreat. When the retreat ended, he went to visit Chan Master Yan at Yunmen.
Yan asked, "Where have you recently departed from? He replied, "I crossed at Cha. Yan asked again, "Where did you spend your summer retreat?
He replied, "Baoci in Hunan. Yan asked, "When did you leave there? He replied, "The twenty-fifth of the eighth month. Yan said, "I let you go."
Three blows of the staff were struck. At first, [Yunyan] was bewildered for a long time. He then asked again, "In my previous response, I saw no fault;
yet I have been granted these blows. Truly, I do not understand. Yunyan rebuked him, saying, "You rice-bag! You are already deliberating over the teachings of Jiangxi and Hunan!

At first, Yunyan silently grasped the meaning and said, "In the future, when it is truly the right time, I shall dwell in a place where there is no human habitation and will not store a single grain of rice."
He provided rice for the monks of the ten directions and departed that very day. Traveling north, he reached the territory of the illegitimate Han dynasty at Xianghan.

In the first year of the Qianyou era, the assembly requested that he reside at Dongshan. He settled there according to the monastic rules and told his students: "Within words there are words; these are called dead words."

Within speech there is no speech; this is called a "live word. Everywhere people possess only the eye that perceives the simultaneous moment of the hen’s peck and the chick’s hatch, yet they do not possess the function of that simultaneous pecking and hatching.
Reaching this point, it is truly difficult to find anyone. They merely cherish remaining unmoved by a single speck of dust and not disturbing a single object.
Seeing things as they are, one speaks: if these types of people are traveling east, west, south, or north, their number is unknown.
To truly break free from the nest and the trap, and to bring life to the eyes of men—this is not to say it does not exist at all, but rather that it is scarce.

They all sit bound by failing to reach the root source, falling into the realm of the shadows and mistakenly taking this for a place of rest. Knowing they have fallen into stagnant water, they dangle with a tailless monkey. Wax...
On the thirtieth day of the month, the drum was already broken and the monkey had fled; his hands and feet were in a frantic scramble, but by then it was too late for regret.
Had he been a true monk (*śramaṇa*), even if he were to die of cold or hunger, he would never have donned that "vulture-stink" cassock.

In the sixth year of the Taiping Xingguo era of our dynasty, the Minister of Revenue, Lord Shi Gongxiang, and the Regional Commander, Lord Zhao, submitted successive memorials [recommending him], stating that he initially possessed the practice of the Way.
He transformed this land and assisted in the holy transformation [of the state]. By imperial decree, he was granted a posthumous title and a purple *kāṣāya* robe to mark his extraordinary virtue.

He dwelt on the mountain for forty years, and his Way spread throughout the world. In the seventh month of the autumn of the first year of the Chunhua era, he passed away while sitting cross-legged without illness.
He had lived eighty-one years and had completed sixty-five summer retreats.

Venerable Master Nanshan Yan, whose Dharma name was Ziyen, was born into the Zheng clan in Tong’an, Quanzhou. At the age of eleven, he left his home and became a novice under the śramaṇa Qiyan at Woxiang Temple in Jianxing.
At seventeen, he received full ordination as a bhikṣu. He then traveled to various regions.
In Luling, he visited the senior monk Yunhuo at Xifeng. Huo was a high-ranking disciple of Chan Master Qingliang Zhiming and a direct descendant of Yunmen.
Emperor Taizong once issued an imperial decree summoning him to the capital, where he was housed in a residence within the Northern Imperial Garden.

After practicing meditative concentration for a long time, he earnestly requested to return to the mountains. The Master stayed with him for five years, attaining a secret realization of the Dharma of the mind.
Upon taking his leave and crossing the Huairen River, there was a dragon that frequently harmed travelers. The Master recited a verse to admonish it, and the dragon immediately departed.
