"Why is he here, beneath Śākyamuni’s assembly, listening to the Dharma? [The Master] said: "He does not contend over self and other. Question:
"What is the Bodhisattva Red-Crested King? [The Master] said: "Why ask this red-headed fellow? Question: "When the body lies horizontal and covers all, it is like..."
"What? [The monk] asked. "Can one still cover it over? Question: "Why did the little snake swallow the snake? The Master said: "What harm is there to the principle? Question:
"At the point where all Buddhas cannot speak, can you, Master, speak? He said: "Tell me, where is there anything that the Holy Ones cannot speak?
Question: "When one encounters a fierce tiger on the road, what then? He said: "A thousand people, ten thousand people—none encounter it."
"You have already encountered it. [The monk] asked, "What is it like when one stays alone on a solitary peak? He replied, "I am idly occupying the seven-bay monks' hall;

who told you to stay alone on a solitary peak? [The monk] asked, "An ancient said, 'If you wish to maintain this matter, you must stand atop the highest mountain peak and walk within the deepest ocean. What is the meaning of this? He replied, "A high peak and a deep ocean."
"The ocean is vast and remote, solitary and perilous. Is it as soft and warm as you are within your inner chambers? He asked again, "The monastic communities (*saṃgha*) are fond of much discussion;
what is the matter regarding those of noble status? He replied, "I want you to know that the Son of Heaven of the Great Tang does not issue written decrees.

Do you understand? His realization was profound and subtle, his practice clearly verified. In responding to stimuli and dealing with things, he transcended all measures and calculations; he was a patriarch of the world.
The Master lived for over eighty years and passed away without illness. Zhang Chong, the military governor of Luzhou, erected a stupa for him on the mountain itself.
The eulogy states: "Dayang Ming'an once commented on the words of Yaoshan, saying: 'High atop the high mountain, the banner cannot be seen.'"
Deeply hidden at the bottom of the sea, it does not sink; his descendants have inherited and followed this, considering themselves to have wondrously grasped its essential meaning.
Yet upon hearing Yunju’s words, they were like a true tiger crouching on the ground and roaring, causing all the beasts to tremble with fear.
Only then did they realize what Ming’an had shown them—it was indeed the tiger of Pei Min. For their sake, I composed this verse: Standing tall atop the high mountain, deep...
Wandering at the bottom of the deep sea, the place where the Way-man walks and stands—whom in the dusty world can vie with him? Without interval, his merit is not established;
he is born into a state of noble dignity. To repay your perverse desires, a single branch of a withered tree flourishes.
*Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks of the Chan Forest*, Scroll Nine and Scroll Ten.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huìhóng of the White Hermitage in the Song Dynasty.
Chan Master Chongyun Hui:

The master’s name was Zhìhuī. He was a native of Xiánqín and was born into the Gāo clan. During his childhood, whenever he went to a monastery, he would invariably stay there as if it were his own home.
When Chan Master Wēn of Guīfēng saw him, he marveled at his character and shaved his head. At the age of twenty, he received full ordination.
Regarding his precepts: he served Chan Master Benren of Baishui in Gaoyang for ten years before returning to the capital of Luoyang.

Finding the mountains and waters of Zhongtan delightful, he built a dwelling there to reside, naming it the Wenshi Monastery (Warmth Chamber). He spent his days performing the work of distributing water and providing medicine, such that no one could fathom the depth of his character.
In the fifth year of the Kaiping era of the Liang dynasty, he suddenly desired to return to Guifeng; as he traveled through the mountains, he was serene and profound.
He went and sat among the rocky crags as he had always done when resting. Looking about, he saw his patched cassock, prayer beads, copper pitcher, and bamboo hat hidden within a stone wall;
upon touching them, they immediately crumbled to pieces. Closing his eyes for a long while, he said, "These were the ritual implements from my previous life.
Consequently, he established a monastery at that site to fulfill his long-held aspiration. Just as he was clearing away the weeds, auspicious clouds emerged from amidst the peaks. Thereupon—
It was named Chongyun (Heavy Clouds). Tigers and leopards retreated. There was a dragon pool that was so treacherous and malevolent it could not be approached.
Daohui supervised the laborers to level and fill it in to create a road; the dragon also moved elsewhere, leaving only clouds and thunder following after him.

Later, Emperor Mingzong of the Tang dynasty heard of this and praised him, granting the temple the name Changxing (Long Prosperity). He served as abbot for over forty years. The Regional Commander Wang Yan...
Chao Weishi once traveled with Huī and wished to become a śramaṇa. Huī looked at him intently and said, "Your worldly ties are deep;
you shall serve as the protective wall for my family. Later, Yan Chao indeed governed Yongxing and observed the rites due to a disciple.

In the summer of the third year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty, [Huī] went to Yongxing to part from Yan Chao, entrusting him with the protection of the Dharma. Yan Chao wept and said, "Sir, you have truly..."
"Can you bear to abandon your disciple? Hui smiled and said, "Even if we were to borrow a thousand years, this would be but a single parting.
On the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month, he wrote a verse: "I have a small cottage, Built for me by my parents.
I have lived within it for eighty years, And lately I have noticed its decay. I had intended to move elsewhere long ago, But such matters involve likes and dislikes; I shall wait until it collapses."

At that time, as there was no obstruction for either of them, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away. He had lived in the world for eighty-four years and spent sixty-four summer retreats in meditation.
Initially, when Huī was at Zhongtān, there was a sick bhikṣu whom the community had cast out due to his evil condition.
The bhikṣu lamented, saying, "I have white leprosy due to my past karma; Master, could you wash and massage me? Huī performed this service without any expression of difficulty. Suddenly—

There was a divine light and an extraordinary fragrance. Just as [the disciples] were marveling at this, it suddenly vanished. Upon returning to examine the scabs of the sores, they too were permeated with an extraordinary fragrance.
—Master Chan Shiliang of Rui Long.
The Chan Master’s name was Youzhang. He was the nephew of the Tang Prime Minister Xiahou Zhi.

At the beginning of the Dazhong era, his uncle, the Minister of Works (Sikong), went out to govern Guangling. Zhang was then seven years old; while visiting Huizhao Temple, he heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* being recited.
Thereupon, he knelt before his uncle and requested to leave the household life. His uncle hesitated, whereupon Zhang ceased eating and drinking.
Having received permission, he followed Master Huiyuan to shave his head. Ten years later, at the age of twenty-five, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
He then traveled to various regions and arrived at Gao’an, where he met Bai Shui; he also visited Mount Shu, and both of these great elders esteemed and approved of him.
In the thirteenth year of the Xiantong era, he encountered Master Teng-teng at Jiangling. Teng-teng entrusted him with these words: "You..."
He went to Tiantai to seek a place of stillness in which to dwell, staying wherever he encountered peace.
Later, he met the Venerable Hanzhan, who patted him and said, "Forty years from now, there will be a Bodhisattva beneath Mount Jingshan who shall rule over Jiangnan;
at that time, my Dharma will flourish. Having said this, Hanzhan departed. Daizhang then proceeded to Mount Tiantai and established Foji Temple in Jing'an Township.
At Tangyuan, he already fulfilled the prophecy of "flying up. He later resided at Yilongyuan. In the fourth year of the Zhonghe era, famine and pestilence ravaged the region of Zhedong;

Chang collected and buried several thousand corpses across the three prefectures of Wenzhou, Taizhou, and Mingzhou. At that time, he was called the Great Being of Compassionate Magnanimity (Beizeng Dashi).
During the Qianning era, Xuefeng once met him and bestowed upon him a *zōnglǜ* whisk before departing.
In the third year of the Tianyou era, Qian Shangfu dispatched the envoy Tong Jian to enter the mountains with robes and incense to invite him to his residence.

He was appointed as the Great Master Zhide and lodged at the Gongchen Monastery. Shangfu questioned him on the Way day and night; when he requested leave to return to the mountains, Shangfu would not permit it.
He then established Rui Long Temple within the city to welcome him. Zen practitioners flocked there like clouds.
Furthermore, this accorded with his "Dumb-Dumb" (Hanhan) saying. He once said to his disciples: "In years past, I traveled beyond the Yangtze River, through Lingnan, Jing, and Hu.
There was no monastery of a master where I did not go to inquire and seek instruction. This was solely for the purpose of gathering together with you all today."

I understand. Each of you must know the destination. However, throughout all quarters there is ultimately no divergent teaching; it simply instructs people to cease their frantic minds and stop seeking from others.
Just follow the situation and let things be as they are—yet there is not even a "reality" to be let be. Enjoy yourself according to the occasion.
There is no time when it could be used. Even if you were to show compassion and speak with bitter words, you still cannot call day night;

even with further skillful means, you ultimately cannot point east and call it west. Should you somehow be able to do so, that would merely be a supernatural manifestation of a marvel and has nothing to do with me.
As for those who merely parrot words, they fail to reflect upon themselves and recognize their error, seeking instead to pluck [flowers] from the empty sky.
Flowers. Can you take the moon from the waves and bring it back to your own mind? Today, each of you should reflect in solitude.
If you suddenly agree, only then will you know that the old man of Rui Long had no choice but to go to such great lengths. Do you agree?
In the fourth month of the second year of Tiānchéng (the Dīnghái year), Zhāng requested a burial site from the Imperial Father. The Imperial Father smiled and said, "The Master is already like this."

He dispatched Lu Renzhang to select a site in Xiguan to construct a stupa. When the stupa was completed, Renzhang went to take leave of Shangfu (the "Venerable Father"), entrusting him with the protection of the Dharma and the relief of the people.
He then returned and sat peacefully until his transformation [death]. He had lived for eighty-seven years and had spent seventy summers in seated meditation.
By imperial decree, the name of the Tiantai mountain retreat was changed from Yilong to Yiji ("Hidden Trace").
Chan Master Linyangduan, whose name was Zhiduān, was the son of the Yu family of Fuzhou. He received his monastic training at Nanjian Temple.
At the age of twenty-four, he went to visit Chan Master An guo Hongtao. A monk asked him, "Among the myriad phenomena, how does one’s true body alone manifest? Hongtao—
Dongshan raised one finger. The monk withdrew, bewildered, yet Dongshan suddenly attained awakening.
That night, he went to see Xuefeng Taoguang and said, "Today, upon seeing the Master raise one finger, I have come to understand the Master's point. Taoguang asked, "What principle have you seen?
Dongshan also raised one finger. Taoguang laughed and sent him away. Subsequently, Dongshan resided at Linyang, where he was asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?"
He said: "A wooden horse gallops like smoke; a stone man cannot catch up. A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? He replied, "Bamboo chopsticks: one for each, in pairs.
A monk arrived at the abbot’s quarters at night with his patched robe drawn over his head. The monk suddenly pulled back the robe and asked, "Who is there?
The monk replied, "It is so-and-so. The abbot said, "Sugarcane from Quanzhou; betel nuts on the ship. The monk did not understand.
Duan stared with wide eyes and asked, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not. Duan said, "If you were to understand, you would sweep away the five aggregates and swallow up the ten directions.
He further told his disciples: "The Buddha-dharma is not so manifold; it is simply that the single truth of both ordinary people and sages still involves the barrier of views.

Where views exist, one is an ordinary person; where emotions are forgotten, one is a Buddha. In the teachings, this is called 'dependent origination according to nature' (chengxing yuanqi). Thus, he looked down...

In looking up and advancing, in bending and stretching, there is not a single dharma that can be transformed. Since there are the characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, how could one possibly engage in theoretical discourse within the gate of our Patriarch?
On the eighth day of the eighth month in the first year of the Kaibao era, he composed a verse:
"On the second day of the second month next year, I shall temporarily part from you. I will burn my ashes and scatter them upon the Long River; do not occupy the land of a donor. Dao...
The common people all recorded this in writing. On the twenty-eighth day of the first month of the following year, the people of the commandery entered the mountain.
On the first day of the second month, the Prefect also arrived. His attendants, runners, and clerks scouted the area, and for two nights it was as crowded as a marketplace.

On the second day, after the meal, he ascended the seat with dignity and recounted the beginning and end of his journey; then he took leave of the assembly. An elder named Yingyuan stepped forward from the crowd and asked:

[The assembly] said: "The clouds grieve and the mists darken; the great assembly is choked with sobs. We have not yet had our leave-taking; we pray you grant us one word. Duan [Changzong] extended one foot. [The assembly] stepped forward and said: "If the Dharma-mirror does not appear in this land, where else will the Precious Moon shine? Duan said: "It is not within your realm. [The assembly] said: "If it is so, then as bubbles arise and bubbles perish, they return to the water; as masters depart and masters arrive, it is the fundamental source. Duan said: "You have spoken well. He then returned to his quarters. The next day, he passed away. His disciples wished to erect a stupa for him, but Duan said: "I am a wandering monk; I have no fixed abode.

Do not trouble yourselves to build a stupa. His disciples said: "We wish to record your life and deeds to transmit them to future generations. Duan said: "I have neither life nor death; how can there be deeds? You must not speak of me to others. He then composed a verse himself: "Thirty years ago, I left home; In thirty years, I have returned. The white clouds and blue mountains— Where is my body? Having finished the verse, he passed away. His disciples then built a stupa for him at Mount Shuangfeng. It is said that when Duan was first ordained, he studied under Master Baizhang at Dongshan. Later, he visited Master Mazu at Gonggong Mountain. When he asked about the meaning of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West, Mazu struck him with his staff and drove him out. He then went to study under National Teacher Huairang. One day, while Huairang was tending the ox, Duan asked: "What is the ox? Huairang replied: "You do not even see the ox; how can you ask what the ox is? Duan said: "I do not see the ox. Huairang said: "You do not even see the ox; how can you say you do not see it? Duan was greatly enlightened by these words. He then stayed at Huairang’s side for several years before departing to travel. He eventually settled at Mount Shuangfeng, where he lived for over forty years. His teaching style was simple and direct, and he did not rely on verbal explanations. His followers numbered over a thousand. During the Tianfu era of the Tang dynasty, he was posthumously titled Great Master Zhenji. His teachings were compiled into the *Recorded Sayings of Master Duan*. It is said that whenever he preached the Dharma, the earth would tremble. Thus, he was known as the "Earth-Trembling Master. His remains are enshrined at Mount Shuangfeng in Jiangxi Province. To this day, his legacy continues to inspire practitioners throughout the world.
Changduan made a sound like a sigh. After exchanging several more words with the monks, he returned to his quarters.

At the hour of Hai (9–11 p.m.), he asked the assembly, "On what day did the World-Honored One pass into parinirvāṇa? They replied, "On the fifteenth day of the second month at the hour of Zi (11 p.m.–1 a.m.).
Changduan said, "Today, before the hour of Zi," and then he passed away peacefully. He had lived for seventy-eight years and sat in meditation for sixty.
Summer. Chan Master Jingqin of Shuangfeng.
The master’s name was Jingqin. He was a native of Yizhou and born into the Zheng clan. Having become a monk at a young age, he resided at Mount Emei.

At Heishui Temple, he traveled south from Shu as far as Shaoshi and Yunmen, where he attained the Dharma-method. He immediately established a vihāra beneath the Two Peaks to reside in, naming it Xingfu.
On the day he opened the hall for formal teaching, Chan Master Kuangzhen personally attended to witness and certify his realization.
A monk asked, "Pindola makes offerings throughout the four worlds; does he do so everywhere? Qian replied, "It is like the moon entering the water.
The monk asked again, "How is it that one acts without confusion? Qian replied, "Before the Hall of Bright Moon, jade dew hangs down; within the Palace of Crystal, true pearls are scattered.
Thereupon, Kuangzhen considered this to be similar to his own teaching and treated him with increased reverence. (Taiping Xingguo Era)
In the third month of the second year, he said to his disciples, "I shall not remain for long. You should construct a 'egg-stupa' (ovata).
On the twenty-third day of the fifth month, the work was completed. Yanqing said, "Tomorrow at the hour of the rat, I shall depart.

When the appointed time arrived, it so happened that Chan Master Yunmen Shuang and the elders Wenmen Shunfeng and others were engaged in a night conversation. The attendant announced that it was the third watch. Yanqing asked for incense.
He cremated [the remains]. With palms joined, he passed away. He had lived in the world for sixty-eight years and sat in meditation for forty-eight summer retreats.
Regarding Chan Master Jiupeng Quan: his name was Daoquan.
He was born into the Liu family and was a native of Anfu in Jizhou. Even as a youth, he abandoned his home to become a monk under the Master.
He served Master Shisi, under whom he shaved his head and received full ordination. Having heard of the reputation of Chan Master Huilun of Changsha, Shisi went to see him once.
At that time, the Ma family had usurped control of Jingchu, which bordered Jiankang. Zhen, being over twenty years of age, formed a friendship with others and braved the dangers to travel there.
It happened that the Ma family was extinguished and Liu Yan took possession of the land, appointing Wang Kui—
Liu Yan was acting as his deputy in charge of the matter. When Sengquan and his companions were seen by Yuan Kui, Kui suspected them of being spies from the Jiangbiao region;

he bound them and intended to throw them into the river. Sengquan remained composed and showed no fear. Kui found this extraordinary and asked Daolun, "This practitioner regards death as looking at the tip of his own nose.
What kind of person can be so capable? Daolun replied, "He is surely one who has forgotten his own body for the sake of the Dharma."

Having heard of the old monk’s reputation for emptiness, I have come specifically to resolve my doubts. Daokui explained the matter to him with increasing respect, but Huichuan departed with an air of arrogance.

He remained with Yan-shou for ten years; after Yan-shou passed away, Huichuan returned to Mount Lu. At the beginning of the Qian-de era, he established a hermitage at the foot of Niu-shou Peak to the southeast.
In the fifth year of the Kai-bao era, Lin Ren-zhao, the Regional Commander of Hongzhou, invited him to reside at Jiu-peak and bestowed upon him the title of Great Śramaṇa.
A monk asked, "I have heard it said that you, Master, personally met Yanshou; is this true? Quan replied, "Has the wheat ripened in front of the mountain yet?
The monk asked, "Is there still Buddha-dharma within Mount Jiufeng? Quan replied, "There is. The monk asked, "What is the Buddha-dharma of Mount Jiufeng?
Quan replied, "The large stones are large; the small stones are small. The monk asked, "What is the study [of the Way]? Quan replied, [as before].
Regarding the person themselves: Quan said, "The bed is narrow, so one lies down first; the porridge is thin, so one sits down later.
When asked about the ancient saying, "It is not the wind moving, nor is it the banner moving," Quan replied, "Tomorrow there will be a market at the crossroads.
In the first year of the Taiping Xingguo era, Zhang Nanjin, the Governor of Nankang, moved him to reside at Guizong. On the second day of the eleventh month of the second year of the Yongxi era—

On the night of the eighteenth day, he sat in the full lotus posture, took leave of the assembly, and passed away. He had lived in the world for fifty-six years and spent thirty summer retreats in meditation.
This was Chan Master Zhong of Guiyang.
The Chan Master’s name was Huizhong. He was a native of Quanzhou and belonged to the Chen clan. In his youth, he received full ordination at Guiyang Mountain.
Later, he traveled to Huazhou to visit the practitioner Daoyi of Cao’an, where he remained for over ten years. Upon returning south to his former mountain, he secluded himself in profound obscurity.
At the beginning of the Huichang era, an imperial edict was issued throughout the empire to abolish the teachings of Śākyamuni. When Emperor Xuanzong ascended the throne, he issued a decree...
He restored [the temple] once more. Zhong then smiled and said, "Those who ascend to the realm of the immortals do not necessarily receive the registers of ordination;

those who attain Buddhahood do not necessarily require the status of a monk. Thereupon, he ceased eating after midday and practiced dhyāna without opening his eyes. He did not leave the mountain for thirty years, revealing his realization through three verses which say:
"Only after the snowfall does one know the steadfast nature of the pines and cypresses; Only when the clouds disperse can one see the division between the Ji and Huai rivers. It is not because..."
The Lord of the World has ordered me back to secular life; how can one distinguish a flock of chickens from a flock of cranes? For many years I have been tossed about in the dust and grime;
though I wear the *kāṣāya*, I am not yet a monk. Today I return to fulfill my original vow; it does no harm to let my hair grow while awaiting the lighting of the lamps.
Though appearances may change, the Way remains constant; though one blends with worldly customs, the source of the mind does not grow dim.
Try reading the verses on Sudhana’s pilgrimage—how could he have been considered a mere śramaṇa at that time? He said to his disciples: "As for sentient beings who cannot attain liberation..."
"It is merely a matter of emotional entanglement. To awaken to the Way is easy; to clarify the Way is difficult. The questioner asked, "How can one attain clarity regarding the Way?
Zhong replied, "Simply shed your emotional views, and the Way will clarify itself of its own accord. Now, as for the word 'clarify' (ming), it means 'to trust.

It is like a snake-handler who, trusting in the power of his incantations and the power of his medicines, can coil and play with snakes, even handling them within the folds of his robe without difficulty. Yet, he does not yet know the actual power of those incantations and medicines."
[The disciples] were terrified and fled, but [the Master] simply observed his own mind with clarity, and their emotional attachments were immediately shattered.

As for those who now harbor a thousand doubts and myriad anxieties and cannot put this into practice, they are those who have not yet seen their own minds. Suddenly, after requesting incense to be burned, he sat peacefully and passed away.
His entire body was interred to the east of the stupa of Master Wuliao. Several years later, the stupa suddenly split open on its own, revealing a continuous flight of stairs.

It was over ten feet tall. As the temple was about to move it, the monks examined it; that night, while in a state of meditative stillness, they saw Chan Master Wuliao, who said, "There is no need to move it further.
It shall now serve as the true-body relics for the two sages, Shen and Chen. Wuliao was born into the Shen clan and once met Mazu.
The encomium states: In recent times, there have been few such elders who have sacrificed their bodies for the sake of the Dharma. Observing his words, they are all concise yet clear;
examining his practice, it was sincere and unadulterated. Thus, he was able to manifest clear and manifest verification at the moment of death and rebirth.
Yet, from the beginning, we have never heard of him presiding over ten thousand people or receiving the four types of offerings.
Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks of the Chan Forest, Scroll Ten;
Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks of the Chan Forest, Scroll Eleven.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huìhóng of the White Hermitage in the Song Dynasty.
Chan Master Dongshan Cong:
The master’s name was Xiaocong. Born into the Du clan, he was a native of Qujiang in Shaoyou Prefecture. In his youth, he received full ordination at Yunmen Temple.

His skull was remarkably prominent, and he wore a single robe through both winter and summer. He traveled extensively throughout the Jing and Chu regions, becoming thoroughly acquainted with various monastic communities and serving alongside the assembly.
[The Master] sighed. There was no one who understood him. While he was at Yunju, it was reported that the Monk Sengqie was in Weiyang.
Thereupon, a Chan practitioner stood up and asked, "Since you are the Sengqie of Sizhou, for what reason have you appeared in Yangzhou?
Cong Posuo came from the side; the assembly playfully urged him to respond. Cong said, "A gentleman loves wealth, but takes it by righteous means. The assembly looked on and laughed.
When Master Xiang of Lotus Peak heard these words, he said in astonishment, "Are there still descendants of Yunmen?
That night, he spread out his sitting mat and prostrated toward Yunju; thus, he became renowned throughout the monastic community. Later, he went to Dongshan to rely upon Chan Master Quan.
In the second year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, Quan moved to reside at Qixian and appointed Cong to succeed him on the seat.
Guo succeeded Wen-shu Ying-tian, the Chan Master Zhen; Zhen was Yuan-ming Mi, a fourth-generation descendant of Yunmen.
Whenever a monk came with a question, Cong would glare at him with wide-open eyes and say, "I possess the art of striking tigers; you do not understand it—go away! One day, he himself carried...
Chaideng was ascending the mountain. A monk met him and asked, "Since you dwell on the mountain, why are you carrying firewood down from the mountain?
He replied, "One needs firewood to burn even on the mountain. At that time, Yunju Shun, an old man, was young; he was intelligent and was sent to beg for alms at Ezu.
A layman asked, "How was it before the ancient mirror had been polished? Dōgen replied, "Black as lacquer. The layman asked, "How is it after it has been polished?
Dōgen replied, "It reflects heaven and reflects earth. The layman laughed and said, "Has the Master not come from Dongshan himself? Shun remained silent and felt ashamed.
He galloped back and recounted this to Cōng. Cōng spoke in place of the former words, saying, "This is not far from Hanyang.
He spoke in place of the latter words, saying, "Before the Yellow Crane Tower is the Parrot Isle. Thereupon Shùn realized its meaning. Cōng addressed the assembly, saying:
"The entire Great Canon of the Teachings is the character 'this' (之). The Patriarch’s coming from the West is the character 'right' (右) [or 'hand' (手)]. What is the correct meaning? Liáng...
Jiuzhi said: "The sky is clear, so I have roofed the house; taking advantage of the leisure, I have harvested the grain. Having paid the king’s tax, I beat my belly and sing aloud.
He personally planted ten thousand pines on the eastern ridge while reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The people of the mountains named that ridge "Vajra. While he was planting the pines, Master Bao arrived; at that time, Cong came personally from the Fifth Patriarch.
Question: "How do you express the phrase regarding 'ascending the ridge'? Shi said, "It would kill people with its urgency.

Cung, holding his hoe, scolded him, saying, "Where did you get this habit of generating interpretations based on mere words? When asked about ascending the ridge, you immediately say it would 'kill people with its urgency.

If that were so, the Buddha-dharma would instead become something merely spread abroad. Baoshou requested Cung to provide a substitute statement for him. Cung said, "Why not say, 'It would kill people with its gasping breath'? Xiaoyao asked.
"The ridge is here. Where is the Vajra? Cong pointed and said, "This single pine tree was planted by this old monk myself.
Formerly, when Xu Gongshi, a Minister of the Ministry of Justice, was serving as the Governor of Nanchang, he passed by Lotus Peak and heard of Master Xiang.
Xu said, "The practitioner Cong is in Jiangxi; let us go seek him out. This monk is the eye of men and gods. Thus spoke Lord Xu.

Upon his arrival, he heard that Yongcong was following the tradition of the Shanjia school. He composed a poem to send him, saying: His speech is entirely unhindered; He treads high upon the tracks of the Patriarchs.
At night he sits upon the cloud-reaching rocks; In spring he plants rain-soaked pines. The mirror divides the candles of the golden hall; The mountain answers the bell of the moonlit tower.
If anyone asks about the meaning of the Westward Journey, He faces the distant peaks from within the empty hall. The eighth day of the sixth month, the eighth year of the Tiānshèng era.
One day, he manifested illness and observed a fast for seven days without eating. He gathered the monastics and the laity and said, "As for the Dharma seat, you must let Zibao maintain it.
Thereupon, he recounted his realization of the Dharmakāya to his disciples and spoke this verse: "Do not be in such a hurry when studying Chan and the Way;

Ask until you have penetrated the Dharmakāya hidden within the Northern Dipper. I am now old and decrepit, exceedingly frail and weak; I lack the strength to engage in further discussion with others. Only..."
One who possesses a hoe knows my Way; when planting pines, he ascends again to Vajra. Having finished speaking, he passed away.

This is not the universal path of the world. When you see the establishment of the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan), you divide them into the "substance of the mystery," the "phrase of the mystery," and the "mystery within the mystery.
Yet, regarding the three essentials of the ultimate teaching (Yao), why do you alone fail to analyze them?

You recently criticized scholars for being mired in intellectual views and unable to awaken to the Way; yet when explaining that a single phrase contains these three essentials, you instead cite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The meanings of the *Śūraṅgama*, the *Vimalakīrti*, and other such texts establish this: the principle of nature is boundless, and the phenomena of events are boundless.

They interpenetrate without being confused, and they blend without becoming one. Why, then, should one doubt that within a single word, the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials are not fully present?

Furthermore, are the exposition of principle and the exposition of events not themselves forms of knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*)? Moreover, since the scriptural vehicles already embody this intent, why should one need to establish [them] anew?

In the Zen school, those of old who possessed a temperament that overwhelmed others would disparage the scriptural teachings as mere intellectual views (*jñāna-dṛṣṭi*), yet when their own school’s principles were not fully understood, they would again cite such intellectual views as proof. This is the first error.

What do you mean by saying that Baolin’s three phrases do not recognize the "live word"? I say: Baolin truly grasped the essential intent of Yunmen. Now, a phrase within a phrase is called a "dead word."
Within speech there is no speech; this is called a "live phrase. When asked about the school of Deva, he replied, "It is the non-Buddhists.

When asked about the "razor-sharp sword," he replied, "It is the keen blade. When asked whether the teachings of the Patriarchs and the scriptures are the same or different, he replied, "They are not the same.

Thus, [if one understands] these as literal words, one falls into the trap of dead language and becomes ensnared within the confines of verbal expression. Now, if we examine these three responses, to call them "speech" is illogical, yet to call them "not speech" is likewise untenable.

To say that [these teachings] are all "live phrases" suited to the capacities of those who come to them is an error of the ancients; this is the second fault. What do you mean by dividing [the self] into two kinds?
Do you not realize the difficulty with which the Sage established his words? It is said in a verse of the World-Honored One: "The *ālayavijñāna* is subtle;
its habitual tendencies are like a torrential stream. Fearing that one might confuse the real with the unreal, I have never openly expounded it. By this, [he shows...]
Regarding the eighth consciousness: if one says it is real, there is the concern that [the listener] will be deluded into thinking it lacks self-nature;

if one says it is not real, there is the concern that [the listener] will be deluded into thinking it is subject to annihilation. Therefore, it is said: "I do not openly expound this. The difficulty lies in the formulation of the words.
To provide instruction for Ānanda, the principle that the false is itself the true is simply stated as "two kinds of erroneous cultivation": the first is...

To take the攀緣心 (pān-yuán xīn, the mind that clings to objects) as one's own nature is the second error. Furthermore, the essence of consciousness is perfectly luminous and capable of giving rise to all conditions;

yet, that which is left behind by these conditions is still not clearly distinguished. This is because [the author] was unwilling to interrupt the flow of the discourse, fearing that within a single teaching two interpretations might arise.

Chan Master Fuchang Shanshi, whose name was Weishan, was a man of unknown origins. He resided at Fuchang Temple in Jingnan and was a dharma successor of Chan Master Mingjiao Kuan.
As a person, he was reverent and dignified, and he held the Way of the Dharma in profound esteem. When he first took up residence there, the monastery consisted of only some ten dilapidated rooms.

The community consisted of several dozen monks. Morning incense and evening lamps were maintained with care; when he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, it was as if he were facing a thousand-fold assembly.

All that is required for the sustenance of a Zen monastery was prepared in full readiness. When guests arrived, he received them with solemn reverence. It took more than ten years before his disciples finally gathered to the number of about a hundred.
Whenever a visitor came, Master Shan would invariably examine and test them. There was one monk who had only just entered the abbot’s quarters...

Hua-yuan drew a circle and presented it as auspicious. Shan-he said, "Stop you, you wild fox spirit! The monk then made a gesture as if throwing something. Shan-he pressed him with his foot three times.
Shan-he said, "A reed arrow! The monk bowed, and Shan-he struck him. He then asked the monk, "Where have you recently come from?
The monk replied, "Da-bie. Shan-he said, "In Da-bie for how long? The monk replied, "Three years. Shan-he said: [The text continues with the dialogue regarding the monk's realization.]
The Water-Ox—what person can match him? [The Master] said: "I have never touched so much as a single grain of his rice.

[The monk] replied: "Anzhou. [The Master] asked: "What thing comes in such a manner? [The monk] replied: "Please, Master, discern it for me. [The Master] said: "Before the donkey, behind the horse."

Shanshan struck him. The monk was speechless. Shanshan shouted, saying, "You blind donkey! Even if you were to kill ten thousand of them, what crime would there be?
Go to the hall! There was a monk who called himself "Reflecting Bodhidharma. As soon as he entered the abbot’s quarters, he held up his sitting cloth and said, "If it is spread out..."

this will not hinder anything and will prevent you from being troubled by interference. What is the principle of “paying according to one's means” with “just a little”? Simply cut off both extremes.
Regarding all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, the sentiments of ordinary and sage beings are exhausted; the essence reveals the true permanence, and fact and principle are non-dual.
This is precisely the Buddha of Suchness (*tathatā*). If one can be thus, then every dharma is without dependence;

To have an insight that merely penetrates the subtle is not called 'seeing the Way. One must investigate authentically and realize authentically. The Great King Yama does not fear [mere words]."
[The author] speaks much.

The commentary says: "Those who do not wish to contend over empty breath within the realm of outward forms, but strive solely to achieve real efficacy beyond the bounds of words and intentions—this is the discourse of this dull old man.
As I observe the Divine Cauldron (Shendǐng), it is nearly equal to this statement; it has attained the Way."
At that time, he was not yet mature. He lived in seclusion on Mount Nanyue for twenty years, after which he assumed the position of abbot.

Another twenty years passed before he finally opened the hall to preach the Dharma. Yet all these events arose through external circumstances and were truly not his own intention; they were like the moon traveling through the sky at night.
He proceeded spontaneously until he reached a place of sweet, withered, and austere simplicity, thereby fulfilling his long-held aspiration.
By dwelling among the forest thickets for the remainder of his natural life, he was able to emulate his teacher.
Chan Master Gushan Chong: The master’s name was Xingchong. His place of origin is unknown. Initially, he resided at Ba’en Temple in Fuzhou; later, he resided at Gushan Temple in Tanzhou.
He was a successor of Chan Master Baofu Zhan, who was a direct grandson of Xuefeng. Chong said to his disciples:
The disciple said: "Though I am not present, I have never failed to act for the sake of my brothers.

If you truly understand how to repay this debt of gratitude—that is, how to act as a human being—I shall grant you release from conceptual thoughts and intellectual understanding regarding the field of the five aggregates. If you cannot yet fulfill this obligation, you must still wait to repay it;

only when you open these two flaps of skin [your mouth] will you truly be a human being. I guarantee that you have not yet emerged from the realm of conceptual thoughts and intellectual understanding."
The ancients called this "the livelihood of ghosts. You are a guest beneath the frog’s robe.
If you wish to attain swift resonance, then right now, standing as you are, realize and verify it; what fault could there be in that?
If not, and your faculties and thoughts are hesitant and slow, then for the time being, investigate and seek it out day and night. Suddenly, one day you will see it; do not hesitate further.
A little is enough. Yet you can further investigate and exhaustively penetrate this until you reach even the brothels and wine shops;
whether things are defiled or pure, good or evil, observe them with what you see and compare them to the Teaching—they are all entirely within this realm. To enter it is to enter the Vinaya.
If you were to see even a single phenomenon as small as a hair’s breadth that did not accord with this reality, I would call that the cataract of ignorance.
You must directly fail to perceive any dharma as being a separate entity; only then will you attain perfect completeness.

Reaching this point, you can further exercise mastery over the turning and casting [of phenomena], such that their opening and closing leave no trace or seam. It is like water entering water, fire entering fire, wind entering wind, and space entering space.
If you can act thus, you may directly draw a single sword and sever the heads of all people under heaven.
The net of doubt is exactly like that of non-action. Thus the ancients said: "When great functions arise in profusion, every movement is entirely true.
If there were such a person who reached such a state, who would dare to step forward and speak of right or wrong?
Why is this? Such a person is a true man; they transcend all limitations and break through cause and effect, remaining unbound by anything anywhere.
People cannot attain it. If you, brothers, can act in this way, then it will suffice. If you have not yet reached such a state, you must simply give with sincerity;
do not speak or breathe recklessly, lest you sink back down for immeasurable kalpas. Do not let it come to such a time.
He then said, "I speak of repaying kindness; I do not speak of it.
Zan remarked: "Master Dongshan Qingbing composed the *Chengxin Tang Lu* (Record of the Hall of Clarified Mind), which records the words and phrases of Master Chong. One should savor them closely."
His bone and spirit were no less than those of Yantou; it is a pity that we cannot see more of him.

At the beginning of the Chongning era, Chong arrived at Gushan, where the stupas and burial mounds could not be distinguished and his deeds had fallen into ruin, leaving nothing for investigation. Sitting there and sighing deeply, he composed this verse:
Having traveled the ten li of pines in Xiangxi, I stand before the gate and count the various peaks. Nowhere can the traces of Master Chong be found.
"Spring mud beneath the courtyard reveals tiger tracks.
Master Yuanzhao of Huilin Monastery was named Zongben.
He was of the Guan clan and a native of Wuxi, Changzhou. By nature, he was upright and straightforward.

He had few ornaments and his appearance was robust and full. His speech was free from flowery elaboration. At the age of nineteen, he took Master Daosheng of Yong’an at Chengtian Monastery in Suzhou as his teacher.

At that time, Daosheng’s reputation for the Way was so weighty that those who sought refuge in the monastic community gathered there like clouds. [Zhaozhou] wore tattered clothes and kept a dirty face;
he handled the mortar and pestle and managed the cooking fires to provide for his master. At night, he would enter the room to inquire about the Way. Daosheng said, "A *dhūta* bears..."
"Are you not weary of the many hardships? Are you also exhausted? He replied, "If one were to abandon even a single dharma, it could not be called the fulfillment of bodhi.

Since I truly desire to realize it through bodily witness in this very life, how could I dare speak of weariness? Shengyin marveled at him. Ten years later, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He served him diligently for three years before taking his leave to travel and seek instruction from various masters. Upon first arriving at Jingde Monastery in Chizhou, he visited Master Yihuai.
Under the Master’s words, he attained realization, though none among the assembly were aware of it. He once served as an attendant; however, he was prone to sleeping and would snore loudly.
Those who heard this grew weary of him and reported it to Yihuai. Yihuai laughed and said, "This man is the banner of diligence in my house."
"You all should rely upon him in the future; do not speak of this much. The assembly was then struck with awe.
When Master Huai moved his residence to Tiantai Monastery in Yue and Jianfu Monastery in Changzhou, Yuanben followed him in both instances.

At the beginning of the Zhìpíng era, Master Huai retired to Shèngshòu Monastery on Wújiāng. When Commissioner Lí Fùguī visited Master Huai, they conversed late into the night, saying: "The Dharma of Ruìguāng..."
The seat was vacant, and it was hoped that a monk of the Way might take charge of it. Huai-zhi said, "None surpasses this practitioner.
Once he arrived at Rui-guang, he gathered the assembly and struck the drum; however, the drum repeatedly fell, spinning and vibrating with a thunderous sound.

The crowd retreated in alarm, but a monk stepped forward and cried out, "This is an auspicious sign that the Dharma-thunder of this Master shall shake the earth! Suddenly, the monk vanished from sight. From then on...

This Dharma assembly flourished daily until the congregation reached five hundred people. Chen Gongxiang, the Governor of Hangzhou, earnestly invited him to the two monasteries of Chengtian and Xingjiao;
although he wished to go, the people of Suzhou urged him to stay even more fervently. Furthermore, Jingci Monastery requested him with great persistence, saying:
"We beg you to lend us your presence for three years to plant the seeds of merit for this region. We dare not detain you for long. Benchao replied: "I shall do so."
Who would not wish to cultivate merit? The people of Suzhou understood his intention and permitted him to go there; the students there were twice as numerous as those at Ruiwang Monastery.
Subsequently, the people of Suzhou requested that he choose between the two monasteries of Wanshou and Longhua to reside in, and more than a thousand people came to welcome him.
He said, "I first borrowed my teacher for three years; now nine years have passed. By right, he ought to be returned. I wish to take him back.
The Magistrate of Hangzhou dispatched a County Magistrate with soldiers and attendants to guard him, so [the monk] did not dare to take him away.

In the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, he entrusted the Daochang Monastery to his disciple Shanben and resided at the Ruipeng Hermitage. When the people of Suzhou heard of this, they plotted to seize it.
Fearing that his strength would not suffice, he wished to depart but did not yet dare. At that time, Zeng Gong Xiaoxu, a Court Attendant, happened to be in Suzhou;
having once sought the Way from Yuanben and attained its essential core, he went to visit him at the hermitage.

He prepared a boat at the river crossing, and once he had taken his leave and departed, Yuanben saw him off as he boarded. Amidst conversation and laughter, Yuanben carried him back on board to comfort the people of Suzhou.
He reflected on this and returned to Fuzhen Yuan on Mount Qionglung; at that time, he was sixty-three years old.
Not long thereafter, Emperor Shenzhong reorganized the sixty-four cloisters of Xiangguosi Temple into eight, consisting of two Chan and six Vinaya (Lü) schools.

The high-ranking official Liang Congzheng was appointed to oversee the affairs. The abbot of Benzhushan Huelin was summoned by imperial post; once he arrived, an envoy was dispatched to inquire after his well-being for three days.
An edict then ordered him to expound the Dharma at the gate of the temple. A multitude of ten thousand people prostrated themselves in veneration, and the dharma assembly was exceptionally sublime.
It was believed that Maitreya had descended from heaven to the human realm. The following day, he was summoned for an audience at the Yanhe Hall.

The officials had him practice the ceremonial protocols before leading him in. Once the audience began and the "Mountains Cry" (shanhū) greeting was concluded, he ascended the hall and was granted a seat;

he immediately sat down with his legs crossed in the full lotus position (*paryaṅka*). The attendants looked at one another in astonishment, yet he remained composed. When tea was served, he raised the cup and took a long draught. Furthermore—
As Dao-han was departing, the Emperor asked him at which monastery he had received his training. He replied, "Chengtian and Yong'an.

The Emperor rejoiced in his honest analogy and, as the Chan school was then flourishing, deemed it appropriate that he should skillfully expound its guiding principles. After Dao-han had retired, the Emperor watched him with his eyes until he was out of sight.

He said to his attendants, "This is a monk of true merit and wisdom. On the day of Shangyuan, when the imperial carriage visited Xiangguo Temple, the master remained among the assembly of Chan practitioners and did not go out to welcome the Emperor.
Honoring the Emperor’s wise appreciation, he propagated Buddhist affairs throughout the capital and the four quarters.
In the year of Great Faith (1084), when Emperor Shenzong passed away, [Fozhao] Ben was summoned to the Funing Palace to preach the Dharma.
Seeing that Ben had once been honored and respected by the late Emperor, those around him wept uncontrollably at the sight of him. Emperor Zhezong bestowed upon him the title of Chan Master;
the Imperial Uncle, Prince Jing, personally delivered the imperial edict to confer it upon him. In the first year of Yuanyou (1086), he requested to return home on account of old age.
The imperial court granted his request and issued an edict permitting him to wander freely as he pleased, stipulating that wherever he went, no one was to compel him to take up the position of abbot.
Consequently, he joyfully ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying: "I am originally a guest with no home; how could I bear to wander at will?
With a favorable wind, I add oars and sweeps to my boat; the boatman sets off for Yangzhou. Once he had left the capital, carriages and horsemen followed to see him off by high officials and nobles.
They were closely associated. Ben once instructed them, saying: "The passage of years and months cannot be toyed with; old age and sickness do not wait for anyone.

Only through diligent cultivation without indolence can one truly act as a true friend. Those who heard this did not fail to shed tears. That Zhen was so able to guide others through his benevolence and compassion was not merely incidental.
While he resided at Ruiguang Temple, there was a man who had been slaughtering oxen. The ox escaped and ran toward Ben, kneeling before him.
If he petitioned on his own behalf, they eventually purchased him and kept him. While he was residing at Jingci Temple, there was a great drought and both the lakes and wells ran dry.
In the western corner of the temple, a sweet spring gushed forth spontaneously, and golden eels were caught. Consequently, they dredged it to form a well and cast the fish into its depths;
the more than a thousand monks of the temple drew from it without it ever failing. A woman of the Zhang family had a daughter who died, and she dreamed that her mother said to her: "I..."

She regarded her transgressions as snakes. Having awakened to this, she found the snakes beneath the coffin and took them to the Master. He then preached the Dharma for her and returned them to their original place.
Suddenly, black cicadas flew over the coffin and the snakes vanished. Her mother made a vow, saying, "If I am indeed your daughter, you shall enter the cage;
I shall take you back to Jingci Temple. It happened exactly as she had vowed. The Master once again preached the Dharma for her.
That evening, she appeared in a dream and said, "The two karmic retributions have already been liberated. Her manifestations among different species were likewise like this.

Originally, in her daily life, she was humble and modest, never making a practice of rhetorical skill or erudition; yet when it came to preaching the Dharma, she showed no concession whatsoever, even toward those of great fame or high status.
The Sengtong (Patriarch) of Goryeo, Uichon, having been sent as an envoy by his royal father on a national mission to our country..."
In the morning, he heard his original name. He requested to see him with the etiquette of a disciple and asked what he had attained. [Yun-chu] replied with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The Master said, "Regarding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, does the Buddha who speaks it possess the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), or the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*)?
Ui-t'ien replied, "It is spoken by the Dharma Body. Yun-chu said, "The Dharma Body pervades all lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. At that time, where were the listeners sitting?"

Lil stood there, his mind blank and lost in confusion; his admiration and submission increased all the more. Li Gongduanyuan, the Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince, was one who had long been renowned for his Buddhist studies.
He asked: "The ten directions gather together, and each person studies non-action (*wuwei*).
Since it is called 'non-action,' how does one study? Li Gong was unable to answer. The Dharma of Xuedou reached its greatest flourishing during the time of Master Ben. Old...
Residing at Lingyan, he remained with his door closed and appeared dejected; yet followers from all directions were seen one after another, never ceasing their pursuit of the Way.
On the day of Jiazi, the twelfth month of the second year of the Yuánfú era, as he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he bathed and lay down.

His disciples gathered around him and entreated him, saying: "The Master’s Way pervades the world (one version says: 'Your fame fills the world'). Today you must not be without a verse. We pray that you exert yourself."

He rose and sat upon his seat. Looking at him intently, he said, "Foolish son! Even in my ordinary moments I am too lazy to compose verses; what are you trying to accomplish by doing so today in particular?
Ordinarily, when I wish to lie down, I simply lie down; I cannot sit up specifically for you today.

He then took up his brush and wrote five characters in large script: "The final affairs are entrusted to Shouryō. Having cast aside his brush, he lay down in a state of profound stillness. Although it appeared as if he were fast asleep, [the disciple] shook him.
He had already passed away. His disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa at Lingyan Mountain. He lived for eighty years and sat in meditation for fifty-two summer retreats.
A eulogy states: When the Duke of Zheng, Fu, resided in Luoyang, he met Daoyong of Huayan; hearing Yong recite the words of the *Benji*, he composed a verse and sent it to him.

It is said: (One edition reads: "The Duke of Zheng, Fu Bi, attained the essential heart of the teachings from Master Yonghua. He sent a verse to the original [text] which says: 'Because of meeting Master Yong, I have realized the profound entry;

through this auspicious connection, I have transmitted the Teacher’s mind. Though one may idly speak of the distance between the rivers and mountains of the southeast, my eyes face the Lingguang and Miaoyin stupas.
Wang Xianmu Han-zhi, upon first seeing the original text as it ascended the seat, looked around with his eyes and thereby verified the original mind. I heard this from Ma..."

The inscription states: "When the Tathāgata was in the world, the physical and mental faculties of sentient beings were preeminent; when he uttered his perfect voice but once, each understood according to their own kind.
Now, more than two thousand years have passed since the Buddha’s era, yet he has been able to cause kings, dukes, and nobles to awaken upon hearing his reputation."
By beholding his countenance and attaining realization, one may know those who followed him constantly and were intimately nurtured by him.

Thus, while there were eighty-odd people in Jiangxi, the number in the capital was double that; in recent times, the flourishing of the transmission of the Dharma has been such that none can surpass it.

Were it not for his vow to propagate the Way of the Dharma and his practice being in accord with the Buddha’s mind, how could he have reached this state? (According to one manuscript, from "by beholding his countenance and attaining realization" onwards, it simply reads: "then his great vow and true compassion...")
...the power [of this work]. It is one who possesses no shame regarding the duty of perpetuating and exalting [the Dharma].

Composed by the Sòng Dynasty monk Huìhóng of Míngbái Ān:

The Zen Master Quán of Héngyuè, whose name was Gùquán, was a native of Quánnán. From his youth, he was intelligent and quick-witted; by nature, he could endure filth and impurity, and his speech was bold and irreverent.

The common world detested him. He left to become a śramaṇa, but cast aside the precepts and acted according to his own whims. He looked down upon the monastics; wherever he went among the monasteries, he would immediately deface them.
He paid no heed to the springs [of discipline]. He traveled to Fenyang to pay his respects to Chan Master Zhao, who marveled at him and secretly bestowed upon him a prediction of enlightenment.
Returning south, he wandered through Xiangzhou. Hearing that Ciming was residing at Daowu, he went there to visit him.
Jian went to visit Ciming. Ciming asked, "White clouds hang across the mouth of the valley; from where have you come, O man of the Way?
Jian looked left and right and said, "Where was the fire last night that burned out the ancient tomb? Ciming scolded him, saying, "Not yet—speak further! Jian then let out a tiger's roar.
Ciming struck him with his sitting mat, and Jian caught it, pushing him onto a rope bed. Cimi... [text ends]
Ciming also made a tiger’s roar. Quan laughed loudly. On the mountain was a pool where a venomous dragon lay dormant;

whenever a fallen leaf touched the waves, thunder and rain would rage for days. Those passing by did not dare even to breathe. When Ciming returned home in the evening, it was still the heat of autumn.
Quan grabbed his robe and said, "We may bathe together. Ciming pulled back his arm and walked straight away. Thereupon, Quan took off his clothes and leapt in; a clap of thunder followed immediately.
It arrived. A raw wind blew and rain fell; the trees and forests shook and swayed. Ciming crouched amidst the grass, thinking that Yiquan was dead.

After a short while, the sky cleared and the sun shone; suddenly, [Yiquan] extended his neck out from between the waves and said, "I am here! Later, he ascended the summit of Mount Heng to Lingfeng Temple (some say...).
[He resided at] Yunpungsa Temple. He lived at Nanzan Rock and later moved to Bajiyo. As he was about to move to Bojin, he wrote large characters on the wall, saying:
"In this Bajiyo Hermitage of mine, I dwell in seclusion amidst the massed clouds. Though I have no leisure to enumerate all its diverse wonders, First, look at these three or four stunted pine trees.
When cold comes, I burn the withered cypress; When hungry, I eat large purple taro. Now, I abandon it and depart."
He learned that someone had come to reside at Baozhen Hermitage. This was a place of extreme peril in the regions of Heng and Xiang.
At night, while he sat on the ground beneath Mount Zhurong, a large python coiled around him. He untied his sash and bound it around his waist; by midnight, it had vanished.
The next day, he took up his staff and searched the mountain thoroughly for it, finding the sash wrapped around a withered pine tree—it was a pine-demon. Furthermore, after this...
Dong carried a stone statue on his back to Nantai. The statue weighed several hundred catties, yet the assembly of monks was struck with amazement, having no idea how it had arrived.
Later, the monks at Dong also had no knowledge of its departure. Consequently, it was passed down as the "Flying-Arival Arhat.
Once, while passing through Hengshan County, he saw a butcher hacking meat; he stood by his side, assuming a pitiable expression, and pointed first at the meat and then [at himself].
The butcher asked him, "Are you mute? He nodded his head. The butcher took pity on him and cut a large piece of meat, placing it in his bowl.

Quan was overjoyed, beyond all expectation; he bowed in thanks and departed. The entire market laughed loudly, yet Quan remained unconcerned. Carrying a large wine gourd upon a staff, he wandered back and forth through the mountains.
When people asked what was inside the gourd, he replied, "It is the elixir of the Great Way. Thus he made it himself.
The verse says: Who am I to govern you, Heaven? Who am I to govern you, Earth? Clad in a tattered paper robe, I do nothing but excel at sleeping. Let the golden crow rise in the east as it pleases;
let the jade hare fall in the west. What concern have honors or disgrace for me? What relevance have prosperity or decline?
With a single staff and a gourd, I wander idly between the Southern and Northern Mountains. I lie drunk upon the mountain paths.
In the meantime, a heavy snow began to fall. He composed a verse, saying: "Today’s snow is most excellent; It falls in profusion like the autumn moon.

Mañjuśrī does not show his head; Samantabhadra reveals his clumsy ugliness. He kept a servant named Tiāogǔ (Tiao-gu), whom he would daily order to gather firewood and draw water from the mountain stream.
Sometimes he would call for him to sit together upon the rocky crags and present him with a verse, saying: "I have a mountain boy named Tiāogǔ; He does not recite [the scriptures]..."
The Sūtra says: "Do not pay homage to the patriarchs. He understood how to split firewood to ward off the winter cold;
his clothes were tattered and never mended. He knew how to plant vegetables and could grow taro. He traveled through thousands upon thousands of mountains without fear.

A-ha-ha! What place is there to seek? When Ciming moved to reside at Fuyan, Xuequan went to visit him again. After staying for a short while, he returned and sent a verse to him, saying: "Since we parted..."
Now another half-year has passed; I know not with whom he has been conversing on Chan.
Amidst the same exquisite scenery of Mount Xiang, you yourself guide your followers while I sleep. Ciming merely smiled and then ordered Master Nan to visit Master Quan again.
When Quan spoke with him, he was astonished, saying, "Is there such a bald-headed practitioner within the jurisdiction of the Five Prefectures? Master Nan spent the summer at the Dharma [seat].
Lunquan then wrote a verse and invited him, saying: "Ever since I discussed the Great Way with you, Master, it has been rare for anyone of equal caliber to arrive.
Now you have cast aside this old mad monk and gone instead to sit atop Mount Jiuliu amidst the vast, drifting snow."
The cries of the monkeys were hushed; he chanted alone and sang songs by himself. "How marvelous! The Great Way is difficult for those who understand it to find.
On what day shall the solitary cloud return to the mountain, so that we may sit together upon the *pāṭhaka* rock before the hermitage?

Master Nan criticized him for his forthrightness and playfully replied with a verse: "Kāśyapa sat in meditation for kalpas; Potaipusa wandered aimlessly for years. A scabby dog has no wish to be born."
"O Heaven! You merely laugh at the white crane in the clouds. When Master Yunfeng Yue visited him, Shuiquan presented him with this verse:
"High-talented Chan practitioner Yue, Your mind is like a child’s, your appearance that of a mountain dweller. You have come from afar, specifically leaning on your staff to seek me out;

I have seen you for three years, yet you remain as you were at first. You do not practice Chan, nor do you inquire about the Way; In your daily life, you simply chant the *Yujia’ao* (Fisherman’s Joy). Chan person!"
He saw that the other was as cold as ashes; the other saw the Chan practitioner to be as indifferent as black lacquer.

There were those who traveled in a group to Changning to pay homage at the Śarīra stupa enshrined by King Aśoka, to whom [the author] sent this verse: "Various Chan practitioners travel in a group to visit the Jade Stupa."
The sacred traces and sublime landscapes are recorded in my heart; returning, I shall show them to you to see what they are like.
How could they compare to the seamless stupa of the mad monk? This seamless stupa is most difficult to depict. How could it be the same as white jade for others to tread upon?

Across the five lakes and four seas, clouds rush everywhere; how many pairs of shoes and sandals have been worn through? The seamless stupa is perfectly encompassing; only when meeting a fellow traveler does it truly begin.
The answer: Suddenly extending his hand, he borrowed the model to look at it, and then struck him across the cheek with a single blow.

During the Jiayu era, the man Li Qing was executed for spreading seductive rumors; because Quan had previously stayed at Qing’s hermitage, he was sentenced to flogging and banishment to the labor camp in Binzhou.

During the height of summer, he carried earth across a main thoroughfare. Setting down his burden, he spoke a verse, saying: "Today is the sixth day of the sixth month; the valley springs are choked by the heat.
I am neither ascending to heaven nor entering hell. Having finished speaking, he smiled and passed away with serene composure, like a cicada shedding its shell.
His cremation yielded countless relics (*śarīra*). The people of Chen built a stupa for them, which is still enshrined as a shrine to this day.
Chan Master Fahua Ju was named Quanju.

As a person, he was refined and strict, upright and honest, and had completed his full course of training under Fenyang, who held him in particular esteem.
