Whether manifesting both [the provisional and the real] or speaking of only one, he sought only the sharpness of the vanguard and the joy of Zen. He opened up expedient means not to compete for cleverness; he extended his radiance only for the sake of..."

Distinguishing the worthy and the wise: there is the perfect mark, there is silent discourse. From a thousand li away one brings it forth; with eyes fixed, a blink. Of ten thousand kinds of ingenuity, there is but a single perfect emptiness.
The *śakara* eye penetrates through faith. Zhi said: "This describes the lineage of the Miao-yang school. Sometimes they fully present [the teaching], sometimes they fully employ it.
Though the myriad phenomena are dense and vast, they are truly not shared; the green mountains do not obstruct the flying white clouds. Deeply resonant.
"The golden phoenix penetrates the dais. Zhi said, "This describes the lineage of Shitou and Yaoshan:
Xianggu’s mirror, Dizang’s moon; Xuansha and Chongshou shine without deficiency. Through a question posed by a guest, he points back to the source;
the intent for those who come is bright and pure. Zhi said, "This describes the lineage of Xuefeng and Dizang: sometimes called 'raising,' sometimes 'picking up.'"
The monk in his true colors strikes out long and far; within the phrase, the human matter is most precisely clarified. A master hand is like driving a wedge with a wedge:
sometimes raising up to recommend, sometimes lowering the hand to guide. It is essential that the mind be empty to open the mouth easily;
failing to recognize the ancestors' Great Compassion, those who merely hold torches wander about illuminating the streets. Zhi said: "This describes the Yunmen lineage. Deshan’s staff—"

Linji’s shout alone breaks forth from heaven and earth, unraveling all horizontal and vertical strokes. Who cares to manage the chaotic divisions from the very beginning? This talkative old master cannot describe it.
Seizing the opportunity, he releases; seizing the opportunity, he snatches away. His swift and sharp wit flashes like lightning. Heaven and earth are held within the palm of his hand;
the spirits of the bamboo and wood have their skulls split open. Whether as guest or host, whether through discernment or selection, he fully unfolds the Chan Way.

The Eye of the Righteous Discernment of the School: the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials serve to meet the capacity of the practitioner; the four propositions and hundred negations are all leveled at once.

I urge my fellow practitioners: do not force a conceptual understanding. If those who consider themselves precocious remain as before obstructed by their own intellect, they will fail to know the lineage of the school and fall into aimless confusion.
For eternal kalpas they shall sink long into the sea of birth and death—hard to encounter, hard to meet, and hard to hear. With a fierce and resolute mind, quickly attain thorough liberation. *Zhi*.
It is said: This records the lineages of Deshan and Linji. Ciming had an excellent attendant named Mingyan Yue.
Having heard of the reputation of Fenzhi, he went from Shishuang to Dayu to enter the master’s room. When Fenzhi kicked out a single sandal, Yue withdrew his body and stood there.
As Fenzhi bent down to pick up the sandal, Yue suddenly tripped him over. Fenzhi rose and sat facing the wall, pointing at Jin with his hand.
He painted it on the wall three times. Shanchang stood behind him while Zhi spun around and struck him with his shoe as they reached the Dharma Hall.
Shanchang said, "To act as a teacher in such a manner is to blind the eyes of an entire city. There was also a monk who claimed to lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Question: "If one has such faith and understanding, how can the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) not arise?
At that time, there was a dog lying in front of a rope-bench. Zhi kicked it, and the dog got up and left. Zhi asked the monks, "Do you understand this? The monks said, "We do not.
Zhi said, "If you understood, it would constitute the characteristics of dharmas. He then composed a verse: "Oil in sand is a pitiable matter; Cuiyan chews his rice to feed an infant. One day..."

One who knows the ultimate point of good and evil finds that their former face was once covered in ash. He entered nirvana at the beginning of the Jiayou era and was interred in a stupa on West Mountain.
The eulogy says: "Dayu and Cuoyan were both my old gardens; in my youth, I traveled back and forth between these two mountains. There was an old..."

My late grandfather was a friend of Master Zhi. He spoke of the time when Zhi was free from illness, saying: "The assembly never numbered more than thirty members. The buildings were old, and he would often prop up the leaning parts with wooden beams;
passersby suspected they might collapse at any moment. Yet Zhi, carrying his rain hat, traveled daily through cities, walled towns, and villages.
Temples were like way-stations for him, and there were times when even the supply of rice gruel failed. Recalling his lofty character, I have composed [this verse]."
The verse says: The halls and pavilions of Mount Lu seem as if naturally formed; In every dining hall, meditation seats lie broken.
These three gates of mine are like cold ashes; All day long, wind-blown leaves swirl through the corridors.
*Chànlín Sēngbǎo Zhuàn*, Scroll Sixteen and Scroll Seventeen.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huìhóng of Míngbái Ānjū during the Song Dynasty.
Chan Master Fushan Yuan, whose name was Fayuan, was a native of Zhengpudian. He was born into the Wang family. At the age of nineteen, he traveled to Bingzhou.
He went to see Chan Master Sengxiao of Sanjiao and requested the Dharma for transcending the world. Sengxiao said, "You must shave your head and join the ranks of the Triple Gem;
only then may you receive the Dharma. Huiyuan asked, "Does the Dharma distinguish between monk and layperson? Sengxiao replied, "Rather than being a layperson, why not become a monk?
It is because as a monk, one can continue the life-span of the Buddha. Thereupon, he cut his hair and received full ordination. He then went to visit [Master Shenhui of] Fen.
He visited State Preceptor Zhao of Zhuzhou and also paid his respects to State Preceptor Xing of Ruhuai; both conferred upon him the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
During the Tianxi era, he traveled through Xianghan, Sui, and Ying, eventually reaching Dayang. There, his spontaneous discourse reached a deep accord with Ming’an Yanchong.
Yanchong sighed, saying, "I am old now; will the lineage of Dongshan finally have no one to carry it forward? He then showed Yuan the cassock and leather sandals he had worn throughout his life.
[Daowu] said, "I shall keep these robes and sandals for you; how about we find someone to entrust them to?
Yan agreed, saying, "If you should indeed find such a person in the future, produce my verse as proof. The verse said: "The grass before Mount Yangguang— Rely on you to wait for its price.

Where the strange sprouts flourish, The numinous root remains deep and firm. The colophon at the end states: "One who attains the Dharma shall remain hidden from the assembly for ten years before [emerging]."
"May you propagate [the Dharma]. Yuan bowed in acceptance of these words and departed. He followed Chan Master Jue of Langya in Chuzhou;

subsequently, at the invitation of Taiping Xingguo Temple in Shuzhou, he preached the Dharma and became the successor to Master Xing. Next, he resided at Tianping Mountain in Gusu, and later at Fushan.
Having grown old, he retired to Huisheng Rock. There, while reading Ban Gu’s *Discourse on the Nine Schools*, he composed a work modeled after it.

He composed the Nine Bands (*kū-hai*), which set forth the teachings and meanings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, extensively gathering the pivotal sayings of former worthies to provide mutual verification and realization.
The first is called the Band of the Buddha’s True Dharma Eye; the second, the Band of the Buddha-Dharma Treasury; the third, the Band of the Penetration of Principle;

the fourth, the Band of the Penetration of Phenomena; the fifth, the Band of the Vertical and Horizontal Interpenetration of Principle and Phenomena; the sixth, the Band of the Winding Path; and the seventh... [text continues].
The seventh is called the "Exquisite Clasp with Dual Straps. The eighth is called the "Golden Needle Double-Chain Belt. The ninth is called the "Even-Minded Constantly Substantial Belt.
Once the students had memorized these, Yuan said, "If we rely on the Dharma-gate of Perfect Fulfillment, there are originally ten such items."
These nine bands have now been explained for you all. Is there yet another band that you can perceive?

If you can perceive it with intimacy and clarity, then please come forward and speak of it. If you can explain it clearly, I shall grant you the perfectly luminous eye of the Way, including the previous nine bands.
If your perception is not intimate and your explanation does not correspond to the truth, and you rely merely upon my words, [then you have failed].
If one understands it for oneself, that is called slandering the Dharma. When the assembly reached this point, they were speechless. Yuan scolded them and sent them away.
[The Master] raised a case where a monk asked Jia Shan, "What is the realm of Jia Shan? He replied, "A monkey carries its young back behind the green peaks."
"A bird carries a flower and alights before the green cliff. Fayan said, "For twenty years, I have taken this to be a statement about the objective realm (*viṣaya*).
Yuan said, "I do not take it as a statement about the objective realm. How do you understand it? The monk asked, "What is your meaning, Master?

Fayan replied, "The rhinoceros develops its horn from gazing at the moon; the elephant receives flowers in its tusks from being startled by thunder. (Alternatively, Yuan said, "Even if you do not take this as a statement about the objective realm, you still have not yet understood. Why is that?")

"The rhinoceros develops its horn from gazing at the moon; the elephant receives flowers within its tusks from being startled by thunder. Yuan’s jade-like bones protruded from his forehead, and his gaze shot outward;

his appearance was like that of a prince, majestic and awe-inspiring. Initially, when the Duke Wenzhong of Ouyang heard of Yuan’s extraordinary talent, he visited his quarters but found nothing remarkable about him.
While playing chess with a guest, Yuan sat beside them. Once the game ended, Wenzhong requested that Yuan expound the Dharma based on the principles of chess.
Thereupon, he struck the drum, ascended the seat, and said: "If one discusses this matter, it is like two families playing at chess. What does this mean?
When the opponent is a true connoisseur, one must not yield in the moment of action. If you are trailing by five points or leading by three, you must open up another path before you can succeed."
There is a certain class of people who only know how to ply their trade behind closed doors; they do not understand how to seize the corner or break through the barrier.
Their stubborn rigidity matches the tiger’s maw, yet once the position is broken, their efforts are in vain. Therefore it is said: "The fat edges are easy to find, but the lean belly is hard to seek.
In practice, they often lose their grip; with coarse minds, they constantly strike their heads against obstacles. Do not boast of being a national master; it is all in vain.

He spoke of the immortal. "When one wins the board and loses the counters, it is no longer a matter for questioning. But tell me, when black and white have not yet been distinguished, where does that first move fall?

After a long silence, he said: "Of the nineteen paths from of old, how many have been lost in delusion or awakened? Wen Zhong sighed in admiration for a long time. Yuan’s verses and words were subtle and profound;
those of all quarters acknowledged his mastery. Master Song of Sanjiao praised him, saying: [The original Chinese text follows: 說神仙。贏局輸籌即不問。且道黑白未分時一著。落在什麼處。良久曰。從前十九路。迷悟幾多人。文忠嘉歎久之。遠偈語妙密。諸方服其工作。三交嵩公贊曰。
Gold beaten into brass chopsticks; white jade carved into ivory combs. The Thousand-Handed Avalokiteśvara cannot pick them up; the Silent Boy sighs in secret.
He also composed a eulogy for Master Yan Ming’an, saying: A black dog with hooves of burnished silver; A white elephant ridden by the Kunlun.
Unimpeded in these two matters— A wooden horse neighs amidst the flames. Yuan Ya called himself... [text ends].
Chai Shi was a man of rustic simplicity. At the time of his death, he was already over seventy years old. In his youth, he traveled through Shu with Da-guan Ying-gong, Xue Da-tou, and several others;
they nearly encountered a violent disaster, but Yuan rescued them through his wisdom. The group relied upon him for his expertise in administrative affairs.
He was titled Master Yuanlu.
Chan Master Touzi Qing’s name was Yiqing;
he was originally a native of Qingdu and the son of the Li family. At the age of seven, he displayed extraordinary intelligence. He left Miaoxiang Temple...
He left home to become a monk at the temple. At fifteen, he tested his knowledge of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and was ordained as a full bhikṣu.

His teacher ordered him to study the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*, but he sighed and said, "The path of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* is far and long; what benefit is there in exhausting oneself? He entered Luoyang and studied the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* for five years.
Looking back at the written words, he saw that they were all like meat on a skewer; everywhere, their meaning and flavor were the same.

Once, while lecturing on the verse concerning the Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin Bodhisattva (sometimes referred to as Zhulin Pusa), he suddenly had a sharp realization and said: "The Dharma transcends words; how can it be lectured upon?
He immediately abandoned his studies to travel abroad. Upon reaching Fushan, he found that the Chan Master Yuanjian Yuan had retired from his seat and was residing there.

Huiyuan of Shengyan Rock had long dreamed of obtaining a fine hawk and kept it. Upon waking, Qing happened to arrive; Huiyuan took this as an auspicious omen and treated him with exceptional courtesy.
Qing stayed for three years. Huiyuan asked: "When an outsider questioned the Buddha, he did not ask about words, nor did he ask about wordlessness.
At that moment, how was it? The World-Honored One remained silent. How do you understand this? As Qing was about to offer a reply, [Huiyuan struck him].
Dafu suddenly covered his mouth with his hand. Thereupon, Qing was enlightened; he bowed and rose. Dafu said, "Have you attained a wondrous realization of the primal mechanism?
He replied, "Even if there were a wondrous realization, it must be spat out. At that time, Attendant Ziji was standing nearby and said:
On this day, Qing Huayan was like a sick man who has broken a sweat. Qing turned back and said, "Shut that dog’s mouth!
If you chatter on further, I shall vomit immediately. He served [his master] diligently for another three years.

Yuanjian then gave him a pair of sandals made from the skin of a large sun (dayang) and a plain cassock, saying, "Continue the tradition of the Dongshan school on my behalf. My stay in this world will not be long; take good care of yourself. Do not...
He remained there for some time. Qing then took his leave and departed from the mountains, where he studied the Tripitaka at Huiri Temple on Mount Lu.
In the sixth year of the Xining era, he returned to Longshu. Monastics and laypeople requested that he reside at Baiyun Shan Haihui Temple. Calculating from the year he received the Dharma...

It had been nearly ten years since he arrived there. Eight years later, he moved his residence to Mount Touzi. His reputation for the Way grew daily, and those who came as practitioners increased day by day.
There were many who attained realization through hidden penetration and silent certification; thus, the extraordinary sprouts flourished once more, truly fulfilling the previous prophecy.

Throughout his life, Qing never kept any possessions beyond what was necessary, possessing nothing more than worn-out robes and a paper quilt. Initially, when he first opened the mountain, there was a record by Ciji which said:

"If my stupa were red, it would mean I have returned. Later, when the people of the district happened to refurbish the stupa and it took on the color of agate, it was not long before he assumed the duties of the head of Qingling Monastery.
Previously, there had been no water in the mountains, which the community had long considered a hardship.
Suddenly, a spring emerged from among the mountain rocks—sweet, cool, and pure. Prefect He named it "Jewel-Returning Spring" (Zailai Quan). The sixth year of the Yuanfeng era.
At the end of the fourth month, he manifested a slight illness. He wrote a letter to take leave of the local officials and various donors.

On the fourth day of the fifth month, after bathing and ascending the seat, he bid farewell to the assembly. Having finished, he wrote a verse: "In my tenure at these two places, there was nothing to assist the Way.

Take care, all you people; there is no need for further seeking. Thereupon, he passed away peacefully. His remains were cremated, and his relics and sacred bones were collected in the intercalary sixth month.
The stupa was erected to the northwest of the monastery, behind Sanfeng Hermitage. He lived for fifty-two years and sat in meditation for thirty-seven summer retreats.
Yang Jie, known as the Master of Non-action (Wuwei zi), composed a eulogy for his portrait, saying: "A single sandal, two ox-hides; where the golden crow crows, the wooden cock flies.
At midnight, the oil-seller breaks into laughter; the white-haired man has fathered a black-headed child."
[One version says: "A black-headed man gives birth to a white-headed child. There was a preeminent Dharma heir named Chan Master Daokai.
Chan Master Tianning Daokai was a native of Yishui in Yizhou. He was born into the Cui family. By nature, he was resolute, firm, and independent. From [the age of]...
In his youth, he was able to abstain from grain while studying the Way, living in seclusion within Mount Yiyang. Later, he traveled to the capital and registered his name at Shu Tai Temple.
There, he underwent examinations on what he had studied, received ordination, and attained the full precepts. He then visited Qing Huayan at Haihui Monastery on Mount Huai, where he asked:
"The words and phrases of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are like the daily tea and rice of a household. Apart from these, are there any other words and phrases for the sake of others?
Qing said, "You say that when the Son of Heaven issues an edict within the realm, does he still require the aid of Yu, Tang, Yao, or Shun?
Kai attempted to respond, whereupon Qing struck him with his whisk and said, "From the moment you first conceived the thought [to speak], you already deserve twenty blows. At this—
"It is so," said Kai, realizing the essential meaning beneath the words; he bowed twice and departed immediately. Qing called out, "Wait a moment! But Kai did not look back.
Qing asked, "Have you reached the stage of non-doubt? Kai covered his ears with his hands. Later, when Kai was presiding over the community's meals, Qing questioned him.
[The Master] said, "The kitchen duties are truly arduous. [Fengxue] replied, "I dare not [complain]. [The Master] asked, "Are you cooking rice? Or boiling congee?
He replied, "The laborers wash the rice and set the fires; the attendants boil the congee and cook the rice. [The Master] asked, "What do you do?
He replied, "Out of compassion, the Master has allowed me to remain idle. Furthermore, once while following Qingyuan to visit his garden, Qingyuan handed his staff to Kaier and said:
"It is only right that it should be so. Daopi replied, "To carry the Master's shoes and hold his staff for him would not be considered beyond my duty.
Daopi said, "There is another companion here. Daopi replied, "That one does not accept instruction. Qing then withdrew.

When evening came, Qing said to him, "The conversation we had this morning was not yet finished. Daopi replied, "Please bring it up again. Qing said, "Born in the Rabbit year, born in the Dog month. Kai—
He immediately lit a lamp and came forward, saying, "Coming and going, it has never been in vain. [The Master] replied, "You have been by my side; it was only natural that this should be so.
He said, "A slave or a servant—whose household does not have one? He replied, "As you are of venerable age, Master, I could not do without him.
He said, "To be so diligent! He replied, "It is my lot to repay your kindness. In the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, he returned north to Yishan.
He lived in seclusion at Mount Ma’an and subsequently entered the world to preach the Dharma. Initially, he resided at Xian-dong in Yizhou;
later, he moved to the Zhaoti Monastery at Longmen in Western Luoyang, and then again to Dayang in Yingzhou and Dahong in Suizhou.
In each case, eminent officials and high-ranking dignitaries of the time urged him to accept these invitations. Thus, the tradition of Dongshan shook the northwest. (Chongning 3rd year...)
In that year, an imperial edict was issued for him to reside at the Jingshan Jingyin Chan Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
In the winter of the first year of the Daguan era, he moved to Tianning Monastery, where he was escorted in by an imperial messenger; he was not permitted to decline the appointment.

Shortly thereafter, Li Xiaoshou, the Governor of Kaifeng, submitted a memorial stating that Fajie’s spiritual practice was preeminent within the monastic community and that he should be honored and distinguished accordingly. Thereupon, he was granted a purple *kāṣāya* robe and the title Dingzhao (Fixed Illumination).
Chan Master Kai burned incense to express his gratitude for the imperial favor and then submitted a memorial to decline it, saying:

"I humbly acknowledge that, by Your Majesty’s compassionate grace, you specially dispatched Tan Zhen of the Zhangshan Pavilion to bestow upon me the title of Chan Master Dingzhao and a certificate for purple robes.
Grateful for this sagely bounty, I have immediately burned incense and ascended the seat to offer prayers for the longevity of Your Majesty. Now, I humbly reflect..."
Your servant’s conduct has been circuitous and superficial, and my power of the Way is meager and thin.

I have long since made a vow not to accept profit or fame, and I have steadfastly maintained this intention for many years, hoping thereby to transmit the Way in this manner. Since then, I have devoted myself exclusively to the Buddha-dharma.

Although I have now received extraordinary favor, were I to continue to occupy this position by mere presumption, I would be violating my own long-held vow; how then could I instruct others? How could I possibly...
I look up to and extol Your Majesty’s intention in commanding me to serve as abbot. Regarding the aforementioned imperial decree, I dare not accept it.

I humbly pray that Your Sacred Compassion will examine my humble sincerity; this is not a mere matter of formal rhetoric. I beseech you to grant special permission for me to practice the Way until the end of my days, thereby repaying the Heavenly Grace.
Having reported this to the Emperor, he entrusted the matter to Li Xiaoshou, who went in person to [deliver the message].

The imperial edict expressed the court’s intent to honor the virtuous; yet Kai remained resolute and would not yield. The Governor of Kaifeng reported the matter in full to the Emperor, who grew angry and ordered Kai to be seized and handed over to the judicial authorities.
The officials, aware that Kai was loyal and sincere (one version reads: "aware that Kai was simple and dull-witted"), knew he had merely offended the Imperial Majesty.
The official asked, "Venerable sir, are you suffering from illness? Kai replied, "I have been ill in ordinary times, but now I am truly not.
The official said again, "If one says they are ill, they are exempted from legal punishment. Kai said, "How could I dare seek to evade punishment by feigning illness? The official sighed deeply;
thereupon he accepted his penalty, donned a scholar's robe (*seungyeok*), and was sent into exile in Ji-zhou. This was at the Daodong Monastery.
Laypeople who saw him wept, yet Hui-kai’s countenance remained calm and composed. He went to Zizhou, where he rented a house to live; his students grew even more devoted to him.

In the winter of the following year, an imperial decree was issued allowing him to live as he pleased. He built a hermitage in the middle of Fuyong Lake, where several hundred people surrounded him while sitting or lying down.
Fearing disaster—or perhaps seeking to avoid it—Hui-kai ate only a single cup of congee each day, and those who could not endure this gradually departed.
There were still about a hundred people remaining. In the winter of the seventh year of the Zhenghe era, an imperial edict granted the name Huayan Chan Temple to the hermitage where he resided.
On the fourteenth day of the fifth month of the following year, he passed away without illness. Prior to his death, he wrote a verse and entrusted it to his attendant, saying:
I am seventy-six years old; my worldly ties are now exhausted. In life I did not crave heaven, and in death I do not fear hell.
Casting off my hands and laying down my body beyond the three realms, I roam freely and spontaneously—what constraints could there be?
When Xuefeng Kai was at Dayang, Qing Huayan sent the attendant Guo with Dayang’s leather sandals and a straight robe to entrust to him. Kai then entrusted them to [Master] Xiangzhou.
Dongshan Daowei. After his retirement from the monastic administration, he returned to Zhejiang Province and passed away at the Small Temple of Shuanglin.

Now, [his remains] have been brought back to Lumen Mountain, where a pavilion has been constructed to enshrine them, called the "Clothing Repository. His verses are profound and purposeful; he composed five gāthās to describe the tradition of his school.
The first is titled "The Sublime Song Does Not Depend on the Tongue," and the verse says: "In every land, in every atom, in every place..."

Tán. Without the need for laborious "striking the ball," Sudhana attained realization; Śāriputra likewise understood how to transmit the message. Before the Flower-Rain Rock, even the birds do not carry it away.
Second: A dead snake startled out from the grass. The verse says: Scorched by the sun and blown by the wind, it lies buried in the weeds;
If it stirs against its own venomous breath, it will only become more perverse. If one were to force its dead mouth open in the dark, Cháng'ān would remain as before, with no one coming. Third.
It is called "The Lament of the Withered Bone Unveiling the Needle. The verse says: To live within death is the extraordinary;
his secret application has a distinct excellence. At midnight, a skull chants a single song; the red flames on the frozen river are yet cool and refreshing.
The fourth is "The Iron Saw and the Three Platforms. The verse says: It is not the mode of *gong* or *shang*; who can join in this performance? What can Boya do about it?

This song has long been popular. Fifth, it is said that there is no gap between the ancient and the modern. A verse says: "A single dharma is fundamentally non-existent; the ten thousand dharmas are empty.
Within this, how could one seek to realize perfect penetration? It was thought that the news from Shaolin had ceased, yet the peach blossoms still smile at the spring breeze.
Kai formerly lived in seclusion, with tigers as his neighbors. The tigers once suckled his four children for over a month. Kai watched for them to go out and went [to their den].

Upon looking at them, their stench was beyond description. He secretly took one back. When the tiger caught the piglet and dragged it to the mouth of its den, it lay on the ground, delighted to see the spine and tail;
however, seeing its three cubs angry, it pawed the earth with its paws and roared. Flocks of birds all cried out and wheeled above it.
Gao Kai immediately released it and returned it. He sent a verse to Han Chengyi, the Magistrate of Iyang, which began: "Old age loves..."

Relying on the mountain, human affairs are rare; tigers are tame, so I wonder why I have come so late to the hermitage. The stone chamber is desolate and filled with dust; I know not what day shall be the day of my return.
It is also said: For several li there is no one who comes; only when the mountains turn yellow do I realize it is autumn.
A single sleep among the crags causes me to forget the anxieties of a hundred years.
The commentary states: The Chan school prizes the succession of the lineage; thus, if one follows the secular rites of propriety, being the successor is equivalent to being a son.
To cause the "Green" (Qing) tradition to continue the fallen framework of the Dongshan school is precisely this.

Yet, Qingyuan and Linji—father and son—faced heavy responsibilities and a long path, both of whom were able to endure rigorous austerity. Through this, they ultimately brought about a sudden and vigorous resurgence. How truly worthy they were!
*Chànlín Sēngbǎo Zhuàn*, Scroll Seventeen and Scroll Eighteen.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huìhóng of the Míngbái Ān Residence during the Song Dynasty.
Chan Master Dajue Lian’s name was Huailian;
his courtesy name was Qizhi. He was the son of the Chen family of Zhangzhou. Initially, his mother prayed before the image of Sengqie of Sizhou and obtained him [as a child];
thus, his childhood nickname was Sizhou. From early childhood, he possessed a profound air, and his intelligence and wisdom were extraordinary.
The man remained a śramaṇa for his entire life; he was skilled in calligraphy and his reputation was widely renowned.

Wandering through various regions, he took a particular fondness for the sublime excellence of Mount Heng and resided in the Three Lives Storehouse (Sāṃsārika-kośa) for many years. The monastic community there called him "Lian the Three Lives.

Having heard that the Zen Master Cheng of Shimen in Nanchang was the legitimate heir of the Fifth Patriarch Jie, he went to pay his respects and served him as a disciple for over ten years before departing to travel.
At Mount Lu, Yuan-tong served as the Secretary of the Monastery under Chan Master Foyun Dao-ne.

In the first month of the second year of the Huangyou era, an imperial edict was issued appointing him to reside at the Shifang Jingyin Chan Monastery in the capital. On the nineteenth day of the second month, he was summoned for an audience at the Huacheng Hall.
He was questioned on the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and his responses pleased the Emperor’s mind. He was granted the title Chan Master Dajue (Great Enlightenment).
Upon the conclusion of the vegetarian feast, an imperial decree was proclaimed that he should follow the ritual protocols of the Southern Chan monasteries to open the hall and expound the Dharma.

Furthermore, Qingman, the Great Master Ciyun and Vice Registrar of the Left Street, was commissioned to deliver the formal invocation, beginning: "The spring returns to the Imperial Garden; the assembly of the Royal House is convened. Since the Ten-Thousand-Wagons Sovereign has arrived..."
In the Hall of Emperor Shun, both streets were graced by the presence of Yao’s eyebrows. Now that this is a season of harmony and warmth, it is truly the day for proclamation and exaltation.

To expound upon the ancestral Way is to fully accord with the Imperial heart. When the questions and answers concluded, he said: "Within the halls of the Ancient Buddhas, there has never been any divergent teaching;
yet within the phrases that circulate, there are indeed many discourses. Those who attain them find their wondrous function unimpaired; those who lose them—"

The creature roams at will; to capture it, simply pull on the end of the rope. For a young calf, stroke it with the grain of its fur, for fear that its four hooves might slip on a steep slope.
The sun is already high; stop feeding it grass. Grip its nose firmly—no distinction between young and old—and lead them all at once into the pen to sleep.
Watch them as they stumble east and west in the mud. Upon awakening, silently attain the *samādhi* of their play. Thus it is said.
In the capital, he stayed with Master Li for over a month, and Master Li indeed passed away. At the moment of his death, he drew a circle and offered a verse to the Master.
The verse said: "The world has no support; mountains and rivers offer no obstruction. The great ocean is but a mote of dust; Mount Sumeru fits within a mustard seed.
Lifting up the head-wrap, unfastening the waist-belt— If you seek birth and death, ask the leather bag. The Master said:
"What is the original Buddha-nature? Li Gong replied, "Today is as hot as yesterday. As soon as he heard these words, [the questioner] asked, "What is your one phrase for when you depart?
Gong said, "Originally there is no obstruction; wherever one goes, one may act with flexibility."
Lord Li said, “I am weary from the evening; I shall not answer you further. Lord Li then passed away in serene stillness.
Emperor Renzong, who had particularly applied his mind to the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), heard of Lord Li’s transformation and his exchange with Yuan.
He marveled at this for a long time. [The Emperor] wept bitterly for him and bid him farewell at the burial site. An imperial edict was issued.
He was granted an official boat for his journey south. Midway through the trip, he said to his attendant, "I have suddenly contracted a stroke;
look, my mouth and lips are already slanted. The attendant stamped his foot on the ground and cried, "What shall we do? Throughout your life you reviled the Buddhas and cursed the Patriarchs!"

"Now it has come to this," he said. The Abbot replied, "Do not worry; I shall set you right. With his hand, he adjusted [the monk's robe] so that it was as it had been before. He then said, "From now on, I will no longer neglect you.
Subsequently, in the first year of the Xinghua era, on the fifth day of the first month, he bathed, took leave of the assembly, sat in the lotus position, and passed away.
He had lived for thirty-four years and spent thirty-two summer retreats in the monasteries. — Recorded by Lord Li.
This man had his conduct inscribed on a stele at Xinghua, while his entire body was interred at Shishuang.
Throughout his life, he practiced the "unimpeded in all things" (sarva-vastu-asaṅga) with his mind; neither ordinary nor holy beings could fathom him.

While sitting in meditation within his quarters, he placed a blade of meat across a basin of water and set a straw sandal beside it, instructing those who came to seek instruction to provide a response. None, however, could harmonize with his spiritual pivot. Furthermore...
He composed a verse for his disciples, saying: "Black, black, black. Way, way, way. Bright, bright, bright. Attainment, attainment, attainment.
Furthermore, during winter, he posted these characters on the Sangha Hall: 二 (two), 三 (three), 二 (two), 三 (three), 儿 (er), [田/?][曲-曰+口][(巨-匚)@二]才. Below them, he added a note:
"If anyone can recognize these, they will not be separate from the four modes of deportment. When the Head Seat saw this, he said to him, "The Master has today released..."
"San. When Ciming heard this, he laughed and said: "The commentary states:
'Only when there are clouds and waves reaching the heavens can one accommodate a fish that swallows a boat; only with a wind of ninety thousand *li* can one support wings that defy the sky.
The heavy responsibility of the Dharma-seal of the Tathāgatas of the three periods—how could it be sought [by those of limited capacity]? "

As for the timber of constancy, can it bear the weight of a yoke? I have observed Ciming: with an extraordinary and magnificent bearing that transcends ordinary men, his conduct was not entangled in the affairs of either the mundane or the sacred.
In jest and laughter, he raised up Linji when he was about to fall; with a single roar, he slew the thieving mind of Huanglong.
Observing his deeds, one sees no tracks left behind; yet before three generations had passed, he died as a perfect standard. This is a proverb.
It is said: "When a character is transcribed three times, 'wu' (a crow) becomes 'ma' (a horse). Although these words concern a minor matter, they can serve as a metaphor for great principles.
