Compiled by the Chan monk Huìhóng of Míngbái Ān, Song Dynasty.
Chan Master Huánglóng Nán was surnamed Zhāng and named Huìnán. His ancestors were from Yúshān in Xīnzhōu. From early childhood, he was profound and serious.

He possessed the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*). He abstained from pungent vegetables and did not indulge in frivolous play. At the age of eleven, he left home and took Huaiyu as his teacher at Zhiluan of Dingshui Monastery.
Once, while traveling with Zhiluan, he saw a shrine along the road; he immediately struck it with his staff, set it on fire, destroyed it, and departed.
At nineteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination. He traveled afar to Guizong on Mount Lu, where an elderly master was presiding over the assembly while seated upon a cushion.

The Master leaned back against it and occasionally blinked at him. From that time on, whenever he sat, he invariably sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), and whenever he walked, he invariably gazed straight ahead.
Later, he stayed at Xixian under Chan Master Yi; Yi managed the assembly with disciplined decorum, and the Master took him as his model.

In his third year [of ordination], he took leave to cross the Huai River and relied upon Chan Master Sanjiao Cheng. Cheng was renowned at the time; upon seeing him, he recognized his potential and granted him his approval.
When Cheng moved his residence to Letan, the Master accompanied him there as well. Cheng had him share the teaching seat to receive disciples.

Later, when Wen Yue of Nanchang saw him, he would sigh whenever he returned to his quarters, saying, "This man possesses the vessel for the Way in the South. It is a pity that he has not yet received the *Platform Sutra*."
Shize was like a pair of tongs and a hammer. Once, when they were traveling together in the Western Mountains, they discussed the Dharma-way of Yunmen during the night.
Shize said, "Although Master Cheng is a successor of Yunmen, his Dharma-way is different. The Master asked why it was different.

Shize replied, "Yunmen is like nine-refined cinnabar; it can transform iron into gold. Master Cheng’s medicine is quicksilver and silver—it may be admired for its appearance, but as soon as it enters the forge, it flows away."
He departed. The Master grew angry and threw his pillow at him. The next day, Yuanze apologized for his transgression.
The Master said again, "Yunmen’s bearing was like that of a king; could he have been content with dying under my words? Master Cheng possessed the Dharma; he accepted people's 'dead words.

But how can dead words bring people to life? Yuanze then turned his back and left. The Master called after him, saying, "If it is truly so, who else could satisfy your mind? Yuanze replied, "Shishuang."
The skillful means of Chu-yuan surpass those of all other quarters. If you wish to see them, you should not delay. Gong pondered this silently to himself, saying:
"This is a matter of great importance for my pilgrimage. Although I admire Master Cuiyan, he has sent me to see Shishuang. If I gain something from seeing him—"

"What joy could there be in this? That very day, he prepared his travel gear. On the way, he heard that Ciming was not diligent in his duties and treated the monastic community with arrogance and contempt;
he regretted his departure and wished not to go. He stayed in Pingxiang for several days, then joined a companion and traveled from Shou County up to Mount Heng.
While residing at Fuyan, the venerable elder known as Xian Chashou—a successor of Dayang Ming’an—appointed the Master to serve as his secretary.

When the dharma-brothers at Letan heard that the Master had not entered the community of Shichuang, they dispatched a messenger to inquire after him. Shortly thereafter, Xian passed away, and the local authorities appointed Ciming to lead Fuyan.
The Master was pleased by this turn of events and wished to observe the man for himself, in order to verify the words of Yue.
When Ciming arrived, Master Gong saw him from afar; both his heart and countenance became solemn.

Upon hearing his discourse, which largely disparaged and critiqued various other schools while enumerating point by point what he considered erroneous interpretations, Gong returned home with his spirit drained, realizing that these views were all secretly transmitted teachings from Lestan.

Recalling the words he had spoken in his usual state of mind, Huineng suddenly changed his tune and said, "A man of great character—how can there be self-doubt or obstruction within one's own heart and core?
He hurried to the chamber of Ciming and said, "I, Huineng, am ignorant and deficient; though I look toward the Way, I have not yet seen it."

"I have recently heard of your night assembly; it is like a person lost in the wilderness finding a guiding chariot. Yet, out of great compassion, please bestow further Dharma-gifts so that my remaining doubts may be exhausted.
Ciming smiled and said, "The Secretary has already led his disciples on a journey abroad and his fame resounds through the monasteries.

Even if he had doubts, he would not have discarded me for being aged and humble, but would have sat with me to deliberate upon them. Is this not possible? He called to his attendant to bring [the Secretary] forward."

[Zhang] Gong invited him to sit upon the couch. Gong declined firmly, his entreaties becoming increasingly earnest. Ciming said, "As a secretary who has studied Yunmen Chan, you must surely be well-versed in its essential meaning.
Regarding the saying, 'He bestowed three blows of the staff upon Dongshan'—at that time, was Dongshan deserving of the blows or not?
Gong replied, "He was deserving. Ciming, assuming a solemn expression, said, "To hear the sound of the three blows of the staff is itself to have received the blows."
"Then from dawn until dusk, you hear the cawing of crows, the chirping of magpies, and the sounds of bells, fish-bells, drums, and wooden clappers;

you should also be struck with the staff for these. When will such beatings ever end? The Master (Fengxue) stared back and withdrew. Ciming said, "At first I doubted that you were fit to be my teacher;
now it is so. He then had him prostrate himself. As the Master rose from his prostration, Ciming resumed his previous argument, saying, "Suppose it were as you say..."
Having grasped the essential meaning of Yunmen’s intent, one recalls Zhaozhou’s former remark: "The old woman of Mount Tai has been exposed by me.

If you attempt to point out the specific point where she was exposed, Master Gong’s face would flush with heat and his sweat would pour down; he would not know how to answer and would withdraw. The next day, when he went to see him again, he was once more met with abuse.
Gong, ashamed before his attendants, immediately said: "It is precisely because I do not understand that I seek a resolution. Is this abuse truly an act of compassion?"
Regarding the manner of giving the Dharma, Ciming smiled and said, "Is this an insult? Thereupon, the official silently realized its meaning and exclaimed, "Letan was indeed speaking words of death.
He then offered this verse: "Prominently rising from the forest is Zhaozhou; The old woman’s discernment leaves no room for further inquiry.
Now the four seas are as clear as a mirror; May travelers not regard the road as an enemy. Ciming—
He pointed at the character "Mu" with his hand and looked at Master Gu. Master Gu immediately changed it, and he was inwardly impressed by its subtle and profound mastery.

After staying for over a month, he took his leave. At that time, Ji was thirty-five years old. Later, while traveling through Fangguang, he visited Donghou and met Master Quan. They stayed together during the summer retreat;

although Quan’s status as either ordinary or sagely was unfathomable, his wit and eloquence surpassed all others. Placing a hand on Master Gu’s back, he said, "You belong to the same lineage as Fenzhou; take care of yourself."

In the following year, Ciming traveled to Jingzhou and met Xiyue at Jinkuan. Looking at one another, they both laughed and said, "Had I not had you, my elder brother, and Guquan as friends, how could I have come to know Ciming?
That autumn, he returned north and entered Leshan Tan alone; his former ties with Master Cheng were now exhausted.
From Yunju, he traveled to Tong’an. An elderly master named Shenli, observing that the Master was weary from his travels, [advised him to stay].
Yue said, "I have resided on this mountain for a long time without contributing anything to the religious teachings. I venture to entrust the affairs of the monastery to you.
Furthermore, the local governor has long known your reputation; at his request, I could not but accept. A monk was sent from Ledu Tan to examine Yue’s words of instruction, which included:
"The ocean of wisdom has no inherent nature; it becomes ordinary through the awakening to delusion. Since the awakening to delusion is fundamentally void..."
If one sees the Buddha with an ordinary mind, one should simply let it rest; this is what Tong’an meant by "no settlement.

It follows whatever you desire in your delusions—seven Southern Stars, eight Northern Stars. When the monk Gui reported this to Cheng, Cheng was displeased. Shortly thereafter, he heard that [Tong’an] had succeeded to Shishuang.
Many of his dharma companions at Ledu abandoned him. He resided at Guizong, where the monastery was consumed by fire overnight. He was imprisoned for his offenses. For...
The official sought his vulnerabilities in a hundred ways. The Master remained composed, accepting the blame upon himself and not involving others;
he simply ceased eating. Only after a long time was the official released. Throughout his life, the official never spoke of the Master’s indignities.
He built a hermitage by a stream at Huangbo, naming it "Accumulated Green" (Jicui). Later, he retired there, saying, "I shall grow old here. At that time, the Yangtze River...
People from Hu, Min, and Yue, hearing of his reputation, came to reside there; they vied with one another to join him, scrambling along the road for fear of being left behind.

Even those who had previously lived in leisure and abundance, considering themselves to have more than enough, were struck with dismay and self-doubt upon arriving, and enrolled themselves among the ranks of his disciples.
Pan Xingsi Yanzhi, a man of high integrity from Nanzhou, once asked him:
Therefore, Duke said: "If the father is strict, the son will be filial. The instruction you have given today shall be the model for future days.
It is like the earth: that which is high it lowers, and that which is hollow it levels. If he ascends to the height of a thousand fathoms, I shall accompany him there;
if he falls into the depths of the ninefold abyss, I shall likewise accompany him there. When his skill is exhausted, then [his] delusions..."
"When [the process] is exhausted, one is naturally liberated. It is further said: "Nurturing and fostering are the means by which spring and summer bring forth life;
frost and snow are the means by which autumn and winter bring things to fruition. I wish to remain wordless—is this possible?

Using these three phrases—"Buddha’s hand," "Donkey’s feet," and "Birth conditions"—he questioned his students, yet none were able to realize their essential meaning. The monastic communities throughout the land designated them as...
There were three barriers. Whenever someone attempted to pass, the Master neither approved nor disapproved; he simply closed his eyes and sat upright, and no one could fathom his intention.

When others pressed him further to ask why, the Master said: "Those who have already passed through the barrier wave their arms and walk straight on; how would they know there are officials at the barrier?"

He asked an official whether it was acceptable [to leave]. This was because he had not yet passed through the barrier. During his flourishing tenure at the Dharma seat of Huanglong, he rivaled Letan, Mazu, Baizhang, and Dazhi.
On the seventeenth day of the third month in the second year of the Xining era, he prepared a meal for the two special envoys from the Fourth Patriarch’s monastery, Huiri.
After the assembly concluded, he sat cross-legged before his quarters; the great assembly surrounded him for a long while.
He manifested his passing. On the day before, he spoke a verse. Seven days later, his body was cremated, and five-colored śarīra relics were obtained.
A stupa was erected on the front ridge of the mountain. He lived for sixty-eight years (some say sixty-six years) and sat in meditation for fifty *varṣas* (or, as some say, thirty-seven *varṣas*).
This occurred in the spring of the fourth year of the Daguān era.
The imperial posthumous title was conferred as Pujue (Universally Awakened). The eulogy states: Regarding the Linji school’s fundamental tenets, Master Shangu (Huang Tingjian) said:

"It is like Han Gaozu’s reception of Han Xin—whispering in his ear to enfeoff him as a king, yet seizing the seal within his own bedchamber; feigning a journey to Yunmeng to bind him with strongmen, and deceiving him with congratulations."
He beheaded Chen Ping in the Bell Chamber. Indeed, the High Emperor of Han possessed no sword for killing men; even the heart of Han Xin did not die.
The patriarchs’ way of receiving people was often like this. The essential principle of Linji was simply to achieve immediate clarity;
the tongs and hammer were entrusted to his true sons and grandsons. In my view, Huanglong used the "Three Barriers" to forge away both the holy and the ordinary;
these were indeed the authentic tongs and hammer for those who were his true sons and grandsons.
Chan Master Yunfeng Yue was born into the Xu family;
his name was Wen Yue, and he was a native of Nanchang. At the age of seven, he received the tonsure at Longxing Temple.

He was short in stature yet possessed a refined beauty and a keen discernment. At nineteen, he took up his staff and traveled extensively throughout the Jianghuai region, often sitting in silent meditation.
The Record: Recalling the words of the Venerable Elder, he harbored doubts and said: "I have heard that when Linji was at Huangbo for three years, Huangbo did not recognize him.

It was the Venerable Chen who instructed him, ordering him to inquire about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma; though he asked three times, he was beaten each time. I have never heard it said that Huangbo taught him earnestly.
It was only upon reaching Dayu that he attained enlightenment and became the founder of the Jiangxi school. The Venerable Elder—
"Teach me. My intention is not in vain; it is simply that what I wish to hear is different. At that time, there was Shan at Jinnian in Jingzhou and Zhi at Dayu in Junzhou.
Xuemo wished to go first to visit Zhi; if they did not reach an accord, he would then proceed to Jingzhou.
Upon arriving at Dayu, he saw that the buildings were old, the monks were few, and the place was as desolate as a roadside inn. Zhi himself carried his rain hat and went out every day.

Yue was in the marketplace when he returned home at dusk; he bolted the gate and lay back with his pillow high, feeling a sense of joy and remaining free from lingering attachments. He intended to pack his bags and depart, but just as he was about to leave, it began to rain.
When the rain stopped, Zhì ascended the seat and said, "Everyone gathers here to eat this stalk of vegetable relish.

If you call it 'a stalk of vegetable relish,' you will enter hell like an arrow shot. He descended from the seat without saying another word. Yue was greatly startled and went that night to the master’s chamber. Zhì—
He asked, "What do you seek by coming here? The man replied, "I seek the Buddha’s Dharma of the mind. Fazhi said, "The Wheel of the Dharma has not yet turned; the Wheel of Food must turn first.

You, a person of later birth, possess physical strength—why not go and beg for food on behalf of the community? I have no leisure to endure hunger; how could I have the leisure to preach the Dharma for you?
Yue did not dare to disobey and immediately requested to depart. Upon his return from Fengchuan, Fazhi moved his residence to the west.

Yue went again to follow him at Mount Cuoyan. At night, he went to the master’s chamber. Zhi said, "Do you wish to seek the Buddha-mind Dharma again? You do not consider that you have only recently settled here;
the walls of this house are drafty and leaking, and it is cold with snow. I have been looking forward to your arrival day and night so that you might provide charcoal for the assembly.
How could I preach the Dharma while enduring such cold? Can I truly teach you the Dharma [under these conditions]? Yue did not dare disobey and entered.

While the charcoal for the city encampment was being transported back, the *vina* (monastic administrator) was absent. Huaiye went to the abbot’s quarters at night. Zhi said, "The Buddha-dharma does not fear being ruined.

One office of the Hall Administration—I now entrust it to you. Huaiye could not speak and departed. The next day, the *ganzhui* (wooden gong) was struck, and he was earnestly invited [to take the post].

Huaiye showed a look of reluctance; having bowed and risen, he wished to leave. However, since his labor had already been extensive, he eventually desisted because of the long-standing circumstances. Nevertheless—
Frustrated that Zhi would not leave his mind, he sat on the rear rack. A bundle of broken buckets and basins beneath the rack fell from it;

at that moment, he suddenly attained awakening and instantly saw the previous applications of Zhi’s [teachings]. He ran, adjusted his *kāṣāya*, and ascended to the sleeping hall. Zhi met him with a smile and said:
The *vinaya* master said with joy, "The great matter is now concluded. Yue bowed twice, perspiring profusely, and departed without uttering a single word.
He served diligently for eight years until Zhi passed away. He then traveled east to the Three Wu regions; wherever he went, the monasteries were transformed.

Chan Master Xuedou Xian held him in such profound reverence that whenever he gathered the assembly for tea, he would set out a special couch crosswise to show his exceptional respect. Hearing of [Yue’s arrival] from the South...
The Chan Master resided at Tong’an. Having traveled from Sanqu to Poyang, he came to pay his respects to the Ancient Pagoda Master (Guta Zhu) and subsequently led the assembly of monks on Mount Zhi.
Later, Nan Chan Master sent an envoy to invite him, whereupon he again led the assembly at Tong’an.

After some time, Nanchang issued an official document requesting that he reside at Cuiyan. When he finally arrived, the Head Seat went out to meet him and asked, "Regarding the Dharma-treasury of Deshan—"
He did not ask what it was that constituted Linji’s great function. Yue addressed him sternly, saying, "Where have you come from? As the Head Seat prepared to answer, Yue struck him with his palm.
When the monk attempted to speak further, Yue shouted, "Lead your assembly back! Thereupon, the entire assembly stood in awe and reverence.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "In years past I visited here; today I come again. Not only has human affairs flourished once more,"
"Moreover, these forests and springs increase the vital energy. Now tell me, what is the single phrase regarding the principle of not harming things?

After a long silence, he said, "The heavens are high in the southeast; the earth slopes toward the northwest. He asked a monk, "Fenzhou said, 'If you recognize this staff, the business of traveling on pilgrimage is finished.
Holding up his staff, he said, 'This is the staff; which one is the business of traveling on pilgrimage? The monk was speechless.
He replied, "Yes. Yuanhe said, "Go straight into the thousands and tens of thousands of peaks. He then asked the monk, "Panshan said:
'It is like the earth upholding a mountain, unaware of the mountain's loftiness; it is like a stone containing jade, unaware of the jade's flawlessness. What does this mean?"
The monk had no reply. Yue said, "It is like the earth supporting a mountain, or a stone containing jade. From where did you obtain such news?

While living in seclusion on the mountain, he was frugal and personally labored in the fields. One night, a farmer tunneled through the ridges to steal water. Yue dispatched two laborers to patrol the area and caught him.

The farmer, in his desperation, pushed the first man (A) into the water; when they looked, he was already dead. The second man (B) fled and reported the matter to the county office. An official arrived to investigate.
Jiā Gài was a deceiver; he was imprisoned for his crimes. He was ordered to wear lay robes (*fèngyè*).

An elderly monk named Lóngxīng, who entered and left the prefectural seat on medical business, heard of this at night and went there to earnestly petition the magistrate, saying: "Rúyuè is a dragon-elephant of the Buddha-dharma;
how can he be allowed to leave the monastic community? The magistrate said: "The law is such. What can be done? I shall issue him a certificate of ordination (*dùjié*)."
Yue was able to travel by night and took refuge at He Mountain in Jizhou. There were those on the mountain who resented him and intended to harm him.
Yue then went to Nanyue to rely upon Chan Master Qinqin of Chengtian Temple. For ten years he did not leave his quarters, and his Way subsequently became widely renowned;
students turned their hearts toward him. He then left to reside at Falun Temple, where he personally supervised everything from the pounding of grain to the supervision of the reaping.

When he saw someone arriving carrying a bundle under their arm or on their back, he would look upon them with joy. But when he saw someone carrying a load on a shoulder pole, he would knit his brows and say, "Not yet;
in another thirty years, you shall be riding a horse on pilgrimage. Yuanxue was close friends with Chan Master Xian of Xinghua in Tanzhou.

Because Xian had resided there for a long time, he grew weary of the constant coming and going of visitors. Yuanxue repeatedly urged him to abandon it all and return to life among the forest trees. Xian—
He did not succeed. One day, while escorting a guest, he fell from his horse and injured his arm. He sent a letter to express his grievances to Xue. Xue replied with a verse:
"The Bodhisattva of Great Compassion has a thousand hands; Which great man does not possess them? Master Xinghua broke off one branch, And so he had only nine hundred and ninety-nine.
Xian laughed and said, "I am utterly defeated; there are no words to speak. Shortly thereafter, [Xue] was transferred to reside [elsewhere].

Yunfeng ascended the seat on the eighth day of the seventh month in the seventh year of the Jiayou era to take leave of the assembly. He spoke this verse: "I have lived in this world for sixty-six years;
as a monk, I have spent fifty-nine summer retreats. If those in the Chan lineage ask where my ultimate aim lies, my nostrils point straight down.
Thereupon, he passed away peacefully. His body was cremated, and five-colored śarīra were obtained, which were enshrined in a stupa north of Yuxi.
The commentary says: Huangbo’s great function was like a "poison-smeared drum"—those who struck it died. Two hundred years passed before Linji placed [the drum] back in use;
Master Zhi struck it once more, and Yunfeng died. As I read his words and phrases, they are like green mountains and white clouds, where opening and closing are sovereign;
they are like the bright moon in a blue pool, known only when one reaches out to grasp it. When it comes to his manifestation at Jicui...
Having seen Ciming, he established Heitang; having seen Jixi, he established Jicui. Regarding his public path of Dharma, he possessed the refined resonance of Dayu, Chen, and Muzhou.
Alas, while the monastic communities were sighing that he would never debase his hand [by accepting inferior disciples], those who succeeded him did so without interval.
How could one possibly know the joy of this?
*Chànlín Sēngbǎo Zhuàn*, Scroll 22 and Scroll 23.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huìhóng of Míngbái Ānjū during the Song Dynasty.
Chan Master Huanglong Baojue Xin was born into the Wu clan.
His secular name was Zuxin, and he was a native of Shixing in Nanxiong. In his youth, he was a renowned scholar;
however, at the age of nineteen, he became blind. His parents consented to his ordination, after which he suddenly regained his sight. He then went to seek refuge [with a master].

The śramaṇa Huiquan of Longshan Temple was to undergo an examination of his scriptural studies the following year; however, he alone contributed a poem and succeeded in gaining a place on the list of successful candidates.

He shaved his head and subsequently resided at Shouye Monastery, yet he did not observe the monastic precepts and encountered various adversities, whereupon he abandoned that place and entered the monastic forests to visit Chan Master Yunfeng Yue.
He remained there for three years, but as the Master found him stubborn and difficult to guide, he informed Yue that he intended to depart.
Yue said, "You must go and rely upon Master Huangbo Nan. Xuefeng went to Huangbo for four years; though he knew the Master possessed the truth, his own spiritual faculty did not yet manifest.
He then took leave and ascended to Yunfeng, whereupon Yue passed away. Consequently, he settled at Shishuang, yet still found nothing to resolve through inquiry.
Examine the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Transmission of the Lamp). It records a monk asking Zen Master Duofu:
"What is the meaning of 'a cluster of bamboo at Duofu'? Duofu replied, "One stalk, two stalks, leaning. The monk said, "I do not understand. Duofu said, "Three stalks, four stalks, bent.
At that moment, he suddenly realized that he had personally seen both masters; he returned directly to Huangbo. Just as he was unfolding his sitting cloth, Master Nan said, "You have entered my..."
[The Master] entered his quarters. The Master [Dongshan] was also filled with joy and said, "The Great Matter has always been thus.
Why must you, Preceptor, instruct people to contemplate the phrase and offer responses, searching for it by every possible means?

Nanquan replied, "If I did not cause you to investigate and seek in this manner until you reach a state where the mind has no application, so that you may see for yourself and accept it of your own accord, I would have buried your potential. The Master [Dongshan] remained composed.
He swam [in the depths of the teachings], sinking like a landmass into the midst of the assembly. From time to time, he went to Yunmen to resolve matters of doctrine and phrasing.
Master Nan said, "If you know such a matter, simply rest; why do you expend so much effort? He replied, "Not so. There is still a trace of doubt remaining."
Without reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), how could one move with such freedom—leaping here and there, turning heaven and earth? Master Nanyuan approved of him.
Subsequently, he went to see Chan Master Zhen of Cuiyan. Zhen was greatly amazed by his conversation with him. He remained in attendance for two years, after which Zhen passed away.
He then returned to Huangbo. Master Nan ordered him to share his seat and receive guests. Later, when Master Nan moved to reside at Huanglong, the Master went to pay his respects.
At that time, Chan Master Yue of Letan was renowned for his profound mastery of the subtle meanings of the sutras and treatises;
those in his circle laughed at him, saying he was merely failing to rest from his own efforts and had gone down from the high trees into the deep valleys. The Master [observed this].

He said: "That man uses the attainment of 'having-attained' to protect what precedes and block what follows. I, however, use the learning of 'no-more-learning' to serve as the central point for the hundred rivers.

During my time here at Zhangjiang, where I stayed while convalescing from a minor illness, Xia Yi Gongli—the Judicial Commissioner of the Transportation Office—whose mind was long devoted to Chan studies, met Yang Jie Cigong and sighed, saying: 'When I reached Jiangxi, I regretted not having known Master Nan. Cigong...
He said, "There is an Elder Xinxin at Zhangjiang. You should humble yourself to visit him; you need not wait to see Master Nan.
When Li went to see him, they engaged in a profound discussion until his spirit was completely relaxed and open.

When they reached the point in Sengzhao’s *Zhao Lun* concerning the convergence of all things within oneself, and the fact that the sentient and the insentient share a single essence, there happened to be a dog lying beneath the incense table. Li struck the dog with a ruler. Furthermore—
He struck the incense table and said, "The dog has sentience and thus departs; the incense table lacks sentience and remains.
How can sentience and insentience become one body? The Master could not respond. The Master said, "As soon as one enters into deliberation, it becomes a superfluous teaching."
When have you ever realized that the myriad phenomena are oneself? Furthermore, he once discussed the *Vimalakīrti* with a monk, saying:
"The thirty-two thousand lion thrones made of precious gems entered the small room of Vimalakīrti; why was there no obstruction?

Was this due to the supernatural power manifested by Vimalakīrti, or was it some other extraordinary artifice? Indeed, because it is a dharma difficult to believe, he manifested this auspicious sign. Is there anyone who..."
Regarding "faith": one has already known that which has been inherently present from the beginning; for what reason, then, is one further commanded to have faith? It is said:
If there were no entry through faith, the small would necessarily obstruct the great. Nevertheless, since the dharma of faith already exists, from what does it arise? Furthermore, he spoke a verse:
"As soon as one withdraws the mind before the gate of the pavilion, it opens early without needing a snap of the fingers. Once Sudhana departed, there was no further news;

outside the gate, spring has arrived and the grass grows green of its own accord. These instructions are intimate and direct; such are his skillful means, which are wondrous and subtle. Most of them are like this.
When Master Nangong entered nirvana, the Master succeeded him as abbot for twelve years. However, by nature he was straightforward and did not delight in being occupied with worldly affairs;
he requested to resign five times before finally being granted leave to retire and live in seclusion. Consequently, his students grew even more intimate with him.

When Xie Jingwen (style name Shizhi) was serving as Governor of Tanzhou, he sent an invitation to the Master to come to Daming Mountain. The Master declined three times and refused to go, yet he further instructed those in Jiangxi:
Peng Ruli, the Commissioner for Transport, inquired about the reason why the Master would not go to Changsha.
The Master said, "I wish to see Master Xie; I do not wish to take charge of Daowei. Before Mazu and Baizhang, there was no office of abbot.

"Waymen seek one another only at the shores of empty, secluded, and silent places. Although there have been abbots since then who were honored and venerated by kings and ministers as teachers of gods and humans, it is not so now.

They merely hang their names upon government offices like subjects registered in the census, and are simply summoned by the *wubo* (police runners). How could this ever be done again? When the Master heard this directly, he did not [approve].
"I venture to trouble you with matters concerning our monastery; I wish to see you once. When the Master arrived at Changsha, the Teacher [Dongshan] wished to receive his dharma instructions.
The Master set forth the essential principles for him. His words were luminous and vast, like the clear blue sky made easily recognizable by the sun. Their summary states:

"The teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the canon are no different from describing food to someone who has never tasted it. Since the flavor of the food depends on another's description, its..."
Food must be tasted by oneself directly. Once one has tasted it personally, one can then fully discern its flavor—whether it is sweet or pungent, salty or bland.
The coming of the Dharma Master from the West to point directly at the human mind and see one's nature to become a Buddha is likewise so.
Since true nature is manifested through words and letters, it must be personally seen by oneself. If one can see it personally, then...
One is able to discern that what is currently present is either real or false, and what is birth or death.

Once one can discern the reality and falsehood of birth and death, one turns back to examine all language and text, seeing that they are all merely conventional expressions and possess no ultimate meaning.

If one does not understand this now, where does the illness lie? The illness lies in seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; it is because one does not know the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) as it truly is.

Regarding that which is encountered: one identifies this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing as being what one has personally seen. Yet one fails to realize that this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing all arise through the discrimination of external objects;
if those external objects and realms did not exist, then this very seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing would likewise not exist.
"It would be just like a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns; there would be nothing to which they could be traced. The Master heard this and said, "I have heard what I never heard before.
He further replied to Han Shilang Zonggu’s question, saying: "I have received your instruction that in the past you attained awakening and were free from doubt.

However, as for the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) accumulated since beginningless time, these cannot yet be exhausted all at once. Since there is no dharma remaining outside the mind, I do not know whether these afflictions and habitual tendencies are..."
What thing do you wish to exhaust? If you give rise to such a thought, it will instead become the mistake of mistaking a thief for one’s own son.

From the time of the ancient patriarchs down to the present, every word spoken—even those that prescribe medicine according to the illness—has been intended to treat afflictions and habitual tendencies through the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision;
these are all skillful means and provisional teachings designed to guide and lead others. If there were truly such habitual tendencies...
To claim that the breath can be regulated is to suggest that there is a dharma external to the mind that can be brought to an end. This is like a sacred tortoise dragging its tail through the mud;
as soon as one tries to wipe away the tracks, more tracks are produced. One might say this is "using the mind to employ the mind," which only serves to reveal that the illness has grown deeper.

If one could truly clarify the mind, there would be no dharma outside the mind, and no mind outside dharmas. Since both mind and dharma are non-existent, whom else would you wish to instruct on how to suddenly bring them all to an end? You, sir—

Born and raised in the far south, he devoted himself early on to the propagation of the Dharma. Dwelling among the mountains and forests during an era of great peace, he wished to visit the capital to spend his remaining years.
Upon arriving in the capital, Prince of Jin, Wang Si—the Imperial Son-in-law and Commander-in-Chief—received him with the utmost courtesy.
He established a hermitage outside the national gates, but after a long time, he returned south. He traveled once more to Mount Lu, where Peng Qizhi...
[He was] guarding the Nine Rivers. When the Master (Gong) saw him, he asked with composed dignity, "When a person approaches the end of life, is there a definitive judgment?
Gong replied, "There is. He said, "I wish to hear its explanation. Gong said, "Wait until you die, and I shall explain it.
Qi-zi rose and increased his reverence, saying, "This matter must indeed come from the Master; for among the high officials of the four quarters, [only one] would harmonize with this."

He responded to invitations from a thousand *li* away; yet if the conditions were not right, he would not travel even a few *she*. A verse says: I do not dwell in the temples of the Tang court; Leisurely, I am a monk of the Song land.
My livelihood consists of the three-fold patched robe; My only companion is a single staff. I beg for food as circumstances allow, And go wherever I may.
"When encountering a mountain, climb it as you please; when meeting others, do not mock one another. This is not something that can be mastered merely by being from Lingnan.

From this, one can imagine the character of Master Huanglong Nan. His countenance was that of a man of the Way, and his presence commanded awe; he was extremely difficult to approach, even for those who had long been seasoned within the monastic forests.

Upon seeing him, one’s sweat would break out. When the Duke approached him, he appeared exceedingly relaxed; they would converse and laugh together all day long, such that the roles of teacher and disciple were forgotten.
Throughout these forty years, many among the scholar-officials were inspired and awakened by hearing his influence.

Because his skillful means were boundless and his universal compassion was impartial, those who had not yet seen him might have been arrogant or slanderous; yet once they encountered his countenance and received his words, none failed to be moved to submission.
As for Ying: once the Duke had reached an advanced age, he moved his hermitage even deeper into the mountains and cut off all contact with students.
After another twenty-odd years, he passed away at midnight on the sixteenth day of the eleventh month in the third year of the Yuánfú era. He had lived seventy-six years in this world.

He sat in meditation for fifty-five summer retreats and was granted the title Baojue (Precious Enlightenment). He was buried to the east of Nan Gong’s stupa; these two were known as the "Double Stupas.
His foremost disciple who attained the Dharma was Weiqing, for whom there is a separate biography.
The commentary states: On the day Master Nangong passed away, the Master composed a verse, saying:
"The time when the ancients departed is today; Yet today, as before, they do not return. Since they do not come now, nor did they go then, White clouds and flowing waters linger in vain.
Who says the scale and ruler are level? Within the straight, there is still the crooked. Who says the principles of things are uniform? Planting hemp, one still reaps [linen]."
Millet. How pitiable are those who race about throughout the world! Six times six is originally thirty-six.

Master Nan said, "I shall follow whatever you desire, even your delusions," using such phrases as "Southern Dipper seven, Northern Dipper eight. This old man was a son who truly upheld his ancestral legacy.
Alas, that this great man has fallen; the eye of the world is extinguished. There is nothing I have ever read that does not cause my heart to break. Upon reading this...

These are but traces of the past; yet they are like gazing at the moon in the southeast on a clear evening after the rain has ceased—brightly shining amidst ten thousand stars, one forgets that one’s own body is amidst the spitting mist.

Chan Master Létán Zhènghuì Wén, known as Upādhyāya Zhènghuì, was born into the Zhèng clan of Wénxiāng in Shǎnfǔ. The Zhèng lineage had produced many renowned ministers for generations. From birth, the Master was exceptionally distinguished;
he lost his father in childhood and served his stepmother with the utmost filial piety. However, he did not win her affection, and she repeatedly humiliated and oppressed him. His father grew old...
He felt pity for him and sent him to travel and study in the four directions. Upon reaching the Northern Pagoda in Fuzhou, he heard the Venerable Guang preaching the Dharma;
moved to tears, he tore his formal robes and took him as his teacher. Thus, the Northern Pagoda was named after him, Kewen. He was twenty-five years old.

He tested his mastery of what he had studied, shaved his head, and received full ordination (*upasampadā*). In his study of the sūtras and śāstras, there was nothing in which he did not reach the pinnacle of excellence.
He eclipsed the lecture halls of the capitals of Chang’an and Luoyang, acting as both host and guest, and several times he elucidated profound and abstruse meanings.

While walking along the corridors of the Longmen palace, he saw a clay statue of a bhikṣu with its eyes closed as if in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The Master was suddenly struck with self-reproach and said to his companions: "What I..."
As for his "carrying the burden": it was like the figure paintings of Wu Daozi; although they were executed with ultimate skill, they lacked the quality of being truly alive.

Thereupon, he abandoned them, saying, "I shall travel south to observe the Way. Wherever he went, his debates overwhelmed those present, and people pointed at him, regarding him as one who had reached the full measure of realization.
In the summer of the second year of the Zhìpíng era, while sitting at Dàméi, he heard a monk reciting the words of Yúnmén: "The Buddha..."
"The Dharma is like the moon in the water. "Is it so? [The Master] replied, "In the clear waves there is no path through. At that moment, he attained great enlightenment.
At that time, National Teacher Nan was at Jici. The Master went to visit him. National Teacher Nan asked, "From where have you come?
He replied, "From Mount Gui. Nan said, "It happens that the old monk is not here. He pressed further, "I wonder where he has gone? Nan said, "To Tiantai."
During a communal work session, Nanyue went on a journey and said, "If that is so, then this student may also go with complete freedom.
Master Nan replied, "Where did you get those sandals on your feet? He answered, "I purchased them for seven hundred coins at Mount Lu. Master Nan said:
"How have you ever been at ease? The Master pointed and said, "How have you ever not been at ease? Master Nán was struck with awe by this.

At that time, the Head Seat Hongyīng possessed a sharpness of wit that could not be provoked; he was as renowned as the Master. Yīng was a native of Shǎowǔ and was known among the assembly as "Yīng of Shǎowǔ.
Wén of Guānxī remained for some time before taking his leave and staying with Chan Master Shùn of Cuìyán. Shùn said, "You..."
Your spiritual lineage is eminent and you have attained realization of the vast and great. When Linji was about to fall, it was your strength that sustained him. Cherish yourself well.
When Master Nanyuan resided at Huanglong, the Master went there once again. Nanyuan said, "Just now I ordered an attendant to roll up the curtain; I asked him—"

[The student asked: "What is it like when he rolls up the curtain? [The Master] said: "He illuminates the whole world. [The student asked: "What is it like when he lets down the curtain? [The Master] said: "Not a drop can leak through. [The student asked: "What is it like when neither rolling it up nor letting it down? The attendant was speechless. [The Master said to the student: "How would you handle this? The teacher replied: "Rolling up the curtain is like the rising sun; letting it down is like the setting moon.

When neither is done, the light is extinguished and the world is dark. At that moment, there is no place for the mind to dwell. If you can enter this state, you will see that the ten directions are all one's own body; if you cannot, you will remain lost in the darkness of ignorance."
The Master said, "Only after the Abbot has taken the place of the attendant and entered the Nirvana Hall can it be done. Nan Gong remarked, "A man from Guansi truly has no head.
He then looked at a monk standing nearby, and the Master pointed at him, saying, "Even this monk has not yet seen it in his dreams. Nan Gong laughed heartily.
From then on, those among his disciples who were considered eminent, extraordinary, or broad-minded would shrink back in awe whenever they saw him. When Nan Gong passed away... Nan [Gong].

Having traveled to Mount Heng, he returned to Mount Yang to lead the assembly of monks. In the fifth year of the Xining era, he arrived at Gao’an. The Prefect, Mr. Qian Yi, had previously sent word to him.
When the Master went to pay his respects, a mastiff escaped from behind a screen; as the Master was about to step forward to meet it, the dog retreated slightly, allowing him to advance. Mr.
Qian mocked him, saying, "A Chan practitioner is surely capable of instructing snakes and tigers, yet you are afraid of a dog? The Master replied: [text continues]

It is said: "The tigers in the mountain recesses are easy to subdue, but the dragons protecting the residence are difficult to bring down. Master Qian sighed and remarked, "A person must not have a reputation that is empty of substance.
He resided at the two monasteries of Dongshan and Shengshou for twelve years. Upon retiring from his duties, he traveled east to the Three Wu regions and eventually reached Jinling.

At that time, Imperial Uncle Shu was receiving a stipend as an official in the Imperial Kitchen and was residing at Dinglin Monastery. Hearing that the Master had arrived, he rushed out to welcome him, his shoes falling off as he stepped hastily. The Prince asked:
All sutras begin by specifying the time and place; the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* alone is not thus. Why is this? The Master said:

"That which is expounded in the Sudden Vehicle directly reveals to sentient beings that which is manifest in daily life, belonging neither to the present nor to antiquity. It is simply this very moment between me, the old monk, and you, Excellency."
They enter together into the Great Radiance Treasury (Mahāprabhāsa-garbha), sporting in samādhi, acting as host and guest to one another, regardless of time or place.

Again he asked: "The Sūtra states that all sentient beings have realized Perfect Enlightenment (Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra, etc.). Yet Guifeng [Zongmi] interprets 'realization' (zhèng) as 'possession' (jù), claiming it is a scribal error in the translation.
How can this be? He replied: "If the term 'Perfect Enlightenment' could be changed, then the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* could also be changed. How could the *Vimalakīrti*..."

It does not say: "Nor does one attain realization by extinguishing sensation. Indeed, to attain realization without extinguishing the aggregate of sensation is identical in meaning to the intent of realizing *yuanjue* (perfect enlightenment) universally.
For the active ignorance (*avidyā*) of sentient beings is precisely the fundamental great wisdom (*mahājñāna*) of the Tathāgata.
Guifeng’s statement was incorrect. Emperor Shu was greatly pleased and praised him for many days, bestowing his own residence upon him as a gift.

At the temple, he took Master Yan as the first founding patriarch. King Shu [Huizong], having heard of the Master’s spiritual conduct from Emperor Shen [Shenzong], issued an imperial edict bestowing upon him the title Zhenjing.
Not long after, weary of the bustle of the city, he returned to Gao’an and built a hermitage at the foot of Jiufeng, naming it Toulao (Retirement).
Students came to him from afar; after six years, he moved to reside at Guizong. Two years later, Zhang...

At that time, the Chancellor was serving as the Left Minister when he was demoted to an official post for wine at Jinling. Later, appointed as the Commander of Nanchang, he passed through Mount Lu and saw that the Master was robust and healthy;
he treated him with the utmost courtesy and exerted all his efforts to invite him to reside at Letan. Shortly thereafter, the Master retired to Yun’an.

On the first day of the tenth month in the first year of the Chongning era, he manifested an illness. On the fifteenth day, the illness abated, and he attended to his lifelong collection of cherished objects and ritual implements.
He recorded each of these matters in detail and distributed them among his disciples. On the night of the sixteenth day, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat in the full lotus posture.

When the assembly requested him to preach the Dharma, the Master smiled and said, "This year I am seventy-eight; the four elements are now parting. As fire and wind have already dispersed, there is no need for further talk at the time of departure.
His final instructions concerned entirely the great affairs of the Zen school; he did not speak of private matters. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
He passed away in silence. Seven days later, his body was cremated; flames of five colors blazed forth, and white light ascended into the sky. Wherever the smoke reached, it produced śarīra relics.
More than a thousand monastics and laypeople all obtained them. They were divided and enshrined in stupas at Letan, beneath Baolian Peak, and to the north of Liuyundong Cave at Dongshan.
The encomium says: Yun’an possessed a nature bestowed by Heaven; without relying on the instructions of a teacher, he naturally attained the Way.

He specifically established his own school of thought based solely upon Huanglong. He dismantled the formalistic study of doctrine and exposed its hidden obscurities through his eloquence of joyful exposition.

He washed away the dust from the Buddha-sun, causing King Shu to submit with a heart of reverence and sincerity. Eventually, he presented his name to the Son of Heaven and offered his residence as a jeweled monastery;
thus, his Way became manifest. Yet, he still shook his head and refused to look back, preferring instead to find liberation among the myriad valleys and thousand crags.

Observing his conduct, it was clear that his mind remained unconvinced by worldly establishments. Later, Mount Qin and Caoxi came to be regarded as the primary centers of the school for an entire generation.
The master’s exemplary model serves as a standard for later monastics.
*Chánlín Sēngbǎo Zhuàn*, Scroll Twenty-three;
*Chánlín Sēngbǎo Zhuàn*, Scroll Twenty-four.
Composed by the Chan monk Honghui of the Mingbai Hermitage in Song.
Chan Master Weishi of Yangshan:
The master’s name was Xingwei. He was born into the Shi clan and was a native of Daming. From childhood, he seldom smiled or spoke; he would sit motionlessly upon the ground.

Throughout his life, a "hidden rhinoceros" protruded from his forehead, and his eyebrows and eyes were sparse and elegant; everyone marveled at him. At the age of nineteen, he traveled to the capital.
Hearing that Master Dacheng of Baoxiang Monastery was currently possessed of excellent discernment, he went to visit him. Dachi said, "Your spirit and appearance are extraordinary;

however, you are not one who should be placed among the 'Flying Smoke' or 'Qilin' [figures of the Tang dynasty]. You are precisely the one who should bare his shoulders and bear the burden of the Tathāgata. Thus he was acclaimed.
Dongwei said with joy, "This is my own heart's desire. I wish to serve as your attendant to sweep and clean, while you further devote yourself to teaching and gathering disciples.
Dongwei was content to apply himself with diligence; he pulled carts to transport grain, split firewood to assist with cooking, and did everything that was required for thirteen years.

He then shaved his head and received full ordination. Taking leave of Huikai, he traveled on foot through various regions. Huikai sent him to Luoyang, where he subsequently received the teachings of Xianshou from the Great Tripitaka Master.
He became famous and succeeded to the master’s seat, with a constant retinue of over a thousand followers. He gave lectures without a fixed residence;

whenever his disciples wished to follow him on his southern travels, Fazhao never refused them. Upon reaching the banks of the Huai River, every Zen monastery he visited was filled with widespread acclaim for his reputation.

The Master’s name was Wei. He found this strange and took up residence in an ancient temple on Mount Huai. There he saw his former fellow student, Faliang, wearing a coarse, dark robe that hung loosely;

his skirts were high and his two calves were wrapped in cloth. Startled, Wei exclaimed, "Liang has also fled! He called out for those who had traveled with him, and they gathered to gaze at him with deep sighs.
Liang merely smiled and exchanged pleasantries regarding the weather. Wei asked, "You now call yourself a Chan practitioner. What is the profound mystery of the Chan school?"
Yi Yu said, "I have come. Huilang replied, "Wait until after I am dead, and I shall explain it for you. Daowei asked, "Are you mad? Huilang said, "My madness has already ceased;
yours is now merely burning fiercely. He then immediately departed. Daowei summoned his followers and said, "Huilang’s learning and insight are profound and extensive;
his knowledge of the Dharma and understanding of its meaning are twice that of mine. I accept this now. There must surely be something superior in the Chan school," and he went alone to visit him.
Huangbo went to visit Master Nan and stayed with him for two years. Every time he entered the master’s quarters, Master Nan would invariably close his eyes.
After a long while, Nan would finally speak. Huangbo asked, "When you see Xingwei coming, why must you close your eyes?
Nan replied, "When Magu saw Liangsu approaching, he was carrying a hoe and weeding. Liangsu attained realization at that moment. When I see you coming, I simply close my eyes idly; although you..."

There was no awakening. Yet, he still harbored doubts, which might have been excusable. Weizi did not understand this. At that time, Chan Master Yue of Lestam was sitting in summer retreat with Master Nan at Jicui.
Yue was renowned for his mastery of the sutras and treatises; Weizi had often attended his seat and listened to his discussions.
Consequently, while reading the *Biographies of the Lesser Śākyamuni*, he came across the passage where Minister Wei asked Master Ji of Yangshan: "Chan Master, [what about] Xun..."
"How do you usually receive people? Jì said, "When a monk comes, I always ask him, 'What have you come for? He says, 'I have come to pay my respects.
I then ask again, 'Do you see the old monk? He says, 'I see him. I ask once more, 'How is the old monk like? The monk has never been able to answer."
Wei said, "If you say you see him, how can you account for the donkey? If you say you do not see him, whom are you now paying homage to? Because of this, it was difficult to answer.
Ji said, "There is no one who can analyze this as skillfully as the Minister. Yuegong praised this as excellent, and Wei also agreed.
Nan alone said, "That the lineage of the Guiyang and Linji schools has not reached the present day is precisely because of this flaw. Wei [practiced] day and night.
He pondered this deeply but could not fathom its meaning. Intending to travel westward, he divined a site for a hermitage beneath Mount Songxiao, where he would live as a monk supported by alms.
One night, while sitting together with another monk, the latter asked, "The *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of attaining the *dhāraṇī* of understanding the languages of all sentient beings.
What kind of language is this *dhāraṇī*? Master Nan turned his gaze toward the incense burner. The monk immediately quoted [the passage].

Nanping reached out his hand to check whether there was fire; finding no fire, he again approached and added an incense stick. He then stood in his original position. Nanping smiled and said, "Is this *dhāraṇī*?
Weijing was struck with great surprise and asked, "How do you interpret it? Nanping told the monk to leave for now.
As the monk pulled back the curtain and hurried out, Nanping said, "If you had not understood, how could you have acted like that? Only then did Weijing attain realization.
Fawei was extremely strict in regulating his own conduct; he would sit in meditation, forgetting both night and day. He occupied a single room and declined all social visits.
Whenever someone of superior virtue arrived, he would vacate his own seat to welcome them, rising personally to light incense and standing with palms joined.

When Master Nanyue heard of this, he considered it an extreme form of distancing oneself from others, contrary to the principle of blending one's light with the dust of the world, and he admonished him in person. Fawei replied, "My cultivation of the Way is not yet perfected."

Time flows like a river. For those of great capacity, even Yunmen and Zhaozhou said, "I only employ my mind for the two times of eating gruel and rice," and further, "How could I have leisure time to waste?
How much more so for one of noble character whose daily practice and eons are multiplied by ten thousandfold?
How could such a person afford to be confined by worldly sentiments, engage in idle talk, flatter others, or increase the sense of self? —From the South.

The Duke esteemed him. In the second year of the Xining era, Nan Gong passed away at Huanglong. A messenger from Jiangxi issued an official summons to invite him, and he was brought with great ceremony to reside at Yangshan.
Within less than a year, his Dharma seat became preeminent throughout the Jianghuai region; those who had previously studied under him and were well-known all gathered there.
Both monastics and laypeople honored and served him, regarding him as the reincarnation of Tongzhi. By nature he was firm, and he managed affairs with [dignity].
The monastic regulations stipulated that certain individuals should hold specific offices and perform specific duties, and none dared to disobey them. Once, twelve men were sent out on a mission;

Wei recorded their names and gave them to the *vina* (steward), instructing him to have them all return the following day to receive detailed instructions. However, when they gathered for tea, one person was invariably missing.
Dawe asked who it was. [The attendant] replied, "Suizhou Yongtai. Just as Dawe was in the midst of making arrangements, the Head Seat said, "Tai has gone off on a mountain tour;
please appoint another monk to fill the vacancy. Dawe agreed. Shortly thereafter, someone reported, "Tai is actually here;
the Head Seat is hiding him to deceive the assembly. Dawe assumed a solemn expression and had him searched for. Tai confessed that he had been timid and weak, fearing he would fail [in his duties].
Regarding the matter at hand: the head seat (shouzuo) was truly unaware. Weiming ordered the bell to be struck to assemble the community and announced:

"The head seat has already shared the seat to transmit the Way; furthermore, he is someone esteemed by our late teacher. To act with a darkened heart and deceive the assembly—this would be unacceptable even for anyone else."

"Would you then willingly bring about your own ruin? The head seat (shouzuo) held his breath and accepted the punishment; Yuongtai was expelled from the monastery. All quarters submitted to his impartiality.
Later, Yongtai succeeded to his Dharma and resided at Huangbo Mountain; the head seat resided at Guishan and succeeded Huanglong.
During a great summer night, he sat in a deep forest. Because the Master had eaten mosquitoes and gadflies, his intestines became poisoned; for ten days it did not heal.
He cut off about a foot of the affected section with a knife, but the flow of blood would not stop. His disciples wept and said, "Master, why alone do you not endure this a little longer?"
He said, "Because it obstructs my practice of the Way, I lie prostrate upon this bed, providing no benefit to anything. Would not death be better than life?
On the twenty-sixth day of the eleventh month in the third year of the Yuanfeng era, he spoke a verse and passed away. Three days later, his body was cremated, and five-colored śarīras were obtained;
his bones and stones were found linked together by cords. He was enshrined in a stupa to the east of the temple. [End of] reading.
Sixty-three years in this world; he sat for thirty-three summer retreats.

Yes. Chan Master Chaosheng of Donglin Zhaojue was originally named Changsheng.
He was of the Shi clan from Youxi in Jianzhou. His mother dreamed of a man, tall and stately, with a complexion like gold.

He held three stalks of white lotus flowers and bestowed them upon her; however, she received only one stalk, while the others were dropped to the ground. Upon awakening, she became pregnant and later gave birth to three sons.
Her eldest and middle sons both died in infancy, and he was their youngest. At the age of eleven, he entered the monastic order under Dharma Master Wenzhao of Baoyun Temple.
Eight years later, he shaved his head and traveled to Dazhong Temple in Jianzhou to attend upon Vinaya Master Qisi.

Upon receiving full ordination, his divine contemplation was extraordinary; he moved with the grace of a phoenix and gazed with the intensity of a tiger, his majestic presence eclipsing the ten thousand monks—a truly magnificent figure.
Initially arriving at Heishan in Jizhou, he relied upon Master Cizhi. Although Cizhi was highly esteemed by the public, he treated him with such profound courtesy that he did not detain him.
Hearing of the reputation of Master Nan, he took leave of Cizhi and went to Guizong. After a long time there, having gained nothing, he departed. At that time, Guizong Temple was destroyed by fire.
Tong went to follow Master Nan at the Southern Pagoda of Shimen.

When Master Nan moved from Shimen to Jicui at Huangbo, and later from Jicui to Huanglong, Tong was present at all these locations. Over a period of twenty years, he made seven such journeys back and forth.
Master Nan praised his diligent efforts before the assembly. Tong himself believed that he had secretly received the essential meaning of the Great Dharma.
Jue resolved to greatly support the Linji school, and his reputation spread ever further; monastic communities vied with one another to honor him.

When Master Nan passed away, he wept so deeply that no sound could be heard, lingering there unable to bear leaving. The following year, the Prefect of Hongzhou, Lord Rong, requested that he reside at Letan.
His disciples said to one another, "Mazu has returned! and both clergy and laity scrambled to be the first to follow him.
"I wish to see him. In the third year of the Yuanfeng era, an imperial edict was issued to convert the monastic residence of Donglin in Jiangzhou from the Vinaya school to a Chan seat.

He eventually found it in a remote valley at Shushan in Xin Gan. He then accepted the imperial summons. His disciples further said to one another, "Master Huiyuan once made a prophetic record, saying:

At Haichanyuan, Zongguo repeatedly declared that he was old and infirm and could not comply with the imperial decree. Nevertheless, the provincial and prefectural authorities pressed him with urgency as if fire were falling from the stars.

Such was the way he won the hearts of the multitude. When the mountain gate sent out emissaries for alms, they often went to remote borderlands filled with miasmic fogs; some even died there.

Whenever he was present, [the master] would invariably weep as he established the altar for offerings and performed the funeral rites with full ceremony to deliver the deceased. For this reason, everyone was moved to tears.

On the twenty-ninth day of the ninth month in the sixth year, he manifested illness. Having finished his bath, he sat upright and passed away in profound stillness.
On the eighth day of the tenth month, his entire body was interred to the east of the Yantan Pagoda. He had lived for sixty-seven years and spent forty-nine summer retreats in meditation.

The Eulogy states: I once visited Donglin and gazed upon it with deep sighs, reflecting on the merit of its founding [during the reign of Emperor Zhenzong] and the flourishing state of its monastic community.
Were it not for a Great Being of great aspirational power (*praṇidhāna*), none could have accomplished such a feat. As Su Dongpo’s verse says: "Majestic was Master Tong, a dragon among monks;

It was as if he were conversing and laughing without rising from his seat, yet transforming the area beneath Mount Lu into a palace for Brahmā, Śakra, and the nāgas and devas.

The Chan Master’s name was Mu Zhe. He was born into the Wen clan of Linchuan. The Wen lineage was of humble means, and Zhe had lost both parents while still young.
He went to rely upon Vinaya Master Yuanjue of Yong’an in Jianchang as a novice. Upon testing his studies, he received ordination and the full precepts.

By nature, he was upright and simple, yet possessed profound insight; he made it his vow to uphold the Dharma and disciplined himself with rigorous adherence to the Vinaya. This was Chan Master Zhen of Cuiyan.
While traveling, Zhe was able to recognize him. Zhen truly displayed his strengths to cover over others' virtues, earning the nickname "True Dot-on-the-Chest.
Wherever he went, he provoked the public's anger and was ridiculed by all. For twenty years, Zhe associated with him; even when living among a crowd, [Zhe] did not dare to lose propriety.
When Zhen resided at two monasteries, Zhe secretly assisted him in establishing them as centers for the Dharma. To those who came to study, he would first have them meet [Zhe].
The attendant Zhe said to people, "Thirty years from now, Zhe will perform great Buddhist works.

After Zhen passed away, he enshrined him in a stupa on the Western Mountain and observed the period of mourning for three years before departing to rely upon Huangbo. He then traveled through the region of Xiang, his single almsbowl moving like clouds.

Whether a bird flies away or remains depends on the gravity or lightness of the forest. When Xie Shizhi was serving as the Governor of Tanzhou, he heard of his reputation and took delight in it, yet could not prevail upon him to come.

Shortly thereafter, he was transferred to reside at Dayue, where the assembly numbered two thousand. Bound by his regulations, every person disciplined themselves accordingly. Only...
After the morning gruel, he would receive questions from his disciples; this was called "entering the room. After the midday meal, he invariably held a tea assembly for the great assembly.

While at other monasteries such gatherings occurred only once or twice a month, Master Zhe held them without fail every day. Following the conclusion of the evening session, Zhe personally engaged in manual labor.

His attendants were by his side like strangers. For fourteen years, morning incense and evening lamps burned before him. At night he performed prostrations while holding *māra* grass, watching the lamps in the halls and corridors;
when weary, he would cover his head with his monastic robe and doze in the Hall of the Three Sages. At first he still bathed, but until his old age he did not bathe for over ten years.

At Haeseonwon Temple, the scholar-officials of the capital longed to behold his dignified bearing. Within the monastic community, they respected his wisdom and his inclination toward quietude, fearing the bustle of the world, and did not dare to expect his arrival.
Yet when he received the imperial summons, he accepted with joy and arrived accompanied by several monks. On the day his belongings were unpacked, the entire city came to witness the event;
it was said that it was as if a Buddha had appeared in the world. The temple grounds were narrow, yet the number of monks increased daily until there was no more space.

Dong then lay down on the ground with his head resting upon [Zhe’s] pillow. When someone requested that he set a limit [to his stay], Zhe said, "The Sangha is that from which Buddhas and Patriarchs arise.

Why do you utter such inauspicious words? Zhe loved others through virtue; if matters did not accord with the truth, he would certainly confront and rebuke them. He had little affinity for preaching the Dharma.

[The Master] adorned [the assembly], treating the noble and the humble with equal regard. When asked by a student about the story of Zhaozhou washing his bowl, "How do you, Venerable Sir, understand it?
as the monk was about to respond, Zhe placed his hand upon him and said, "Rest. From the time he shared the seat and welcomed others until the end, he never once altered his fundamental approach.

I observe that while his hidden conduct and subtle functions were found among the mountains and beneath the trees, the manifestations of his wondrous portents at the moment of birth and death occurred instead within the capital of the Son of Heaven. Chan Master Yunju You, whose name was Yuan Yu, was of the Wang clan and a native of Shangrao in Xin Prefecture. At the age of thirteen, he took Bo Shan as his teacher.

He obtained five-colored śarīra relics that emitted light; this light would swallow and eclipse all other lights until they eventually faded. Suddenly, the mountains and forests were covered in white flowers.

He lived for sixty-six years and sat in meditation for forty-two summer retreats. Wǔ was thin and emaciated, and though his hair had turned white, he did not cut it. His demeanor was exceptionally distinguished.
When preaching the Dharma, he enjoyed criticizing and rebuking various quarters, often referring to himself with refined self-deprecation as "the Elder Wáng Wǔ."
The eulogy says: When I was young, I traveled to Mount Lu and paid my respects to the Master at the Daolin Hall by the Jade Stream. At that time, the Master had recently recovered from an illness;
leaning on a staff, he came out and sat upon a rope-cot. His emaciated bones were fully exposed, yet his spiritual bearing was transcendent, like the Subhūti depicted in the world’s paintings.
The few words he spoke were all worthy of recitation. Alas! Today we shall no longer see such an elder. Its...

The Chan Master’s name was Qingxian. He was the son of the Zhuo family of Gutian in Fuzhou. His mother dreamed that a foreign monk gave her a bright pearl;
she swallowed it and subsequently conceived. Upon his birth, a white light illuminated the room. From childhood, he did not approach wine or meat.

At the age of eleven, he entered the service of the śramaṇa Dequan of Mount Sheng in Jianzhou. At seventeen, he received full ordination; at twenty, he traveled far away. His nature was pure and sincere, and he lacked...
He delighted only in the Way, which he pursued with thoroughness. His appearance was robust and his speech was sparse. Wherever he stayed, he remained aloof and rarely engaged with others;
if anyone approached him, he would simply raise a hand and depart. He served Master Nan as his father, and Master Nan held him in great affection.
At that time, he was at Huangbo together with Master Cuiyan Shun; Shun frequently interrogated Xian, who responded with sudden, spontaneous flashes of insight.
He made no concessions and appealed to Master Nan, saying, "I am seeking seclusion and ease; moreover, my words have not yet been fully examined, and I fear they may offend you.
Master Nan said, "The Dharma is thus. To seek seclusion through worldly sentiment is to create right and wrong—is this truly possible? Xian once asked Master Nan:
Regarding Wen Shouzuo (who was Yun’an): How was he when he was at Huangbo? Nan said: "When he was at Huangbo, he was like a man who has suddenly become wealthy;
he spent money as if it were mere soil and dung. Since you arrived, he is like a rich man for several generations, not spending a single coin in vain.

He replied, "The Buddhas have perhaps never reached the realm of Qingxian. [The Master] asked again, "What is the place where you were born? He replied, "This morning I ate white..."

He asked again, "How is my foot like a donkey’s foot? The reply was: "A heron standing in the snow is not of the same color.
Master Nan sighed and looked at him, saying, "Having shaved off your hair and beard, for what purpose do you do so? The reply was: "I simply wish to be without [delusion]."
The Master said, "In that case, 'A few sounds of the clear chime are beyond right and wrong; one idle man dwells within heaven and earth.
Xian said, "What words are these? The Master said, "You are a clever monk. Xian said, "That too is unnecessary. Master Nanyuan said:
"There is an Elder Bian here. You must show your mettle. Xuanzhe replied, "What excellence does he possess? Nanquan said, "He pats your back once;
what do you think of that? Xuanzhe asked, "What is he doing? Nanquan said, "He also extends both hands.
Xuanzhe said, "Where did you learn this empty gesture? Master Nanquan laughed heartily. Xuanzhe then extended both his own hands. Master Nanquan—

"That which you have used for thirty years has been caught and defeated this very morning. Master Nan laughed heartily and said, "In one sense, they are all spirits.
During Master Nan’s lifetime, students already vied to seek his guidance. After his passing, Zhang Gongjian, the Governor of Luling, invited him to reside at Longqing;

His countenance remained unchanged, and when his robes were put on, his hands and feet were supple and soft. Although his hair had been shaved, it grew back again. When the Prefect came to view him, he wished to preserve his entire body.
Sengliyan said, "His final instructions were that he should be cremated. When the wood was exhausted and the fire extinguished, his body remained in the lotus posture, unscattered.

Wherever the smoke reached—in the east, west, south, and north for forty li—all among the grasses, trees, sand, and pebbles, śarīras were obtained."
It was golden in color; when broken, it resembled gold dust. Monastics and laypeople purchased it with gold coins, and commoners picked it up and sold it;

this continued for several days without ceasing. Calculating what was obtained, it amounted to nearly several *hu*. He lived through fifty-five years of the world and sat in meditation for thirty-six summers.

The commentary states: Qian’an told me that Xian was a man of vigorous spirit and rapid speech. Once, while staying overnight together, I saw him sitting and dozing;

At first, I thought it was merely coincidental, but as we shared the same mat time after time, it was always so. This was surely because of his sincere devotion to the Way and his single-minded concentration.

"Therefore, I have emitted smoke; it was merely because I encountered a damp firewood log and relied on the smoke for warmth. Zhi turned back to run away. Yu called out to him, saying, "Come!

He acted with deliberate simplicity, which the Master [Zhaozhou] directly appreciated. He emerged from seclusion to reside at Daowu, where he soon moved to reside at Yungai for ten years.
He was ill in Chanlin, yet his mind remained supple and warm; his aspiration for the Way was tranquil and detached. Those who came to seek instruction would have him shake his head and refuse them.

In the sixth year of the Yuanyou era, he retired to the West Hall and closed his door for thirty years. When the monks of Xiangzhong heard that he had begun to receive visitors and allow them entry into his room, they flocked there.

His hall and chambers were filled [with disciples]. As for his wisdom, he was patient with the austerity and simplicity of human life; even in his old age, he continued to carry a hoe to tend his vegetable garden without ever flagging.
In the fourth year of the Zhenghe era, at the age of ninety, the Master of Tan, Zhou Zhongren, sent the Assistant Magistrate of Changsha to the mountain to request his presence for a meal offering.
Huiyi declined on the grounds of his old age, but the assistant magistrate insisted, saying, "The Governor, due to his official duties, is unable..."
When he entered the mountains, his subordinate officials sent word to come and welcome him with great earnestness; however, Huiyi did not go, fearing it would bring reproach upon the mountain gate.

Huiji boarded the carriage and arrived. Upon entering Kaifu Monastery, the drums were struck after the meal. Huiji asked for the reason, and they replied, "We request that you, Master, take charge of this monastery."

Zhixian realized he had fallen for his ruse; having no choice, he accepted. On the seventh day of the third month of the following year (some say the seventh day of the seventh month), he ascended the seat and spoke this verse:
"Before entering the world, my head was like a horse-dipper; after entering the world, my mouth is like a donkey's snout."
After a hundred years, one must inevitably perish of oneself. Let the world speculate as it will regarding his passing. The Abbot sat peacefully in his quarters; after a long while, he passed away.
During the cremation, five-colored śarīras were obtained. After ten days, commoners sifted through the ashes and still found them among the embers.
He had sat in meditation for sixty-six summers.
The Eulogy says: When I arrived at Yungai and stayed there for two years, I heard in detail about the past events concerning Huangbo and Cuiyan.
It was said that when Master Nan resided at Huanglong, all those in the world who were determined to study the Way gathered there; yet Master Nan looked upon them with dissatisfaction.
He asked them calmly what their intention was, and they replied: "When we saw Master Cimeng, although the assembly was large, it was not so numerous."
All were once majestic dragon-elephants, yet now they are reduced to such meager states that they no longer catch the eye of superior men.
From this day forward, the flourishing and decline of the Buddha-Dharma shall begin. Yun-gai is now old, and fifty years have passed since the time of Master Nan.
Those who were once called "meager" can no longer be seen. Because I have recorded his life story, I have moved by these events and thus recorded them all together here.

While reading the *Huayan lun* (Treatise on the Avatamsaka), I came to the passage stating: "Mount Sumeru stands within the great ocean, rising eighty-four thousand yojanas high;
it cannot be reached by grasping with hands or feet. This is used to clarify that the eighty-four thousand mountains of defilement (*kleśa*) abide within the great ocean of affliction (*kleśa*).
If sentient beings are able to remain within all phenomena without thought or volitional action, then afflictions will naturally dry up;
worldly toil becomes the mountain of omniscience, and afflictions become the ocean of omniscience. If they further give rise to mental deliberation, there is clinging;
thus worldly toil becomes ever higher and afflictions ever deeper, such that they cannot reach the state of the Buddhas.
