The general account: Chen Zhi was a man of great virtue and discernment. When Nan led the assembly, he was simple and dignified, never speaking or smiling frivolously.
Once, while practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*), his hands remained folded naturally at first; by midnight, they had gradually risen until they reached his chest.
His attendants would watch him constantly to await the crowing of the cock. Such was his diligence. He served as abbot for twenty years before moving to the two monasteries of Sijuzu and Kaiyuan.
Wherever he traveled, his monasteries were acclaimed as the foremost. Having grown old, he retired to live at Baoji Rock.
On the sixteenth day of the third month in the fourth year of the Xīníng era, he passed away without illness. He had lived for sixty-two years and spent forty-five summer retreats in meditation.

Chan Master Jingyin (Jìngyīn) was named Dazhen (Dàozhēn), with the courtesy name Bǎixiáng. He was the son of the Dài family of Gǔtián in Fúzhōu. From his youth, he abstained from meat and pungent herbs.
At the age of fourteen, he went to Shangsheng Monastery and practiced the dhūta austerities for another six years.

Regarding the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras, he set them aside and did not read them, saying, "These are merely expedient teachings. He then took a single alms bowl and traveled through the Jianghuai region.

Although he consulted many spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*), he received the definitive resolution of the ultimate meaning from Chan Master Yuan of Fushan at Chengtian Monastery in Jiangzhou, where the vacant seat had been offered to him. It was not [a mere formality].
He traveled to Danyang at his own will and stayed at Yinsheng. One day, while walking along the riverbank, he looked back at his boat and thought silently to himself, "I shall follow wherever I go;
let my karmic conditions take their course. He asked the boatman, "Would it be possible for you to carry me on the stern of your vessel?
The boatman laughed and said, "Where do you wish to go? My boat is bound for Bianzhou. Zhen replied, "I am traveling to the capital to tour it," and so the boatman took him aboard.
He then traveled north to pay his respects to Chan Master Jingyin Dajue Liaan. Liaan appointed him as the head of the assembly at his seat.

When Liaan returned to Wu, the community requested that Zhen succeed him. On the day he began to propagate the Dharma, Emperor Yingzong dispatched an imperial messenger to bestow incense, a purple robe, and a formal title.
The capital was a great center of convergence for all quarters, where tens of thousands of good and evil events occurred; it was frequented by nobles and distinguished persons.

The officials’ days were filled with visitors as they flocked to this single eye [of wisdom]. The Empress Dowager, who had ascended to the realm of immortals, summoned him to the Qingshou Palace by imperial decree.

The Emperor was greatly pleased upon receiving him in audience and ordered a high and spacious seat to be prepared, allowing him to engage in questions and answers at will. Those present—above, below, to the left, and to the right—experienced something unprecedented.
The sound of jubilation shook the palace, and he was granted very generous rewards. The Shenzong Emperor lamented the decline of the Buddha-dharma.
Compassionate toward the defects of names and forms, he first established the two monasteries of Huilin and Zhikai. Whenever he appointed a presiding monk, he invariably selected him himself;
even the most senior elders all followed his lead like grass bending in the wind. Three monks from Goryeo came to study under him.
Dazhen attained awakening according to his faculties, and the Divine Sovereign ascended to the realm of the immortals. By imperial decree, Dazhen was summoned to the Funing Hall to preach the Dharma.

The Emperor decreed that since Dazhen had long possessed virtuous conduct, he should be granted the title Chan Master Jingzhao (Pure Illumination). Dazhen was a man of dignified and tranquil withdrawal, appearing as if unable to speak.
He resided in the western corner of the capital city with more than forty disciples; he remained there in a state of humble seclusion, never venturing forth.
For thirty years, his household remained unchanged as if it were a single day. On the seventeenth day of the eighth month in the eighth year of the Yuanyou era, he passed away.
Previously, he had told his disciple Jingyuan: "In three days, I shall depart. When the time arrived, he bathed, changed his robes, and after reciting a verse of gāthā, he passed away.
He passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. He lived for eighty years and spent sixty-one summer retreats in the monastic community. His nature was profoundly kind and sincere;

he maintained the utmost simplicity in his personal life. For twenty years, he did not change his single cotton skirt, which consisted of only five panels—just enough to cover his calves—and he made no pleats, saying, "It would merely be a waste.
Having no worldly attachments or preferences, he was able to clear the western wall of his quarters and requested that [the Master] paint it.

Wen Yuke painted ink bamboo and said to people, "When travelers behold this, their minds and eyes will feel refreshed and cool; this gentleman [the bamboo] shall serve as my substitute to preach the Dharma.
He first preached the Dharma at the Qingshou Palace. A monk asked, "The Empress Dowager Cisheng has ascended to the realm of the immortals."

"Where do you take ultimate refuge? Zhen replied, "The flowing water originally resides in the sea; the setting moon does not depart from the sky. The Emperor was delighted and treated him with even greater reverence.

[The author] praises him, saying: "When I arrived in the capital, I was still able to see him. At that time he was already eighty years old, with his hair tied back and moving about with a graceful ease; his face..."

Distant mountains form her brows, red apricots her cheeks; She marries the spring breeze without the need for a matchmaker. This old woman, in her youth of thirty-five..."
He also understood how to apply [the teachings] here and there.

Chan Master Fayun Yuan Tong Xiu—Master Xiu’s name was Fa-xiu—was a native of Longcheng in Qinzhou. He was born into the Xin clan. His mother dreamed that there was a monk who was extremely emaciated, with a beard...
Her hair had turned completely white. She took up lodging and said, "I am a nun from Mount Maiji. Upon waking, she found herself pregnant.
Previously, there had been a monk at Mount Maiji whose name was unknown; he recited the Lotus Sūtra daily and was on good terms with the Venerable Lu of Yingqian Temple.
He once wished to travel abroad under Lu's guidance, but Lu, considering him too old, sent him away. As he departed, Lu spoke these parting words: "In the future, you should seek me out at Zhupu."
Before the slope, at the foot of Mount Tieqiang, a boy was suddenly born. When Lu heard of this, he went to see him; the boy smiled at him.

At the age of three, the boy wished to follow Lu back home and consequently adopted Lu’s surname. At nineteen, he mastered the scriptures and became a *bhikṣu*. His celestial bone-structure was lofty and eminent;

amidst ten thousand monks, he stood towering and majestic, appearing as if he were a living portrait. He lectured on the Great Sūtras, analyzing them chapter by chapter and phrase by phrase. Beside...

His penetration was direct and thorough; his sharp wit was unassailable. His reputation resounded throughout the capitals of Jing and Luo. Relying on the *Guifeng Chao* (Commentary by Guifeng) to analyze and weigh various meanings, he nonetheless felt regret that Guifeng had studied Chan and only revered Yuan Huaian of Beiping.

He lamented that Yuan was not a lecturer, saying: [...]* *Note: The original text appears to be a fragment from a historical or biographical account concerning a Buddhist scholar who, while relying on the works of Guifeng Zongmi, expressed a sense of incompleteness regarding the lineage of exegesis.*

If the teachings fully embody the Buddha’s intent, then one such as Master Yuan should not disparage the teachings. If Chan were not the Buddha’s intent, then one such as Master Guifeng should not have studied Chan.
Yet I do not believe that the World-Honored One, outside of his formal teachings, privately transmitted a separate Dharma to Mahākāśyapa;

Because of this, the monk attained awakening. Xiu laughed heartily and said, "How could buddha-nature dare to have possession or lack thereof?"

He departed for Wúwéi Tiěfó Temple and paid his respects to Master Huái. Huái’s appearance was haggard; he sat upright, tears falling until they soaked his robes. Xiù changed his demeanor.
Huishai wiped away his tears and asked, "Master, what sutra do you lecture on? Xiu replied, "The Avataṃsaka. He asked again, "What is the central tenet of this sutra?
Xiu replied, "It takes the mind as its central tenet. He asked once more, "And what is the central tenet of the mind? Xiu was unable to answer. Huishai said:

Initially, when he preached the Dharma at Mount Sishen on the Huai River, his only possessions were his staff, alms bowl, and traveling bag. Disciples flocked to follow him, never wearying of hunger or cold. Xiu felt deep compassion for them.

The ancestral Way was not flourishing, and the monastic groves were withering away; he took it upon himself to restore them. While residing at Xiqian Monastery, there was a monk named Wenqing who was so humble and unassuming that he did not even catch the master’s eye.
When Xiu sent him to oversee the rice harvest at Shiqiao Village, Wenqing took his leave. One who possessed discernment remarked, “Wenqing has been the abbot of Xiangxiang Temple for over ten years;
he is a dharma heir of Chan Master Yungai Yong. Upon hearing this, Xiu dispatched an attendant to pursue him.

He thanked him and invited him back to the mountain. Daoying said, "I shall wait until the rice has been stored in the granaries before returning. Xiu marveled at this in his heart and praised it to the assembly.
Later, he resided at Qixian for twenty years; Xiu was indeed the one who had sent him there. After Master Yuan of Jiangshan passed away, [Daoying succeeded him].

Prince Shu (Shao Yong) used ritual propriety to invite Xiu to succeed him on the dharma seat. When Xiu arrived at the mountain, the Prince went first to pay his respects, but Xiu was then occupied with managing the affairs of the monastic community (*conglin*) and did not see the Prince for some time.
Thinking this an act of arrogance toward himself, Xiu became displeased and departed.

He resided at Changlu in Zhenzhou, where he had a following of a thousand people. An elder from Quanpiao once came to ascend the seat, and the assembly looked on and laughed; no one came forward to pose a question.
Thereupon, Fashu stepped forward and bowed. He asked, "What is the self of Fashu? Quanpao laughed and said, "Fashu has an iron face;

do you not recognize your own self? (The monastic community called Fashu "Iron Face. Fashu replied, "Those who occupy the position are often deluded. Nevertheless, the entire assembly marveled at his resolve to uphold the Dharma.
When Princess Jiguai, the Great Imperial Granddaughter, completed the construction of Fayun Temple, an imperial edict was issued.

Xiu was the first patriarch of the founding of the mountain. On the day he opened the hall for formal preaching, Emperor Shenzong dispatched an imperial messenger to bestow incense and a hand-sewn monastic robe (mòná), while also transmitting the Imperial Words to represent the ritual of the Emperor’s personal visit.

His Imperial Highness, the Prince of Jing, paid his respects at the seat. From this time on, the Yunmen school flourished in the northwest, and scholar-officials sought instruction from him morning and evening.

At that time, Sima Guang, the Duke Wen, had recently been ennobled and was engaged in reforming what he perceived as the excessive flourishing of our Dharma. Xiu said, "Your Excellency is brilliant and a hero among men;
you could not have attained this without the power of the Buddha-dharma. Have you suddenly forgotten your original vows? Sima Guang did not take this to heart.
In the eighth month of the fifth year of the Yuanyou era, he lay ill in bed, and an imperial edict summoned a physician from the Hanlin Academy to attend him.
A physician requested to examine his pulse. Xiu looked up at him and said, "Who are you? I am ill; I shall simply die.
I sought treatment only because I still cherished life. Throughout my life, there has been no distinction between life, death, and dreams."
He brushed it away. Calling his attendant, he changed his robes and sat upright. He spoke three lines of verse and passed away.

He had lived in the world for sixty-four years and spent forty-five summer retreats in meditation. Li Gonglin, whose style name was Bashi, was a master painter of horses, no less skilled than Han Gan.

Xiu rebuked him, saying: "You are a scholar-official who has gained fame through painting; moreover, you paint horses with the expectation that people will ride them. Do you think this constitutes [true mastery]?"
"Excellent! Excellent! [The Emperor] entered the horse’s belly; this was truly enough to cause alarm. Liang Kai (Bo-shi) consequently ceased his brushwork.
Fashou (Xiu) urged him to paint an image of Avalokiteśvara to atone for his transgression. Huang Tingjian (Lu-zhi) composed flowery verses that people vied to transmit. Fashou rebuked him, saying:

Xiu replied, "You stir up the lustful hearts of all people in the world with your flowery words; it will not stop at the horse's belly—I fear you shall instead be born in the Niraya hell.

On New Year’s Eve, he sent an attendant with a letter to address Academician Diao Jingchun of Yangzhou, saying: "I shall depart tomorrow morning; there will be no time for us to meet. Take good care of yourself.
When Jingchun opened the letter, he was greatly shocked and said, "What am I to do? He replied with a letter of parting and nothing more.
At midnight, a messenger reported that a letter had arrived from Yangzhou. As the boat was about to reach the shore, [Chang]ying joyfully dispatched it.

The drum was beaten. He ascended the seat and recounted the origins and history of his succession to the position. He expressed gratitude to those who had assisted in the management of the monastic community and exhorted them not to be negligent in their practice.
He said, "Upon my passing, the Virtuous Karmadāna shall succeed me. Having descended from the seat and finished reading the letter from Jingchun, the assembly crowded around him as he walked away.
He went up to the abbot’s quarters. Xing sat in the full lotus posture and gestured for everyone to stand back at a distance. After a long while, he passed away on the first day of the fifth year.
He had lived seventy-two years and spent fifty-three summer retreats in meditation. Xing’s brilliant spirit overwhelmed all other quarters.

Chan Master Fachang Yu:
The master’s name was Yiyu. He was the son of the Lin family in Zhangzhou. By nature, he was extraordinary and possessed great ambition.

From the moment he shaved his head and received full ordination, he took up his staff and traveled to study under various masters, becoming renowned throughout the monastic communities. Chan Master Fushan Yuan once pointed him out [as a successor].

He said to the man, "This is the model for those who study later in life to travel as a wandering monk. He took his leave of Yuan and went to pay his respects to Guquan, the abbot of Bajiao Hermitage on Mount Nanyue.
Three times he arrived, and three times he was turned away; yet he still sought him out. Guquan lunged at him, saying, "In this place of mine, tigers and wolves roam in all directions!"
The "bed-wetting ghost" came three or five times seeking something. When he encountered [Zhao]quan, [Zhao]quan said, "People say you, the abbot, have seen Fenzhou.
Quan then stripped his clothes and shook them out, saying, "If you think I have seen Fenzhou, how extraordinary would that be?
The ghost immediately prostrated himself and asked, "If it is truly as the abbot says, with what will you entertain a guest? Quan replied, "Yunmen."
Hu-bing (Wu-bing) and Zhaozhou’s Tea. Yunju said, “Thank you for your offering. Xuefeng Quan said, “I have not even had my firewood yet;
why did you thank me so early? For what should one thank? Yunju then departed and went to Chan Master Xian of Beichen, where he asked, “Where have you recently come from?”
Nanyue said, "Fuyan. Fuyan asked, "How long is Dashi’s nostrils? Nanyue replied, "The same as what you saw when you were with the Master.
Fuyan said, "But tell me, how long were they when I saw them? Nanyue said, "The Master seems to have never been to Fuyan.
Xian laughed and said, "He is just one who parrots the words. He then asked, "When you came, was Mazu in good health?"

Yuanwu said, "Jian! Jian asked, "What were you saying just now? Yuanwu said, "I told Beichan not to confuse the lineage. Xian said, "I have considered that you are a newcomer and did not wish to strike you.
Yuanwu said, "Relying on Yuanwu, I shall also let the Master go. Thereupon, he desisted. Consequently, Yuanwu changed his mind and served him as his teacher.
At that time, Chan Master Ciming was residing at Xinghua; when he visited Master Xian’s quarters, Yuanwu was standing in attendance.
Watching their conversation, Xian said, "Fenyang’s lion is indeed terrifyingly fierce. Ciming said, "Have you not heard it said that he bites those who come near?
Xian asked, "If this is truly so, has the Way been cut off at Fenyang’s gate, leaving it desolate?
Ciming raised his whisk and said, "Why has this thing reached the present day? Before Xian could respond, Yu, from the side, remarked, "It is nurtured."
"The son does not equal the father; the family lineage has declined for a generation. Xian rebuked him, saying, "What kind of eyes do you possess that you dare act like this?
Yunyu replied, "If it were a man-eating lion, it would never be like this. Ciming took him away to the shrine of Longya.
Pointing to the image, he asked Yunyu, "Whose image is this? Yunyu said, "Longya's. Ciming said, "Since it is Longya’s—"
The statue was located at Beichen. Yuanwu said, "One color, two prizes. Ciming asked, "The statue is here; where is Longya?
As Yuanwu was about to respond, Ciming struck him with his palm and said, "Do not say you cannot bite people. Yuanwu said, [and continued].

Why? So that we shall no longer rely on others' doorways or lean against others' walls. He then descended from his seat. A monk followed after him...
Later, he shouted loudly, "The county official has arrived! Xian turned around and asked why. He replied, "The monk slaughtered an ox, but has not yet returned the hide and horns.
Xian laughed and threw his warm cap at him. The monk went over to pick it up; kneeling, he presented it, saying, "The weather is cold;
here is the monk’s cap back to you. Xian asked Yu, "What do you think of this? Yu replied, "Recently, paper has become expensive in the city."

he was surely a peer to Mingzhao, the "One-Eyed Dragon. Yet he dwelt in a desolate village and a dilapidated temple; when he struck the drum with his solitary strength, he served as the clay head for eighteen [monks].

Chan Master Yangqi Huai: The Chan Master’s name was Fanghuai.

His secular surname was Liang, and he was a native of Yichun in Yuanzhou. From his youth, he was alert and quick-witted; he possessed a keen sense of humor and spoke with great relish for dramatic wit.

Upon reaching adulthood, he took no pleasure in the study of brush and inkstone, instead registering himself under the merchant tax office, where he devoted himself to managing the collection of duties with the highest efficiency. Because of this...

Being unfit for his office, he was subject to punishment; thus he fled under the cover of night and traveled to Jiufeng in Junzhou (some say to Daowu in Tanzhou). There, he felt as if he were once again in the places where he had previously practiced, and out of deep affection, he could not bear to leave.
He subsequently shaved his head to become a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*). As he read the scriptures and listened to the Dharma, his mind merged with it and his spirit attained realization.
He was able to humble himself deeply and submit to the guidance of the venerable elder Ciming Chanshi, who resided at Nanyuan. Hui assisted him there, enduring hardship with joyful diligence.
When Ciming moved to Daowu and Shichuang, Hui requested and received the appointment as head of the monastery (jianyuan) in both locations.
This was not the intention of Ciming, yet the various treatises all praised it as excellent. He took up a paper quilt and entered the administration of the temple’s gold and grain;

from time to time he would speak in simple, plain language, rubbing against and smoothing over the teachings of Ciming. The various quarters of the world transmitted this as being appropriate. After Ciming had finished his meal, he would invariably go for walks in the mountains.
When Chan Master Dahui asked about the Way, he frequently missed the essential point. Once, when Dahui had not gone far from the assembly hall, Ciming struck the drum to gather the congregation.
Dahui hurried back, and Ciming scolded him, saying: "You young man of the forest! You ascend the seat so late in the evening;
where did you get such a rule? Dahui replied slowly: "This is the evening session (wanchan) at Fenzhou; why would it not be a rule? Ciming was at his wits' end.
Nowadays, when the three-day and eight-day liturgical recitations have concluded in the monastic communities, those who still engage in formal inquiry are the very source of this tradition.
When Ciming moved to Xinghua, he took his leave and returned to Jiufeng. The clergy and laity of Pingshi went to the mountain to invite him to reside at Yangqi.

He ceased and said, "Is there anyone else who wishes to engage in dialogue? Come forth and let us meet. Yangqi’s life today rests in your hands;
you may drag him about as you please, pulling him this way and that. Why is it so? Because he is a true man of great capacity."

Duiyun said, "Second Seat, try speaking on behalf of the head of the assembly. He too was speechless. Duiyun said, "Both of you..."
Xiang left him standing there in silence. His testing of the sharpness of [his disciples'] spiritual faculties was also similar to that of Nan-yuan.
In the sixth year of the Qingli era, he moved to reside at Mount Yungai in Tanzhou, where he transmitted the orthodox lineage of Linji to Shouduan.
Chan Master Baiyun Dan was named Shouduan.
He was born into the Ge clan (some say the Zhou clan) of Hengzhou. From his youth, he was skilled in calligraphy and did not take pleasure in remaining in secular life.
He received the tonsure under Master Yú of Chálíng. When he was over twenty years old, he went to attend upon Master Yóng (or Páng) Chánshī.
After Yóng passed away, Master Huì succeeded him in residence. Upon first seeing him, Huì marveled at his dignified and extraordinary air; he would often converse with him until late into the night.

One day, Huì suddenly asked, "Whose disciple are you, Venerable? Duan replied, "The Venerable Yú of Chálíng. Huì said, "I have heard that he attained awakening while crossing a stream and composed a verse."

"How extraordinary! Can you recite it? Duan immediately recited: "I have a divine pearl; day and night it has been bound and locked by dust (some say 'it is constantly bound and locked by the toil of worldly defilements').
This morning the dust is cleared and its light shines forth, illuminating ten thousand peaks of the green mountains. Upon hearing this, Huì laughed loudly and rose to leave.
Duan stared at those around him in astonishment and did not sleep all night. The next day, he requested entry into the inner quarters to seek further instruction from him.
It was the first day of the year. Baizhang said, "Did you see the wild fox that was acting last night?
Xuedou replied, "I saw it. Baizhang said, "In this one matter, you are not his equal. Xuedou was greatly startled and asked, "What do you mean by this?
Baizhang said, "He loved being laughed at; you fear being laughed at. At these words, Xuedou attained great enlightenment and took his leave to travel extensively throughout Mount Lu.
When Chan Master Yuntong Ne saw him, he considered himself inferior; he appointed him to reside at Chengtian Monastery in Jiangzhou, where his reputation became resplendent.
Furthermore, Ne yielded the abbotship of Yuntong to him, while taking up residence himself in the East Hall. At that time, Duan was twenty-eight years old.

Because he had previously yielded the leadership of the monastic community to his senior, he held himself in profound self-reproach; thus, he treated the assembly with reverent gravity, suppressing his private interests for the sake of public duty.
Consequently, the tradition of our school flourished greatly. Not long after, Master Nǜ grew weary of seclusion and quietude. When the Prefect arrived, he expressed his desire to remain a guest.
The Prefect looked at him with deep sympathy, but Master Duān merely smiled and responded with "yes, yes. The following day, he ascended the seat and said: "In the past, the Dharma..."

Chan Master Yanguan had a verse that said: "Difficult, difficult, difficult! It is the difficulty of dispelling emotional attachments. When emotions are exhausted, there is a single, cold, perfect luminosity.

To use expedient means to dispel emotion is still not it; to further eliminate those expedient means is utterly groundless. The assembly was asked: "Tell me, how are emotional attachments to be dispelled?
He let out a shout, descended from his seat, took up his traveling bag, and departed. The entire assembly was greatly astonished; they tried to detain him, but he would not stay. Thereupon—
He crossed the river and spent the summer in a quiet room at Wuzu’s monastery. At a small temple in Shuzhou called Fahua, the abbot was like a bird in a cage, never forgetting his desire to fly away.
When the Governor of Shu heard of Duan’s lofty reputation and wished to see him in person, he sent an official letter inviting him to take up residence there.
Duan joyfully took up his staff and came; the number of monastics arriving was such that there was no room for them, and the scholar-officials were filled with admiration.
He moved his residence to Baiyun Haihui. Ascending the seat, he looked around and said:
"Before the drum has been struck, and before this mountain monk has ascended the seat—what a fine model of an ancient Buddha!
If anyone can realize it here, they may be said to precede the Śākyamuni of old and not lag behind the Maitreya of today. Listen further to what emerges from my three-inch tongue."
It has long been uneven; one must possess the eye that discerns the uneven in order to restore it to completeness.
Is there such a person? He then said: "I shall further act as an old woman for you. When opening one's mouth, the very last word is precisely what strikes the mark.
When taking a step, the very last step is precisely where one treads. Why, then, are the nostrils not straight? It is because they have become calloused through ordinary perception."
Because he was unwilling to resolve his mind [to leave], he exhorted everyone there that day to depart immediately. After a long while, he said, "One," and then descended from his seat.
Such was the severity and loftiness of his teaching style. A monk asked for instruction; Huichao asked Fayan, "What is the Buddha?
Fayan replied, "You are Huichao. He then composed a verse and showed it to him, saying: "One large coin of great radiance Bought me a piece of oil-cake."
He ate it and let it go into his belly; immediately, he was no longer hungry. Again, he asked: A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the phrase that penetrates the Dharma-body?
He replied, "Hiding one's body within the Big Dipper. Then Du'an composed a verse, saying: "The young master of the nine avenues is accustomed to wandering among the flowers;
The poor scholar who has not yet passed the examinations feels much lamentation. Watching others' wealth and honor from a cold distance, He cannot bear the casual way they wear their head-coverings."
Regarding Touzi Huiqin, Zhan said: "Yangqi was divinely gifted with spiritual intuition and skillfully entered the *samādhi* of playful mastery (*yóuxì sānmèi*).

He delighted in testing and verifying his disciples, preserving the legacy of the ancient patriarchs. Since the Qingli era, he has been acclaimed as a master of the school, while Baiyun was a brilliant youth."
Bian possessed a spirit of such sharp acuity that he truly emulated the excellence of his predecessors. In dealing with the world, he spat upon fame and status;
in preaching the Dharma, he swept away all cognitive views. He was thus of an extraordinary caliber, much like Ji-zhuangzi was to Dayi or Gongchen was to Xuansha.
The lineage of Linji’s Dharma path has not yet become particularly desolate.
*Chànlín Sēngbǎo Zhuàn*, Scroll Twenty-Eight and Scroll Twenty-Nine,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Huìhóng of Míngbái Ānjū during the Song Dynasty.
Chan Master Dàtōng Běn, whose name was Shànben, was born into the Dòng clan. He was a descendant of Hán Zhōngshū. His ancestors originally resided in Zhòngshū Village in Tàikāng;
his grandfather Qí and his father Wēn both served as officials in Yǐng, and thus he became a native of Yǐng. Initially, his mother had no children, so she offered prayers.
Before an image of the Buddha, he made a vow, saying: "If I obtain a son, he must serve the Buddha. He immediately adopted a vegetarian diet and soon became pregnant.

When the child was born, his physical features were exceptionally refined and extraordinary. At one year of age, he lost his father and was raised by his maternal uncle, Zhai. Upon reaching adulthood, he became a man of extensive learning.
His conduct was pure and austere. When his mother died, he mourned her with such excessive grief that it violated the bounds of propriety.

Having no intention of pursuing an official career, he abstained from grain and studied the Way, concealing himself among pen-makers. Nevertheless, his spirit was firm and unbending; he remained silent and looked askance at high officials.

In the eighth year of the Jiayou era, he and his younger brother Shansi went together to the capital, where they registered their names at Xiansheng Dizang Monastery and underwent the examination for their studies to become ordained monks. Their master...
The Vinaya Master Yuancheng Huiyi said to others: "In days to come, there shall surely be one renowned throughout the land; will he indeed be born into my Dharma?
He had Yuancheng listen to and study the *Vinaya*, while he himself took joy in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. One night, he saw a young boy in a dream.
It was like the image of Sudhana painted in the world, with palms joined as he headed south. Upon awakening, he said, "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have bestowed their grace upon me;
they wish for me to travel south to seek out my spiritual friends. At that time, Chan Master Yuanzhao’s reputation resounded throughout the Wu region.

Wenben went directly to Gusu to pay his respects at Ruiwang Temple. Once Yuanzhao had settled into his seat, he looked specifically toward Wenben. Wenben silently realized the essential purport of the school.

He served him diligently for five years until he fully mastered the essentials. His mastery of the principles for rectifying and awakening others, as well as his refined wisdom in discerning distinctions, was so versatile and expansive that it surpassed all previous standards; none among his contemporaries could surpass him.
Yuanzhao relied upon him to expand the lineage. He served the Venerable Xiu of Quanyong as if he were his own elder uncle. When Xiu resided at Qixian on Mount Lu, [he] emerged...

He entered the inner quarters, much like Jizang did at Dongsi Temple. In the spring of the seventh year of the Yuanfeng era, he departed from Jiuyang to travel through the mountains of Huai, paying homage to the ancestral pagodas everywhere.
Admiring the excellence of the rocky thickets of Fushan, he formed the intention to spend the remainder of his life there; he subsequently resided at Taishouyan.

After a long time, he emerged from seclusion to take up residence at Shuanglin in Wuzhou for six years. The monastics and laypeople of Eastern Zhejiang followed him with such veneration that they even said:

Master Fu was reborn and moved his residence to Jingci Monastery in Qiantang. He succeeded Yuanzhao as abbot; the refectory daily served over a thousand mouths, all of whom relied upon the offerings of donors.
The magnificence of the ritual offerings and adornments was so great that travelers suspected they were in the heavens (some say "Western Heavens").

At the time, he was known by the titles Dàběn and Xiǎoběn. Emperor Shenzong (alternatively, Zhezong) heard of his reputation and issued an imperial decree for him to reside at the capital’s Fahu Monastery.
He was granted the title Chan Master Daotong by imperial decree at Yunsi Temple.

Following in the footsteps of Yuantong, his character was naturally upright and solitary, standing with majestic dignity before the assembly—whether it be a thousand or ten thousand followers—as if Mount Tiantu were surrounded by myriad peaks, its lofty coldness beyond compare.

Yet he shared both the refined and the coarse provisions with the community; he never conformed to others through his words, nor did he flatter anyone through his countenance. Kings, dukes, and nobles came daily to offer alms, their gifts filling the gates.
His residence was a hall of ten thousand pillars, plated in gold and adorned with azure-green tiles, appearing as if a jeweled monastery had sprung up from the earth.

Having resided there for eight years, he petitioned the Imperial Court, expressing his wish to retire to old age upon the shores of West Lake. The Emperor’s decree granted his request, and he subsequently returned to the east.

At Longshan Chongde, he shut his door and swept away all visitors, forgetting the world. Another ten years passed; though the whole world longed to see him, it was impossible to do so, for he dwelt alone with the Dharma.
Zi Si and Rui were both [his disciples]. Rui was on friendly terms with me and spoke to me of his master’s life, saying: "For thirty years while presiding over the assembly, he never once smiled.
Yet when he was in private, he would laugh and converse with animated gestures. When asked the reason for this, he said: 'If one is not solemn and reverent, how can one lead the multitude?

In the past, when I served in the monastic communities, I practiced this out of necessity; it was not my true nature. Wherever I went, I saw that..."* *(Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at the end.)*

Regarding images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in standing or walking postures, he did not dare to sit upon them; he would not eat the *kaṣāya* (I-pu-se) food offerings, nor would he consume meat or fish, even those of renowned quality.
His sincere reverence and service, as well as his guarding of the mind to remain free from transgression, were of this nature.

On the *jiazi* day of the twelfth month in the third year of the Daguan era, he bent three fingers and said to those around him, "There are only three days left. Shortly thereafter, he indeed passed away. There was a strange bird [that appeared].

He soared and cried out in the courtyard and departed. His entire body was enshrined in the upper story of the pagoda. He lived for seventy-five (or three) years and sat in meditation for forty-five summer retreats.
The eulogy says: Originally he emerged from the lineage of Yunmen, and in terms of spiritual rank, he was the fourth-generation direct descendant of Xuedou.
In his daily life and conduct, he gazed straight ahead without blinking; yet when he ascended the hall to preach, he would look left and right like an elephant-king turning in a circle.
Many students attained awakening through him. On the evening before his passing, a monk from Yue dreamed that he had returned to Tuṣita Heaven.
Judging his character—his dwelling, clothing, and articles of use, as well as his conduct and his benefiting of others—he daily renewed his virtue;
were he not placed among the various heavens, where else could he go?
As for Chan Master Baoben Yuan, his name was Huiyuan.
He was born into the Ni clan and was a native of Chaoyang. Even as a young child with hanging tufts of hair, he was remarkably dignified;

while other children played boisterously before him, he would simply sit cross-legged with his hands folded in his sleeves. His parents deliberated, saying, "With such talent and disposition, how could this child possibly endure the mundane world?"
"It is sufficient that you intend to serve the Buddha and the Sangha. When Yuán heard this, he immediately stepped forward to bow and take his leave.

He stayed at a vihāra south of the city and recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. At the age of nineteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination. Traveling through various regions, he arrived at the capital.
There, the Dharma Master Huá-yán Yuán-míng saw him and marveled at him, saying, "Venerable sir, you are young in years; from where have you come, and what do you seek? He replied:
Huiyuan came from the South Sea; he brought nothing else but a quest for the Buddha-dharma. Yuanming smiled and said, "In the royal capital, fame and profit are swift paths;
wine and beauty are cages. Those with eyes vie and scramble, with ten thousand affairs daily. Long ago, the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū—"

He sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, yet the Buddha-dharma still did not manifest before him. "Is there truly any Buddha-dharma here? he asked. "The Buddha-dharma is entirely in the South.
Originally from Luoyang, he traveled through Xianghan, visiting famous mountains everywhere and drawing near to spiritual friends wherever he went;
yet he attained no realization whatsoever. In the spring of the third year of the Zhiping era, he arrived at Huanglong. At that time, Nanzen...
The Master came from Jicui. The assembly of dragon-disciples gathered like ants drawn by honey.

Whenever Yuan sat down on his meditation mat, he would invariably reach out his hand, turn it over and examine it, saying, "How can there be any logic in saying this resembles a Buddha’s hand? Only those who know my family lineage will understand. He was from Jieyang.
He then asked again, "Where was he born? After a long while, [the monk] suddenly had his doubts resolved; that very day he departed.
In the first year of the Xining era, he entered Wu and resided at Shousheng Temple on Wujiang. He dispatched a monk to visit Huanglong and deliver a letter of succession for the Dharma.
Master Nán examined the inscriptions on the base of the statue; before opening it, he said to the visiting monk, "Return at once and tell Yuán to come in person.
When the monk returned with this message, Yuán suspended his duties as abbot and set out on foot toward Nanchang. There, he saw Master Bǎojiào presiding over the monastery and preaching the Dharma.
Learning that Master Nán had already passed away more than a month prior, Yuán returned to the region of Wú. Both the clergy and the laity revered him as their teacher.
He further resided at Huayan Monastery in Kunshan for ten years. Once, while returning by boat from Xiachuan at night, he was plundered by bandits.
The crew was terrified and did not know what to do, but Yuan sat calmly and said slowly, "I give all my money and silks to you; do not take human life.
The bandits then departed with their backs turned. In the fourth year of the Yuanyou era, he resided at Chengtian Wanshou Monastery, where the assembly grew even more numerous.
Fengsheng personally carried his alms bowl to Lake Hu. The people of the lake said, "A master makes his home wherever he goes; why do you take such trouble to love only Gusu?

They detained him firmly, refusing to let him return. When the people of Suzhou heard of this, they vied with one another to carry clubs and staves, entering the lake in a tumultuous crowd, saying, "Why have you seized our nation’s virtuous spiritual friend?
We shall see him returned at once, or else we will simply die. Yuan was serene and composed.
He was not stingy with his feelings regarding whether to stay or leave, saying, "I simply follow the conditions. They remained together for over a month;
when the people of Su had consumed all his food, he departed and eventually fell into the hands of the people of Hu. He resided at Baoben Chan Monastery for six years.

On the sixteenth day of the eleventh month, he ascended the seat and spoke this verse: "Fifty-five years of dreams and illusions; Whether one dwells in the east, west, south, or north, who is truly kin? The white clouds..."
"Scattered beyond a thousand mountains, a single new moon rises in the autumn sky ten thousand *li* away. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
At that time, Chen Gongguan Yingzhong, the Right Minister, was in Lake [District] and personally witnessed these events. For thirty years, Yuan’s side never touched his mat;
in his entire life, he alone was able to emulate the Master Nanchan in his regulations for conduct and his every action and repose. His final instructions were to be buried on Mount Xian.
Yang. His disciple Yuanzheng was possessed of talent and eloquence. He asked, "Why do you think only of Mount Xian? Yuan replied, "In the future, a temple may be built there.
Thirty years later, Yuan Daoqi became a Grand Master (Taishi) and Duke of Chu. The Duke petitioned the court on his behalf, and by imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Zhengwu;
his stupa was named Dingying. By special edict, Xianhua Temple was established there, and [a grant was made] for its annual [maintenance].
He ordained monks, saying, "This is to honor the incense and lamps.

Chan Master Heshan Pu was a man of widespread fame and virtue. He was the son of the Pu family of Mianzhou. In his youth, he esteemed integrity and principle; he read extensively and possessed outstanding insight. Upon seeing...
Fule Shanjing Chan bowed with palms joined and said, "This is my teacher. Shanjing found him extraordinary and took him back to the mountains, where he observed him in secret.
His conduct and demeanor were like those of an elderly *dhūta* practitioner. Shanjing remarked, "This youth is by nature bold and unrestrained, yet he is able to humble himself;
amidst the tasks of pestle and mortar and cooking, he makes it his duty to serve the community."
This was truly rare. At the age of eighteen, he received the full ordination and distinguished himself among the lecture halls.

He mastered the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Awakening of Faith*, such that none in the two river provinces dared to challenge his interpretations; he was thus known as the "Tiger of Meaning. He criticized Guifeng’s commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, noting that many of its points were based on mere conjecture.

He pointed out these errors and cautioned students not to place their trust in them, for even the senior masters numbered him among their ranks, saying: "Guifeng [was surpassed by] Qingliang Guoshi..."
"What your teacher has certified, you dare to criticize with the yellowing of ink. You have truly realized the argument of the ant shaking a tree.
He sighed deeply and said, "Students have long been deluded by fame and status. Qingliang and Guifeng did not possess four eyes and eight arms."
How can one willingly accept such self-defeat? The Buddha-Dharma is now in decline; this is its omen. At that time, Master Sheng returned from Jiangxi.
Lü Dafang (style name Weizhong), serving as a *Longtuguo Zhixueshi*, was dispatched to govern Chengdu.

He observed the etiquette of a disciple, visiting [the master] day and night—sometimes at his quarters—to listen in private while the master wore the robes of a Chan practitioner. [Lü] remained there until the end, listening to his discussions.
One day, he could not understand it. Returning home, he lay down and looked at the rafter beams, saying: "In the past, I was once a lecturer with a reputation for excellence.

I used to engage in scholarly debate with Master Lü—who is universally regarded as a man of virtue—and he treated me with such respect and faith. Yet here I am, failing to believe this; how can that be right?"
However, my doubts remain unresolved; this is due to my own lack of learning. I then departed from Shu and traveled to Jinyuan in Jingzhou.

There at night, I encountered a monk—his name has unfortunately slipped my memory—who had met the Abbot Qing’an of Lianshan and was widely known for his thorough mastery of the teachings. He questioned me, saying:

"How can the sutras and śāstras be at fault with the Chan school, such that you, Venerable Sir, frequently criticize and revile them? Nan said, "Because they consist of intellectual understanding and principles, and are within the realm of conceptual thought and measurement;
they cannot by themselves give rise to the holy or lead to the Way. However, if there were those who attained the Way or gave rise to the holy through them," [he continued].

All of these merely serve as conditions. If one does not rely on self-awakening and instead relies solely upon the sutras and śāstras, then those who can read, know, and attain understanding would all have already realized sainthood and attained the Way; how could they still be looking up to or down at people like us?
It is because words of death are themselves an obstacle to knowledge that the Patriarch came from the West (one version reads: "therefore it is clear that the Patriarch came from the West").
[This refers to] the mind). As the sutra says: "All sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning. Do you believe this?
He replied, "How could I dare not believe the words of the World-Honored One? Nan said, "Since you already believe this, why have you come all this way in such earnest?
He replied, "I heard that the Chan school possesses a distinctively transmitted Dharma; therefore, I have come. Nan laughed and said, "If that were so, you do not yet believe. It was not otherwise.
He was able to believe. Fupin asked, "Where does his illness lie? Nan said, "The Master Nanchuan Jicui has been in the world for a long time;

you should go see him before it is too late. If you see him, he will surely cause your illness to be cured. That very day, Fupin set out, arriving at Huanglong in the first year of the Xining era (1068).
He asked, "When Ānanda questioned Kāśyapa, [Kāśyapa replied that] apart from the transmission of the golden robe, the World-Honored One entrusted..."
“What dharma? Kāśyapa called out to Ānanda. Ānanda responded with an assent. Kāśyapa said, “Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate.
What was the meaning? Master Nanyue said, “When you, Venerable One, left Sichuan, did you ever go to Yuyuan? He replied, “I went there.”
He asked again, "Have you ever stayed here before? Nan replied, "I departed after one night. Nan said, "This is the site of the Dharma-center of the Wise One (Zhizhe).

When General Guan offered a ritual feast, it was to establish a karmic connection. Why should it matter when that happened? It does not hinder anything. Nan remained silent for a long while, then repeated his previous question. Nan bowed his head.
Nan stepped out in a great surprise and exclaimed, "The tiger-like masters of the two Sichuan provinces cannot withstand a single spittle from this old man! Eight years [later].
In autumn, he traveled to Luochuan. The Imperial Academician Liu Gong Hǎng invited him to reside at Huíyún Chan Monastery for seven years;
subsequently, he moved to reside at Heshan for twelve years. On the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month in the fifth year of Yuányòu, he said to those around him:

"When the venerable elders of various quarters pass away, the monasteries invariably perform memorial rites. I consider this to be a mere empty formality. When I die, you all should be the first to perform the rites.
He then ordered that preparations for the memorial service be made from this day forward. The assembly, considering him old and fond of humorous speech, asked, "When will the Master pass away?
He replied, "When your memorial rites have ceased, I shall depart. Thereupon, he screened off the meditation hall and sat within it.
In the center, place the offerings and read the ritual text. Kneeling and bowing, present the food; all may drink and eat as they please.

From the chief disciples down to the laborers, each shall perform this in turn day by day until the New Year’s Day of the following year, at which point the ritual ceases. It is said: "If it clears up tomorrow, we shall proceed."
When the time came, the weather was clear, yet suddenly it snowed. When the snow ceased, Pujian sat upright and, burning incense, passed away.
He had lived for sixty-seven years and spent forty-nine summer retreats in meditation. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the left of the temple.
The commentary states: When Yun’an first went from Jiufeng to Mount Lu, practitioners of Chan from all quarters gathered at his gate;
among those who returned were many men of outstanding talent. Yet Yun’an would often knit his brows and say, "As for the Way of the Dharma, from this point forward, it remains uncertain.
When asked about his meaning, he replied, "When my late teacher was at Huangbo, the assembly numbered fewer than a hundred, yet the number of those with 'clear eyes' was nearly [equal to the total]."
Half [of that number]. Although it is now three times what it was then, there are still only one or two people. At that time, I was young and my mind did not agree with their doctrine.
Yet, when I observe the two Chan masters Yuan and Pu, both of whom were late disciples of Master Nan, their conduct is already so preeminent;
if this is the case, then Yun’an’s words are like a patched robe—only when the cold is severe and the year draws to a close does one see their efficacy.

Chan Master Yunju Foyin Yuan, whose name was Liaoyuan and courtesy name Juelao, was born into the Lin family of Fuliang in Raoyou. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations; neither his father nor his grandfather held office.
When Yuan was three years old, he could recite the *Analects* and the poems of various masters with clear and resonant intonation. By the age of five, he had memorized three thousand [verses].
At the beginning, he followed a teacher for a long time and was granted the Five Classics; having gained a general understanding of their major principles, he departed.

At Zhulin Temple, he read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and, becoming deeply enamored with it, completely abandoned his former studies. He informed his parents and requested to leave the household life to transcend birth and death.
He paid homage to the śramaṇa Riyong of Baoji Temple, where he tested himself in the *Lotus Sūtra* and received full ordination. He then traveled to Mount Lu to visit Master Xian at Kaixian.
Xian prided himself on his reputation and roamed freely across the seas, looking down upon those who followed him.
Yuan asked him questions with such quick wit that Xian praised him highly, regarding him as a truly heroic monk. At that time, he was nineteen years old.
Later, he visited Chan Master Netuan of Yuantong, who was struck by his calligraphy and remarked, "His skeletal structure already resembles that of Xuedou; he will be a great successor."
Junya. At that time, the secretary Huailian was about to depart for the west in response to an imperial decree. Nan took over the position formerly held by Lian.
When the Dharma seat at Chengtian Monastery in Jiangzhou became vacant, Nan was also due to be transferred there;

however, the local governor looked down upon him. Nan said, "Yuan is young in years but mature in virtue; even ten thousand veteran monks cannot surpass him. Thereupon, he preached the Dharma for [him].

The successor to Kaixian was at that time twenty-eight years old. Beginning with his initial residence at Chengtian, he moved to Doufang on Mount Huai, followed by Kaixian and Guizong on Mount Lu, Jinnshan and Jiaoshan in Danyang, and Dayang on the banks of the Jiangxi River.
Furthermore, he resided at Yunju for forty years. His virtuous influence transformed both the monastic and lay communities, and his fame reached even the young.
Many among the scholarly elite were his companions. When Su Dongpo was exiled to Huangzhou, Yuan was residing at Guizong on the opposite shore of Mount Lu;
their exchange of exquisite verses vied with the beauty of mist and clouds. Later, when he was at Jinshan, Dongpo obtained...
Shi returned to the Wu region and subsequently went to Danyang. He sent a letter to Yuan, saying: "There is no need for you to leave the mountains;
you should learn from Zhaozhou’s superior way of receiving people. Upon receiving the letter, Yuan came straight away. Dongpo welcomed him with a smile and questioned him.

Yuan offered this verse (or, according to some versions, a playful jest) as a response: "Zhaozhou on that day lacked a bit of humility; He did not leave the three gates to see the King of Zhao. How could he compare to the Golden..."
"The mountains have immeasurable forms; the great trichiliocosm is but a single meditation seat. Dongpo clapped his hands and praised this as excellent.

Once, when Dongpo was visiting his disciple Ziyou at Gaoyang in Gao'an, on the eve of their arrival, Ziyou engaged in a night-long conversation with Chan Master Zhenjing Wen of Dongshan and Chan Master Cong of Shengshou, sitting together on the same bed until the third watch. Suddenly, Zhenjing awoke in a start and said: "By chance..."
"We dreamed that we were visiting the Chan Master Wuzu Ji. We did not think about it beforehand; what auspicious omen is this? Ziyou shook Cōnggōng.
Cōnggōng said, "I have just now dreamed of the Chan Master Wuzu Ji. Thereupon they rose, sat in rows, and laughed, saying, "Is there such a thing as a shared dream?
Shortly thereafter, news arrived that Sūndāo had already reached Fēngxīn. Ziyou took two monks with him and waited for them south of the city.
He established Jiansi Temple. After a short while, Dongpo arrived. Li asked him about the matter of his dream: "Where was Master Jie born? He replied, "In the region of Shanyou.
Dongpo said, "When I was ten or so years old, I often dreamed that my body was that of a monk, traveling back and forth through Shaanxi.

He asked again, "What is Master Jie’s physical appearance like? He replied, "Master Jie has lost one eye. Dongpo said, "When my late mother was pregnant with me, she dreamed of a monk arriving at our door. He was emaciated—"
He was blind in one eye. When asked where his preceptor (Jie) resided, he replied, "Gao'an Dayu; it has been fifty years now. At that time, Dongpo was forty-nine years old.
Later, in a letter to Zhenjing, he wrote briefly: "Preceptor Jie does not recognize people's dislikes."

To force a smile and emerge once more is indeed laughable. Since you are one with whom the Dharma is sealed (or, as some say, a vessel for the Dharma), I pray that you will apply yourself with diligent effort so that you may restore your former splendor.
From then on, he constantly wore a *nāṃsa-vastra* (patchwork robe). Thus, Yuan presented him with a skirt, and Dongpo repaid him with a jade belt, offering this verse:
"My sickly frame can hardly bear the girdle of jade; My dull faculties still fall within the range of the arrow-head. [He] understood.
When begging for alms at the Courtesans’ Quarter, I seized the old cassock from the Clouds-and-Mountains [monastery]. It is further said: "This sash has seen people as numerous as way-stations;
its transmission to me is likewise leisurely. Its brocade patterns are still well-suited; I beg it for the old man Wan-hui, who feigns madness.
The hall where he originally resided was specifically named the "Sublime High Terrace" (Miaogao Tai). Dongpo also composed a poem concerning it:
I wish to board a flying chariot and travel east to visit the immortal Chisongzi. But Mount Penglai cannot be reached; the Weak Water stretches for thirty thousand li.
It would be better to go to Mount Jinshan, where a single sail suffices on a clear breeze. Upon it stands the Wondrous High Terrace, its cloud-peak rising solitary from within.
Gazing upward, there was originally no path; who would have believed it as level as a whetstone? An old bhikṣu within the hall, his azure eyes reflecting upon the window-sill and desk.
With towering bones like jade, he is stern as frost enters his teeth. His sharp wit cannot be provoked; a thousand gāthās flow forth like surging water.
"Why need one seek the Cloud of Virtue? This very bhikṣu is he. While I have not yet had leisure to study longevity, I pray that you teach me how to live long and not die.
Thus spoke Zhang Gongfang, the Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince, during his peaceful travels while serving as the Prefect of Chuzhou, when he visited the Zangyuan Monastery on Langye Mountain.
Hu Titiang opened a wooden chest and suddenly realized his previous life; it was found to have been a monk from the Zangsi Monastery.
He had begun transcribing the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* but passed away before completing it. An Dao continued writing on the remaining scrolls, and the calligraphy remained as vivid as it had been before.

This became known as the "Sutra of Two Lives. An Dao intended to carve woodblocks to print and distribute them throughout the four quarters, but Dongpo remarked: "If this sutra were in the hands of another person..."
This is a rare omen for the age; how much more so for you! I request that you preserve it at home as a source of inexhaustible blessing for your descendants.

Yuan requested Dongpo to compose this on his behalf, which was then carved onto printing blocks at Mount Jin. At that time, among the scholar-officials, they took Ou-yang Wen-chung-kung as their model for the "ancient prose" (ku-wen).
You, sir, assisted Han-tzu in disparaging me for my *Yuan-xing* (On Original Nature), arguing that nature is a principle that is born together with life itself.
This was for the purpose of evaluation; thus, I originally used this to exhort them. Furthermore, he once said to the assembly:

"In the past, Yunmen’s preaching was like clouds and rain, and he absolutely did not like people recording his words. Whenever he saw someone doing so, he would scold and drive them away, saying: 'You do not use your own mouths, yet you record my words.
At some other time, you will come to peddle my teachings as if they were your own. The records of his responses to disciples in his room today are all the work of Xianglin and Mingjiao."

Using paper as clothing, he would immediately write down whatever he heard. Later generations of scholars, who merely fish and hunt for words and language, are just like those blowing on a net in hopes of filling it;
they are either fools or madmen. At that time, the monastic centers (conglin) of Jiangzhe still took texts and words to be Chan, calling this "requesting instruction.
Thus, Yuan used these words to satirize them. The Korean State Preceptor (Sengtong) Uicheon arrived by sea...

Regarding Mingzhou: Tradition holds that when Wŏnhyo (Yitian) renounced his royal status to become a monk, he submitted a memorial requesting to travel extensively through various monasteries to inquire about the Dharma and receive the Way.
An imperial edict was issued for Yang Jie (Cigong), the Court Receptioner, to accompany him as he visited the various temples throughout the region of Wu.
They all welcomed and saw him off with the etiquette due to a king’s minister. Upon reaching Mount Jinshan, Wŏn sat upon his bed and accepted the formal prostration.

When the official asked him in surprise for the reason, Wŏn said, “Uichon is merely a monk from another country. When a monk arrives at a monastic community, such is the rule and discipline; it cannot be altered.
Those of various surnames who have left the household life are all equally called sons of Śākya. It is not as if one buys the status of the Ch’oe or Noh clans to establish one’s lineage.”
Gao An asked about his noble lineage. Cigong replied, "I am humble; I have merely conformed to the requirements of the times and sought to differ from other quarters.
How could this be considered awakening the mind of an elder? Yuán said, "Not so. To bend the Way to follow worldly custom means that other quarters have already lost one eye;

how can such a person demonstrate the teacher’s method to the people of China? When the court heard this, they regarded Yuán as one who understood the great principles. [He was appointed to] Guānwén Diàn.

The scholar Wang Gong Shao’s son, Zichun, was appointed as the Governor of Nanchang. Having long served as a commander at the Western Frontier, he felt that his excessive killings and punishments required atonement;

thus, he turned his mind toward the Emptiness School (Śūnyatā) and sought sublime words to cleanse his karmic stains. Just then, Yuan arrived. Zichun requested that Yuan preach the Dharma at Shanglan Monastery.
Yuan lit incense and said: "This incense is for the General Who Kills Without Flinching; it is for standing upon the ground..."
Upon becoming a Great Layman of Buddhahood, the entire assembly cried out in acclaim, "Excellent! Zizi Chun’s lingering doubts were also naturally dispelled.
When Chan Master Lingyuan Qing was among the assembly, he attended the Dharma seat at Yunju Monastery; though he strictly concealed his brilliance, his reputation naturally spread among the people.
When Yuan ascended the seat, he appointed him as the First Seat of the Hall. The monastic community respected this for its impartiality, not merely—
Master Qing was like Gan Tie-mian, Zhe Zhenru, Bai-zhang Su, and Yang-shan Jian—all of whom Yuan had personally admired and recognized.
Li Gonglin, known as Bo-shi, painted a portrait of Yuan; Yuan said, "You must depict me with a smile. He then composed his own eulogy for it, saying: "Li Gonglin is a stone qilin from the heavens;
he has transmitted the true likeness of the Cloud Dweller (Yunju Daozhe). It is not for the sake of the 'Plucking the Flower' [gesture]."

Clarifying the Great Matter: Opening one's mouth at ease, who is there to laugh with? A clay ox needlessly sniffs the wind; a withered tree unexpectedly blooms in the snow. Facing each other in full presence, neither can be recognized. In this era of Great Peace, one is a body of freedom.

On the fourth day of the first month of the first year of the Yuánfú era, hearing the talk of a guest, I had an awakening in my heart; I laughed heartily and said: [The following is the verse: The Great Matter is clear; opening one's mouth at ease, who is there to laugh with? A clay ox needlessly sniffs the wind; a withered tree unexpectedly blooms in the snow. Facing each other in full presence, neither can be recognized. In this era of Great Peace, one is a body of freedom.

Huà commanded that a portrait of his smiling countenance be painted and offered praise for it; this was no mere formality. He traversed the world for sixty-seven years and sat in meditation for fifty-two summer retreats.
His original bone-structure was prominent and refined; when facing affairs, he was never obstructed or stagnant. What passed before his eyes vanished like flowing water or dispersing clouds.
As a man, he honored righteousness and loathed evil. When first nominated, he was moved by Tièmiàn (Iron Face); later, upon succeeding Tíngān, Gǎn said: "May [he]..."
"It is permissible to manage the gruel and rice offerings for the Sangha of the ten directions. If you wish to have an heir, Ci-gan already has a teacher; Yuan Qi will surely admire him.

He further recommended Elder Xuan to reside at Ganlu Temple. Later, Xuan sold Yuan's property. Yuan reported this to the authorities, saying, "Xuan’s exposition of the Dharma lacks a fundamental principle;
I beg that he be corrected. Consequently, Xuan was eventually driven out. Yang Cigong said, "He was dragged [away]."
It is like someone who tramples another's field with his ox and is then stripped of that very ox; Yuan was not at all concerned by this. Yuan once traveled to the capital to visit the Prince of Cao.
The Prince, impressed by his reputation, presented his name to the Divine Emperor (Shenkao), who bestowed upon him a *mona* robe and the title "Foyin.
Dongpo, being playful in his calligraphy, composed a satirical eulogy for him which people delighted in transmitting; therefore, I have recorded it here in full.
The eulogy says: The Buddha-seal’s lineage was both upright and versatile; his wisdom and discernment were swift and keen, like a newborn colt that has not yet been broken to the bit.
This was because his talent was sufficient to withstand insults. Observing him when faced with affairs, one sees that his resolve to protect the Dharma was profound.
