Chan Master Baofeng Ying, whose name was Hongying, was born into the Chen family and was a native of Shaowu. From his youth, he was alert and quick-witted; when reading, he could read five lines at once.
His parents doted on him and intended for him to become a scholar, but Ying refused to eat and made a fervent vow to seek ordination as a monk.
Upon becoming a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*), he immediately set out to seek the Way. Traveling eastward, he arrived at Mount Cao and stayed with the venerable Master Ya.

After a long time, he took his leave and ascended Mount Yunju. Finding the cliffs and valleys there exceptionally sublime, he resolved to spend the remainder of his life there. While studying the *Huayan Shiming lun* (The Treatise on the Ten Clarifications of the Avataṃsaka), he reached the passage:
"As for true wisdom, it has no substantial nature; because it cannot know itself to be without nature, it is therefore called 'natureless'."
This nature cannot know itself to be without nature; therefore, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

The sixth stage of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that because one does not comprehend the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is designated as ignorance. This is because true wisdom is fundamentally without nature, and thus [ignorance] cannot understand itself.
If it encounters conditions for comprehension and thereby understands, then ignorance is extinguished. This is what is called the essential gateway to attaining Buddhahood. May [it be so].
"In this way, the Dharma shall flourish and the lineage of the Buddhas shall be sustained. However, at that time, who among those in various quarters could be spoken to of this?

After a long silence, he said with joy, "There is the old master Jicui. That very day, he traveled to Huangbo and paid his respects to National Teacher Nan at Jicui. They conversed from night until dawn.
Nan Gong merely added his respect. At that time, the assembly was filled with eminent monks who were like dragons and elephants;

Ying’s brilliant discourses would always captivate the four directions, and his reputation was widespread. Once, while traveling through the Western Mountains, he met the layman Pan of Nanchang and stayed overnight at Shuangling.
The layman said, "The timing of Longtan seeing the Emperor of Heaven perfectly accords with that of Confucius. Ying was startled and asked how this could be verified.
[The Master] said: "Confucius once said: 'Disciples, do you think that I conceal anything from you? I have nothing hidden from you.
There is no action of mine that I do not share with you; such is the person I am. What do you, my teacher, think of this? Ying laughed and said:
"The people of Chu mistook the mountain pheasant for a phoenix; the world has handed down this as a joke. I did not expect that your words, Reverend Sir, would be similar to it. You [then] held up...
"Tea is served. I shall receive it for you. You have come to offer refreshment; I shall accept it for you. You inquire after my health; I raise my hand in greeting.
If he says, "This is what is being said," then what is being said? If he says, "Nothing is being said," how then did Longtan suddenly attain enlightenment?

This is what is meant by: "There is no dharma that can be spoken; this is called preaching the Dharma. Even with the eloquence of the World-Honored One, one could not add anything further than these two lines.
It is merely a phrase. Students should simply seek to understand its meaning. It is like using five colors to paint empty space.
Master Niaokuo had no Buddha-dharma to transmit; he could not remain in silent sitting, so he idly picked up a piece of cloth and blew upon it, whereupon his attendant attained enlightenment.
A student then remarked, "Picking up the cloth and blowing upon it—his entire being was revealed. Such a view has not yet transcended the teachings of the scriptures.
One may truly be called a guest in the lineage of the Patriarchs. When Jiufeng was asked, "Is there Buddha-dharma in the deep mountains?
he could not help but say, "There is. However, when pressed further until he had nothing left to say, he replied, "The boulders are large indeed."

The junior student, being of limited capacity, speculated and said: "If the lands speak, sentient beings speak, and the three periods of time speak with blazing intensity, then this teaching alone is sufficient;
why must one further inquire into the intent of the Patriarchs? One simply wishes to attain clarity through the very essence."
It is like a person with cataracts seeking medical treatment. The physician can only remove the film; he does not bestow light upon them.
The layman pushed his bed back and said in alarm, "I have long worried that the Dharma-way of Jicui would have no successor.
Now I know it rests entirely upon you; take good care of yourself. Chan Master Shun of Shuangling asked, "The old teacher in the hermitage likes to ask questions."
The student was asked, "Shut your throat, lips, and mouth, and utter a single phrase. Has the Head Seat ever uttered one?
Ying laughed heartily and spoke this verse: "The mother-in-law tastes the vinegar with her three-inch beak; The daughter-in-law washes her face and touches her own nose."

Daowu’s response earned him his waist-cloth; Xuansha’s opening of the letter revealed it was but white paper. Thereupon, Master Shun submitted, thinking to himself: "Beneath a great name, there are no empty men.
A fellow practitioner of his was at Shimen, where he shared the seat and received him. Daoying composed a verse to send him, saying:
"The iron caltrops from within the furnace of ten thousand refinements— One must pay a high price; do not bargain with them. Whether they come horizontally or vertically..."
He laughed heartily, leaving it to others to stir up disputes and rumors as they pleased. In the first year of the Xining era, he led the assembly of monks at Lushan’s Yuan Tong Temple;
students flocked to him just as they had to Master Nan. The following spring, Master Nan passed away. In the tenth month of that winter, Ying began to teach the Dharma at Shimen.
In the sixth month of the next year, the administrative officials fell into conflict; Ying attempted to stop them, but they would not listen.
On the ninth day of the first month, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Leading the community without solemnity and sitting upright without virtue—I am ashamed before Huanglong.
He called for the *vinaya-dhara* (the rector) to strike the bell, and when the assembly had gathered, he recounted the beginning and end of his travels as a wandering monk (*caryā-pādaka*), saying:

"After my passing, I shall be cremated, and my remains shall be enshrined in the Pǔtōng Pagoda, to demonstrate that life and death are not separate from the pure assembly. Having finished speaking, he passed away; he had lived for fifty years.
There were nine [monks]. He sat in meditation for forty-three years.
The eulogy states: "The Heroic One loathed the crowds of strife and hastened toward death; furthermore, he instructed that his bones and stone relics be enshrined in the Puguang Pagoda."
How could one treat life and death as mere child’s play? When Wei Shu of the Jin dynasty lost his wife, he ceased after a single outburst of grief, saying, "I am far inferior to Zhuang Zhou.
When the children of Huan Wen and Yin Hao were playing, Wen threw away his whip while Hao took it up.
After warming himself, Wen said with joy, "I have always known that Hao was beneath me. The ancients could verify their own talent amidst such things as weeping and playing;

this is proof of it. Ying sighed and remarked, "To lead a multitude without solemnity while feeling ashamed before Huanglong, and to whip oneself without pardon—this can indeed serve as a model for others."
Chan Master Baoning Ji’s name was Yuanji.
He was of the Lin clan of Fuzhou. His father died when he was only one year old, and his maternal uncle took him in to raise him.
At the age of sixteen, his gaze was brilliant and piercing; when Sengchuan of Yingtian Monastery in Fqing saw him, he marveled at him and said, "If you follow [the monastic path]..."
When I was traveling, Ji looked up at me with joy; I then left, carrying my staff and hat. Shortly thereafter, he tested his training and attained ordination.
He traveled to Eastern Wu and relied upon Tiantai Yihuai. After Huai passed away, he served Huangbo Nan as his teacher, receiving the secret transmission of the dharma-seal.

Fajue possessed a refined natural disposition and was diligent in his efforts. He bore the burden of the monastic community, heedless of cold or heat. He reclaimed wasteland to create fertile fields and planted pines and cypresses to form beautiful trunks.
He held one office for ten years without change; Master Nanyuan praised him as a true son of the Way who had left the household life according to the original essence.

When it came time to move to Huanglong, Master Nanyuan took Fajue with him. In the second year of the Xining era, Master Nanyuan passed away, and after the stupa had been completed, [Fajue remained there].
He took his leave. Master Donglin Zong appointed him as the First Seat (Diyizuo) in the hall; thus, his reputation grew even more eminent.
The monks of Guifeng at Xinzhou and Dayu at Muzhou vied with one another to welcome and invite him, yet Jue remained firm in his refusal and did not respond.
When Chan Master Baojue wished to have him succeed to the Dharma seat of Huanglong, Jue shook his head, resisted the effort, and departed directly; Baojue did not force him. People asked him why.
Therefore, he replied, "My former master cautioned me that I must not act as a teacher before reaching the age of fifty.

When I arrived at Guizong, I was forty-eight years old. Master Foyin Yuan encouraged me to accept the invitation from Cuiyan, at the request of Xie Jingwen (style name Shizhi), the Military Commissioner of Nanchang.
Ten years later, I moved to reside at Yuan Tong, at the request of the Military Commissioner of Jinling."

This was requested by Zhu Yan Shiying. In the second year of the Chongning era, when Shiying was once again serving as the governor of Jinling, he learned that the seat of Baoning was vacant and recommended Zongji to take it from his current post.
When the officials and scholars of Jianghuai gathered for their annual leave, their carriages filled the gates.

As they played chess and brewed tea, they were like clusters of orchids or rows of jade trees; yet amidst them, Zongji sat at the sacrificial table as motionless as a withered stump, though his discourse was profound and spirited.
There was a man named Xu Yi Yanzhou of Suiyang who was keenly intent on investigating the Way. Upon seeing Jueji prostrate, Jueji said, "Do not hang trivial matters upon your mind.
Yanzhou asked, "What is a trivial matter? He replied, "Investigating Zen and studying the Way are [trivial matters]."
Thereupon, Yanzhou attained awakening. After a long while, he said, "The Great Way is exceedingly level and plain; why use so many words and conceptual entanglements?
Guizong called to his attendant and asked him to explain the previous statement. The attendant stared blankly and withdrew.
Guizong said to Yanzhou, "Words and conceptual entanglements must not be discarded either. Since students nowadays are prone to savoring and becoming attached to mere texts, I shall compose a verse."
He said: "I do not study literary compositions nor read books; I remain as I am all day long, appearing as if ignorant.

Although I am unacquainted with a hundred affairs, how could this horse ever be called a donkey? In the fifth year of the Zhenghe era, when Baoning was renamed Shenxiao, he retired to his hermitage south of the city on that very day.
On the ninth month of the eighth year, he manifested a slight illness. On the twenty-second day, after bathing, he spoke.
He passed away with these verses. He had lived through eighty-three years of the world and sat in meditation for sixty-three summer retreats.
Upon his cremation, there were two parts that remained entirely indestructible, interspersed with śarīra relics of five colors. His stupa was erected to the left of the Rain of Flowers Terrace.
The eulogy states: Jiaya styled himself the "Old Man of No-Learning" (Wuxue Lao). He inscribed a verse upon the wall of his dwelling, saying:
"The old man in the Hermitage of No-Learning has been unable to accomplish anything throughout his life. Yet, reflecting upon my many blessings, I have reached old age having become a monk.
This was in the first month of the first year of the Xuanhua era.

The imperial edict was issued, decreeing that all monastics, both monks and nuns, throughout the land were to become lay practitioners, male and female respectively; yet Ji had already passed away more than a year prior.
How could this have been merely a matter of chance?
Chan Master Huanglong Fushou Qing, whose name was Weiqing, style name Juetian, and sobriquet Lingsuan Srou, was born into the Chen family of Wuning in Nanzhou.
While still wearing his hair in a topknot and attending school, he could recite several thousand words daily with effortless fluency. Once, a strange bhikṣu passed by a bookstore.
He saw him and, reaching out his hand, gazed at him intently. Greatly astonished, he said, "Is there such a child among the reeds and rushes?
He informed the boy's parents, who granted permission for him to leave the household life. He took the Vinaya Master Jielü as his teacher. At the age of seventeen, he became a full monk (*bhikṣu*).

Hearing that the veteran Dharma Master Fǎ'ān of Yán'ēn Yuàn was one who possessed the true character of a master, he went to pay his respects and requested to remain there to study under him. Fǎ'ān said, "You are in the ocean of suffering..."
"The Dharma is like a boat; I am but an ordinary person in a ditch—how could I possibly contain it? Master Chan Master Baojue of Huanglong is your teacher. Go at once; do not delay.
At that time, the Master went to Huanglong and lived among the crowd in anonymity. His questions and answers were vague and bewildered, and he knew nothing of the fundamental principles.
One night, he made a vow before the Buddhas, saying: "If I should attain any realization, I vow to devote my entire life [to the Way]."

Shou took the Dharma as his almsgiving (dāna). Throughout successive lifetimes, he exerted himself to propagate the Great Dharma. Once, while reading the records of Xuansha, he grew weary and leaned against a wall;
rising to practice walking meditation (caṅkrama), his steps were so hurried that he left his sandals behind. As he bent down to retrieve them, he attained great enlightenment.

He reported his realization to Baojue, who said, "Those who enter through conditions will never again fall back or lose what they have gained. However, those who have newly attained the emptiness of dharmas often become overly joyful, which leads to..."
He sent Sanluan to the attendant’s quarters to sleep soundly. The Master’s spirit was as clear and cool as ice and snow, yet his penetrating insight far surpassed his contemporaries.
Xu Xi (Dezhan) of the Longtu Academy and Huang Tingjian (Luzhi) of the Bureau of Astronomy were both his teachers and friends;

it was the Master who provided the foundation for them when they met Baojue and received his prediction of enlightenment. Baojue held him in such deep affection that he forgot their relationship as teacher and disciple.

Regarding the deliberations on this matter, he was like a close friend to all quarters; those of various regions called him the "Pure Attendant. He was like Zhaozhou Wen-yuan, Nan-yuan Shou-kuo, and Chancellor Zhang Shang-ying.

When Zhang first served as an envoy to Jiangxi, he held the Master’s character in high esteem and offered him generous hospitality to invite him to reside at Guanyin Monastery in Hongzhou, but the Master did not accept.
Ten years later, Zhu Jing Shichang, an envoy from Huainan, requested that he take up residence there.
He then proceeded to Tàipíng in Shūzhōu, where monks vied with one another to follow him; the grandeur of his assembly was no less than that of Yuántōng.
During his time at Fǎyún and Chánglú, Bǎojié had reached an advanced age. When the Imperial Commissioner from Jīngxī, Wáng Huán, invited him to reside at Huánglóng, he went there without hesitation.
Not long after, Bǎojié passed away, whereupon [Fàn]qī moved to the Zhāomò Hall on the pretext of illness. He sat listlessly in a single room.
The world admired his character; he scraped the clouds and towered above the heavens. At that time, as a brother in the Dharma-gate, I was privileged to hear his discourse, in which he said:
"Among those who study today, none have escaped birth and death. Where does their ailment lie? It lies simply in the fact that their 'thieving mind' has not yet died.
Yet this is not their fault; it is the fault of the teachers. It is like the Han Emperor Gaozu, who deceived and killed Han Xin."
Although it is said that one has died, has their mind truly died? As for the students of antiquity who liberated themselves from birth and death beneath a single word, where was the evidence of this?
It lay in the fact that their "thieving mind" had already perished. Yet, this was not something the student could achieve on their own; it was truly due to the Master.
The tongs and hammer are subtle and precise. It is like Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, who sat in the Great Hall and saw Hou Jing without shifting his voice or expression;
yet the heart of Jing was already withered and exhausted, leaving nothing behind.

What is taught by various schools is not without its beauty, but in essence, it is like Zhao Chang’s painting of flowers—so lifelike, yet not the real thing. His skillful metaphors are of this same nature. *Xianju* (Leisurely Dwelling).
For fifteen years, it would have been appropriate for all those in the world who study Chan to have known him and personally relied upon him.

How could the high officials and great ministers have known of him on their own, and why would they have vied to draw near to him? Yet, without thunder or lightning, his reputation has constantly remained in the ears of men.
"What practice has led him to this state? [The master replied: "Throughout my life, I have simply been devoted with utmost sincerity and felt deep compassion for the Way.

On the eighteenth day of the ninth month in the seventh year of the Zhenghe era, after finishing his meal, he closed his room and sent someone to summon the Head Seat Yixi. When the latter arrived, they spoke together regarding their parting.

He then rose, bathed, and changed his robes. Pointing his finger to the crown of his head, he waited for his attendant to finish shaving his hair; once this was done, he sat upright and passed into stillness.
Ten days prior, he had composed an inscription on his own regarding his birthless, eternally abiding, true refuge, which read:

"I, Weiqing, the forty-eighth-generation descendant in direct line from Śākyamuni Buddha, the fourth honored one of the Bhadrakalpa, although born through the response to conditions from fundamental enlightenment,"
Yet, when conditions are fully understood, they are immediately empty; from the beginning, they possess no inherent nature (*svabhāva*). His clan, lineage, and kin cannot be detailed;
he simply takes the single thought-moment of the true cause as his ancestral heritage. Thus, he is a distant descendant of Śākyamuni, known by the sobriquet "The Old Man of Lingyuan.

Relying on the factor of self-enlightenment (*pratyavekṣaṇā-hetu*), the wondrous nature that is realized within the nameless is merely given a designation for the sake of communication. He is also the "One Without Rank" of Linji.

The True Man is akin to the Heart-King of Master Fu Dashi. Is he not indeed the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvana—something known only through personal realization, which none others can fathom?
Thus, when the Sixth Patriarch asked Master Huairang, "Where have you come from? he replied, "From Mount Song.
The Patriarch asked, "What thing is it that comes thus? He replied, "If one tries to describe it as a thing, it is immediately not so."
The Patriarch asked, "Is there still any need for cultivation and realization? He replied, "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent; however, one must not be defiled.
The Patriarch said, "This very state of being undefiled is the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas. Since you are thus, I am also thus."
